text:
American politics has a serious problem, and it begins with the standards we apply to those seeking power.

Marco Rubio’s record includes service as Speaker of the Florida House, 14 years in the U.S. Senate, senior positions on the Foreign Relations and Intelligence Committees, and the office of Secretary of State. 

His Cuban family history also informs his understanding of communism, authoritarianism, and American freedom.

These are substantive qualifications that can be examined, challenged, and measured against actual decisions and accomplishments.

Now consider Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez’s appearance at the Munich Security Conference.

She traveled to Europe to participate in an international gathering devoted to security and foreign policy. She took her place on a panel specifically addressing the future of American foreign policy, before an audience concerned with the most consequential geopolitical challenges confronting the United States and its allies.

And then came a question about whether the United States should commit troops to defend Taiwan against Chinese aggression.

This was hardly an obscure question. The possibility of a Chinese invasion of Taiwan is among the most prominent national-security concerns facing the United States. 

Anyone preparing to participate in a serious international security conference should reasonably anticipate being questioned about it.

Yet Ocasio-Cortez struggled through an extraordinary succession of pauses, verbal stumbles, and unfinished thoughts before finally producing generalities about avoiding confrontation.

Watch the video linked below. Words barely capture the spectacle.

What makes the exchange particularly troubling is the context. She was not ambushed by an unexpected question outside a congressional hearing. She was participating in a scheduled discussion about American foreign policy on the world stage. Preparation for precisely these kinds of questions was a reasonable expectation.

Nor was she required to make an unconditional commitment to military intervention. America’s longstanding policy of strategic ambiguity leaves considerable room for a sophisticated answer about deterrence, military commitments, and the consequences of confronting China.

The question presented an opportunity to demonstrate that understanding. Her response offered little explanation of any of it.

That distinction matters. There is a considerable difference between disagreeing with a politician’s policy judgment and questioning whether the politician has adequately prepared to defend that judgment.

The presidency requires far more than ideological enthusiasm, political celebrity, and carefully rehearsed applause lines. It requires judgment, historical perspective, diplomatic skill, command of complex issues, and an understanding that decisions made in Washington can have consequences lasting generations.

Yet American political discourse repeatedly elevates personality over preparation and slogans over substance.

Voters have every right to disagree with a candidate’s policies. But evaluating candidates responsibly requires examining their records, their command of the issues, and their ability to explain the reasoning behind their positions.

A democracy cannot continually reward spectacle over substance and then act surprised by the quality of its political leadership.

The electorate is not merely an innocent observer of political dysfunction. Its choices help determine the standards by which the country is governed. 

And when voters decline to demand serious preparation and demonstrated judgment, they bear responsibility for the consequences.

At the heart of this strategy is the critical task of maintaining party cohesion after intense internal primaries. Zulum’s explicit instruction for victorious candidates to reach out and heal rifts with aggrieved aspirants reflects a realistic understanding of political arithmetic: internal resentment erodes turnout faster than any opposition campaign. By coupling reconciliation with firm warnings against subversion, the leadership is attempting to forge an unbreakable front out of potentially volatile factions.

The sheer scale of political unity displayed in Maiduguri underscores the formidable nature of this campaign structure. This public display of solidarity among historical heavyweights signals organizational stability, minimizing space for opposition inroads while keeping rank-and-file members firmly aligned.

Beyond local dynamics, Borno State occupies a unique position on the national political chessboard as the home state of Vice President Senator Kashim Shettima. In this high-stakes arena, sheer victory is insufficient; the turnout margin itself serves as a barometer of political influence. Delivering a massive vote tally is therefore both a local objective and a strategic demonstration of national strength, cementing the state's leverage within the governing alliance.

To turn political influence into actual votes, the campaign relies heavily on record-based persuasion and visible governance dividends. A vital strength of this expanded outreach is the deliberate inclusion of women and youth as core engines of voter mobilization. The strong presence of the women’s delegation led by Borno First Lady Dr. Falmata Babagana Umara Zulum alongside the wife of the Deputy Governor and the wives of party candidates highlights an organized effort to engage families and community networks directly. Demanding structured participation across all demographics ensures that campaign directives actively translate into voter registration and turnout.

DigiPowerX $DGXX said on October 13 that it "did not issue any shares" under its ATM program in Q3.

$DGXX's Q3 10-Q, filed November 13, shows 2.85M shares issued for cash in Q3 for $11.3M, and counts them among the 30.8M shares it sold through the ATM in the first nine months of 2026.

The share count rose 46% this year, from 69.4M at the end of 2025 to 101.4M as of November 12.

The 10-Q also shows three details the Q3 earnings release left out:
1) Prepayment: Cerebras $CBRS, the AI chipmaker that's the tenant at $DGXX's Columbiana data center campus in Alabama, paid a $12M upfront charge in Q3 for building Phase 1. The charge can be refunded, less what's been spent on finished construction, in some cases before Phase 1 starts, including if $DGXX misses the final delivery date.
2) Spending: $145.5M went into property, equipment, and equipment deposits in the first nine months, paid for with $170.8M of net share sales.
3) GPUs: Equipment deposits rose to $23.9M from $8.5M at the end of 2025, and the 10-Q mentions next-generation $NVDA Vera Rubin systems $DGXX has "committed to purchase," without an amount.

$DGXX's Q3 revenue rose 85% q/q to $12.2M, but its $1.0M of net income leaned on $8.6M of gains on its crypto and warrants.

Cash was $95.2M and bitcoin and ether were $24.5M as of September 30.

$DGXX also expects to close a $200M loan syndicated by Goldman Sachs $GS in Q4 2026 to finish Columbiana, with an unsecured $DGXX guarantee until construction is done.

Even with the cash, crypto, and loan, $DGXX is ~$30M short of its 2027 plan (~$350M of capex, mostly for ~10 MW of AI inference capacity and Columbiana's Phase 2) before any Q4 2026 spending.

$DGXX expects customer deposits and prepayments to be a main source of funding, and it has already sold $174.7M of the $175M its ATM prospectus covers.

At $2.28/share, $DGXX's market cap is ~$231M, an EV of ~$112M after its cash and crypto.

If Phase 1 is ready on December 15 as planned, Cerebras starts paying in January 2027, and its $12M prepayment can no longer be refunded.

text:
Three Heads, One Master Plan: Is Sean Payton Saving Denver's Hydra for December?

Everyone is talking about the Denver Broncos struggling to find their offensive identity. But what if they're not?

What if Sean Payton has known exactly what he wanted from this offense all along? What if the inconsistent running game, the changing workloads and the revolving door at running back aren't signs of an offense searching for answers, but pieces of a much larger plan?

And what if everything we've witnessed through nine games has been preparation for something far more dangerous in December and January?

Denver entered its bye week at 7–2, riding a five-game winning streak. The Broncos survived one of the most difficult opening stretches in football, facing Kansas City, Jacksonville, Los Angeles, San Francisco, the Chargers, and Seattle in their first six games. Yet the three-headed rushing attack fans anticipated entering the season has barely had an opportunity to operate at full strength.

That raises an interesting question: Has Sean Payton been managing three running backs independently, or has he been managing their workloads as part of a much larger plan?

It starts with J.K. Dobbins.

Dobbins was the established veteran, the proven NFL runner Payton could trust when the Broncos needed physical yards against difficult opponents. During the first six games, he carried the football 81 times, averaging 13.5 attempts per game. His heaviest workloads came against the Chargers and Seahawks, when he received 18 and 17 carries, respectively.

But there's something else worth considering about how Dobbins has been running this season.

We've seen a more conservative approach from a player whose reputation was built on physicality. Rather than consistently bouncing off would-be tacklers, fighting through additional contact and punishing defenders for every extra yard, Dobbins has appeared more selective about when to unleash that aggression.

What if that's intentional?

What if Payton and Dobbins entered the season with a plan to prevent the veteran from being so physically worn down that he couldn't be available when Denver needed him most?

Last season demonstrated just how quickly the punishment of NFL football can catch up with a running back. Perhaps Payton understood that keeping Dobbins healthy for an entire season would require more than simply reducing his number of carries. It might also require changing how much punishment he absorbed on those carries.

That doesn't mean asking Dobbins to stop being a physical runner. It means choosing his moments.

Let him take enough contact to stay sharp, maintain his football instincts and remember exactly what kind of game he's playing. Sprinkle him into the offense just enough to get punched in the mouth and know it's football season.

But don't ask him to initiate a collision with every defender between September and November.

Because the objective wouldn't be to have Dobbins delivering his hardest blows in October.

It would be to have him healthy enough in December and January to become the Dobbins we all know. The one who does the punching.

And if that was Payton's thinking, it would explain why the veteran's role has evolved so dramatically as the season progressed.

But Dobbins wasn't the only running back Payton trusted during that opening stretch.

RJ Harvey was emerging as something different. Through his first seven games, Harvey recorded 24 rushing attempts for 87 yards, but his receiving production told a more revealing story: 25 receptions for 217 yards, with two total touchdowns.

He had actually caught more passes than he had rushing attempts.

That wasn't the profile of a traditional backup running back waiting for his turn to carry the football. Harvey was becoming a legitimate receiving threat out of the backfield, giving Payton another offensive weapon while Dobbins handled much of the conventional rushing responsibility.

Then there was Jonah Coleman.

Coleman had barely participated in the season opener, but against Jacksonville in Week 2, he finally got an opportunity to demonstrate what he could do in a real NFL game. He responded with 58 yards from scrimmage and a touchdown, including the go-ahead score in Denver's comeback victory.

Payton had seen enough to know what Coleman could offer.

Following that game, Coleman was placed on short-term injured reserve with an ankle injury. He would miss the next four games, including the remainder of Denver's opening six-game gauntlet.

Now consider the sequence.

While Coleman was unavailable, Dobbins and Harvey continued carrying their respective responsibilities. Dobbins provided the established rushing presence. Harvey supplied the receiving versatility and another dimension to the offense.

Denver got through the difficult opening stretch with a 4–2 record.

Then Coleman returned.

And almost immediately, the entire backfield changed.

Against Arizona in Week 7, Coleman stepped back onto the field and assumed a significant role. Dobbins, who had received 35 carries over the previous two games, suddenly carried the football only six times.

The following week, Dobbins received seven carries. Against Carolina, just four.

In three games, his workload had fallen to 17 rushing attempts combined.

Why?

The conventional explanation is straightforward: Coleman was producing, and Payton was rewarding the rookie with additional opportunities.

But there's another possibility.

Coleman was the one running back who could relieve Dobbins of his physical rushing responsibilities without forcing Payton to change the offense.

Harvey wasn't being used in quite the same way. He had already established himself as a receiving weapon, someone who could stretch a defense horizontally, create mismatches and produce through the passing game.

Coleman, however, could take the football between the tackles, absorb contact and move the chains.

Suddenly, Payton no longer needed Dobbins to carry the same workload he'd handled during the gauntlet.

And that brings us to the second remarkable development.

Just as Coleman returned and began assuming the rushing responsibilities, Harvey went onto short-term injured reserve himself.

One running back came back. Another went out.

But what if the timing of those injured-reserve placements wasn't entirely coincidental?

Think about what happened.

Jonah Coleman made his NFL debut against Jacksonville and immediately demonstrated that he belonged on the field. He later explained that he'd hurt his ankle early in that game but knew he needed to keep playing. There was no obvious moment when fans watched him go down and leave the game.

Then Coleman went on short-term injured reserve.

For the next four games, Payton had his established veteran, J.K. Dobbins, and his emerging receiving threat, RJ Harvey, available to navigate the remainder of Denver's opening gauntlet.

When that difficult stretch ended, Coleman returned. And almost as if someone had flipped a switch, Harvey went on short-term injured reserve.

Coleman had received a month away from the punishment of NFL football. Now Harvey would receive his own extended break, with Denver's bye week providing an additional week of rest.

Meanwhile, Dobbins remained available throughout the entire process. But once Coleman returned and proved he could handle the physical rushing responsibilities, Payton dramatically reduced his veteran's workload.

And here's where the timing becomes particularly interesting.

By placing Coleman and Harvey on injured reserve at different points in the season, Denver also gained temporary roster flexibility. Payton could elevate another player at a position of need rather than carrying three running backs he wasn't necessarily planning to use together until December.

So consider the possibility.

What if Sean Payton had been looking at his running back room as a season-long project rather than a week-to-week rotation?

What if the objective was to give all three backs enough meaningful action to remain sharp, while ensuring none of them absorbed an entire season's worth of punishment before the playoff race?

Coleman got his opportunity to demonstrate his abilities, followed by an extended break. Harvey established himself as a dangerous receiving weapon, then received his own. And Dobbins handled the difficult early assignments before Coleman returned to take much of that workload off his shoulders.

Three running backs, each managed differently, but potentially working toward the same destination.

December football. January football. Playoff football.

I'm not suggesting we know what Payton planned behind closed doors. But when two running backs receive consecutive month-long breaks, their roles fit together almost perfectly, and the third remains available while his workload is carefully reduced, it's difficult not to wonder whether there's something more to the sequence.

Maybe it's coincidence.

Or maybe Sean Payton has been managing the entire season while the rest of us have been watching one game at a time.

And now look at the calendar.

Harvey's projected eligibility to return arrives in Week 13, when Denver hosts Miami on December 6.

That would give Payton the opportunity to reunite his three running backs just as the Broncos enter the final stretch of the regular season.

Miami. The Jets. Las Vegas.

Then comes Christmas Day against Buffalo, followed by New England and the Chargers.

Three consecutive games against teams that reached the previous postseason, with playoff positioning potentially hanging in the balance.

And what could Denver bring into that stretch?

J.K. Dobbins, a veteran power runner whose workload has been dramatically reduced since Week 6.

Jonah Coleman, a physical young running back who has spent November gaining valuable experience as the primary ball carrier.

RJ Harvey, a receiving threat capable of changing how defenses align and forcing linebackers to account for another weapon in the passing game.

Three different runners. Three different responsibilities. Three different problems for opposing defenses.

And all of them potentially available together for the most important part of the season.

This is where the three-headed Hydra we've discussed since the beginning of the year could finally become the offense everyone expected.

But there's another element that makes the possibility even more intriguing.

Bo Nix has begun showing more of his mobility, adding another dimension to an offense that already has multiple ways to attack a defense. Payton has also indicated that changes along the offensive line remain possible.

And those potential changes could be critical, because Denver has a genuine problem with its interior offensive line.

Those struggles affect every part of the offense. It doesn't matter how many weapons Sean Payton has at his disposal if the offensive line can't consistently create running lanes or give Bo Nix enough time for passing plays to develop.

Dobbins and Coleman need space to establish their physical running styles. Harvey needs blocking that allows him to exploit his acceleration and receiving ability. And Nix needs a pocket that doesn't collapse before his receivers can complete their routes.

That's why this bye week may be just as important for the offensive line as it is for the running backs. Whether the answer comes through personnel changes, adjustments to blocking assignments, or simply better execution, Payton and his staff have to find a solution.

Because a three-headed Hydra is only as dangerous as the opportunities its offensive line creates.

If Denver can stabilize the interior, combine it with Nix's growing mobility, and bring all three running backs together for December, the offense could look dramatically different from what we've seen through the first nine games.

Imagine those elements coming together at the same time: an adjusted offensive line, a more mobile quarterback and three running backs capable of attacking defenses in completely different ways.

A defense preparing for Dobbins' physicality could find Harvey lined up as a receiving threat. A defense expecting Coleman between the tackles could suddenly be defending Nix on the perimeter. And a defense attempting to account for every possibility would have to do so without knowing which running back would become the focal point of the next series.

That's not simply running back depth.

That's offensive flexibility.

And in December and January, when weather conditions become more demanding, defensive fronts become more physical and every possession matters, having three different ways to move the football could be a tremendous advantage.

Perhaps the apparent inconsistency in the running game hasn't been evidence of a plan that failed.

Perhaps we've been watching the pieces of a plan come together.

Dobbins handled the difficult early assignments. Harvey demonstrated his receiving value. Coleman returned and proved he could carry the workload. And now the possibility exists that all three will finally converge when Denver needs them most.

If that happens, the Broncos team we see beginning in Week 13 could look considerably different from the one that survived the first nine games.

And perhaps that's been the point all along.

This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.

There has been some really encouraging news in the fight against deepfakes. A couple of weeks ago the US Federal Trade Commission announced it is finalizing rules banning the use of deepfakes that impersonate people. Leading AI startups and big tech companies also unveiled their voluntary commitments to combatting the deceptive use of AI in 2024 elections. And last Friday, a group of civil society groups, including the Future of Life Institute, SAG-AFTRA, and Encode Justice came out with a new campaign calling for a ban on deepfakes.

These initiatives are a great start and raise public awareness—but the devil will be in the details. Existing rules in the UK and some US states already ban the creation and/or dissemination of deepfakes. The FTC would make it illegal for AI platforms to create content that impersonates people and would allow the agency to force scammers to return the money they made from such scams. 

But there is a big elephant in the room: outright bans might not even be technically feasible. There is no button someone can flick on and off, says Daniel Leufer, a senior policy analyst at the digital rights organization Access Now. 

That is because the genie is out of the bottle. 

Big Tech gets a lot of heat for the harm deepfakes cause, but to their credit, these companies do try to use their content moderation systems to detect and block attempts to generate, say, deepfake porn. (That’s not to say they are perfect. The deepfake porn targeting Taylor Swift reportedly came from a Microsoft system.) 

The bigger problem is that many of the harmful deepfakes come from open-source systems or systems built by state actors, and they are disseminated on end-to-end-encrypted platforms such as Telegram, where they cannot be traced.

Regulation really needs to tackle every actor in the deepfake pipeline, says Leufer. That may mean holding companies big and small accountable for allowing not just the creation of deepfakes but also their spread. So “model marketplaces,” such as Hugging Face or GitHub, may need to be included in talks about regulation to slow the spread of deepfakes. 

These model marketplaces make it easy to access open-source models such as Stable Diffusion, which people can use to build their own deepfake apps. These platforms are already taking action. Hugging Face and GitHub have put into place measures that add friction to the processes people use to access tools and make harmful content. Hugging Face is also a vocal proponent of OpenRAIL licenses, which make users commit to using the models in a certain way. The company also allows people to automatically integrate provenance data that meets high technical standards into their workflow. 

Other popular solutions include better watermarking and content provenance techniques, which would help with detection. But these detection tools are no silver bullet. 

Rules that require all AI-generated content to be watermarked are impossible to enforce, and it’s also highly possible that watermarks could end up doing the opposite of what they’re supposed to do, Leufer says. For one thing, in open-source systems, watermarking and provenance techniques can be removed by bad actors. This is because everyone has access to the model’s source code, so specific users can simply remove any techniques they don’t want.

If only the biggest companies or most popular proprietary platforms offer watermarks on their AI-generated content, then the absence of a watermark could come to signify that content is not AI generated, says Leufer. 

“Enforcing watermarking on all the content that you can enforce it on would actually lend credibility to the most harmful stuff that’s coming from the systems that we can’t intervene in,” he says. 

I asked Leufer if there are any promising approaches he sees out there that give him hope. He paused to think and finally suggested looking at the bigger picture. Deepfakes are just another symptom of the problems we have had with information and disinformation on social media, he said: “This could be the thing that tips the scales to really do something about regulating these platforms and drives a push to really allow for public understanding and transparency.” 

Now read the rest of The Algorithm

Deeper Learning

Watch this robot as it learns to stitch up wounds

An AI-trained surgical robot that can make a few stitches on its own is a small step toward systems that can aid surgeons with such repetitive tasks. A video taken by researchers at the University of California, Berkeley, shows the two-armed robot completing six stitches in a row on a simple wound in imitation skin, passing the needle through the tissue and from one robotic arm to the other while maintaining tension on the thread. 

A helping hand: Though many doctors today get help from robots for procedures ranging from hernia repairs to coronary bypasses, those are used to assist surgeons, not replace them. This new research marks progress toward robots that can operate more autonomously on very intricate, complicated tasks like suturing. The lessons learned in its development could also be useful in other fields of robotics. Read more from James O’Donnell here. 

Bits and Bytes

Wikimedia’s CTO: In the age of AI, human contributors still matter
Selena Deckelmann argues that in this era of machine-generated content, Wikipedia becomes even more valuable. (MIT Technology Review) 

Air Canada has to honor a refund policy its chatbot made up
The airline was forced to offer a customer a partial refund after its customer service chatbot inaccurately explained the company’s bereavement travel policy. Expect more cases like this as long as the tech sector sells chatbots that still make things up and have security flaws. (Wired)

Reddit has a new AI training deal to sell user content
The company has struck a $60 million deal to give an unnamed AI company access to the user-created content on its platform. OpenAI and Apple have reportedly been knocking on publishers’ doors trying to strike similar deals. Reddit’s human-written content is a gold mine for AI companies looking for high-quality training data for their language models. (Bloomberg) 

Google pauses Gemini’s ability to generate AI images of people after diversity errors
It’s no surprise that AI models are biased. I’ve written about how they are outright racist. But  Google’s effort to make its model more inclusive backfired after the model flat-out refused to generate images of white people. (The Verge) 

ChatGPT goes temporarily “insane” with unexpected outputs, spooking users
Last week, a bug made the popular chatbot produce bizarre and random responses to user queries. (Ars Technica)

The Ys video game series gets its name from a real French legend about a magical city that sank into the sea. As the games grew into a long-running series, the creators also borrowed stories and gods from Greek, Norse, and ancient Middle Eastern myths.

1. The Main Legend: The Sunken City of Ys

• The Real-Life Myth. In old stories from Brittany, France, there was a rich, beautiful city called Ys built right below sea level. A giant sea wall kept the ocean out until someone opened the gates by mistake, flooding the entire city underwater.
• How the Game Changed It. In the first Ys games, the developers flipped this idea upside down. Instead of sinking into the ocean, the kingdom of Ys uses magic to float high up into the sky to escape an army of monsters.

2. Gods and Myths in Other Ys Games

Almost every Ys game takes the hero, Adol, to a new land inspired by real-world legends and gods.

Game Real-World Inspiration How It Shows Up in the Game
Ys I & II The Bible (Tower of Babel) You climb a giant, endless tower called Darm Tower that reaches up toward the floating land in the sky.
Ys VI Noah's Ark / Gilgamesh The story revolves around a giant ancient ark built to survive a massive world-ending flood.
Ys VIII Greek Myth & Hinduism You get shipwrecked on a cursed island inspired by Greek sirens, guarded by a giant sleeping goddess named Maia (based on the Greek earth mother, Gaia).
Ys IX Norse Gods & Joan of Arc The local religion worships gods named Grimnir and Luki, who are direct copies of the Norse gods Odin and Loki.
Ys X Vikings You sail the ocean alongside fierce Viking-like warriors who use magic runestones to talk to their ancestors.

Why the Creators Did This

The world of Ys is actually a fantasy version of Europe and Asia. By mixing real history with famous myths, the creators made each game feel like you are exploring a legendary lost civilization.

Black iron armor refers both to a specific mid-game piece of heavy equipment in the Ys video game series and to historically darkened or "blackened" iron and steel armor used in late medieval and Renaissance warfare.

1. In the Ys Video Game Series

In titles like Ys VIII: Lacrimosa of DANA, Black Iron Armor is a craftable, heavy tier body armor built for maximum physical defense over agility.
• Stats and Traits: It provides DEF +102 and is described in-game as cumbersome armor constructed from multiple overlapping layers of black iron.
• Crafting Materials: Players forge it at the blacksmith using 8 Iron Ore and 2 Accursed Shells.
• Role in Progression: It sits cleanly between early-game Ring Mail (DEF +78) and late-game Lamellar Armor (DEF +148), serving as a reliable mid-game defensive wall.

2. In Medieval History and Gothic Aesthetics

In real-world history, "black" or "blackened" armor was a practical and widespread treatment applied to wrought iron and steel plate armor rather than a separate mystical metal.
• Rust Prevention: Polishing bare steel to a mirror shine ("white armor") required constant maintenance to prevent rust. Applying a dark finish—either by leaving rough hammer-scale intact from the forge or by coating hot metal in oil and wax—sealed the iron against moisture and salt air.
• Cost and Status: Unpolished "rough from the hammer" black armor was cheaper to produce and became standard issue for rank-and-file soldiers and mercenaries in the 15th and 16th centuries. Conversely, wealthy nobles used controlled heat-bluing and chemical browning alongside gold gilding to create striking high-contrast "black-and-white" gothic armor.
• Historical Debate: On Reddit, armor enthusiasts note mixed opinions on early records—while purposeful blackening clearly appears in 15th- and 16th-century art, earlier references to "black" armor around 1400 likely just described unpolished, forge-darkened iron.

In British folklore, mythology, and Gothic literature, black iron—more traditionally known in folk superstition as cold iron or raw wrought iron—serves as a potent ward against supernatural creatures, witches, and the dead. During the Gothic revival era (late 18th to 19th centuries), antiquarians and writers wove these rural British folk beliefs into haunting tropes of spectral knights, cursed armor, and iron-bound graveyards. 
1. British Folk Superstition: "Cold Iron" vs. the Fae

In England, Scotland, and Wales, raw, dark wrought iron was regarded as the ultimate earthy defense against preternatural beings.
• Repelling the Fair Folk (Fae): Highland Scots and English villagers believed fairies, elves, and changelings could not bear the touch of iron. Farmers nailed iron horseshoes above doorways and placed iron tongs or knives near cradles to stop the Fae from abducting infants or young mothers. 
• The "Cauld Airn" Charm: As documented in Ronel the Mythmaker, Scottish fishermen who accidentally uttered a curse or unlucky word at sea would immediately shout "Cauld airn!" and grab the nearest piece of dark iron on the boat to ward off bad luck. 
• Containing the Dead: According to Wikipedia, Victorian and Georgian communities erected heavy black wrought-iron railings around churchyards and over individual graves (known as mortsafes) not just to stop grave robbers, but out of lingering superstition that iron barred restless ghosts from walking. 
2. Why Iron Was Feared by Magic

Folklore offered several explanations for why dark, unpolished iron possessed magical resistance:
• Earthly Purity: On Reddit, folklore enthusiasts agree that "cold iron" meant raw, dark iron worked with minimal refining, preserving an earthly grounding that disrupted glamour and fairy magic. 
• Christian & Mythic Associations: As noted by Sorcerer of Tea, medieval and post-medieval British lore linked iron both to the nails of the Crucifixion—making it abhorrent to demons and fallen spirits—and to the clash between the Iron Age newcomers and older pagan nature spirits. 

3. Black Iron in Gothic Literature and Chivalric Myth

When the Gothic literary movement emerged in Britain (beginning with Horace Walpole's The Castle of Otranto in 1764), authors blended real medieval armor history with dark folklore. 
• The Black Knight Motif: In British Arthurian romance and Gothic revival fiction (such as Sir Walter Scott's Ivanhoe), knights clad in blackened iron or steel symbolized mystery, mourning, penance, or hidden identity.
• Haunted Suits of Armor: Gothic writers transformed museum displays of blackened 15th- and 16th-century plate armor into vessels for ancestral curses, animated specters, and doom-laden prophecies.
• Witches and Iron: In British witch-trial lore, burying an iron knife beneath a threshold or wearing an iron charm prevented witches from crossing into a home or casting the evil eye. 

Victorian Gothic ghost traditions combined ancient pagan winter folklore, elaborate mourning customs, and the rise of Spiritualism into a cultural obsession with death and the afterlife. During Queen Victoria's reign (1837–1901), rapid industrialization, high mortality rates, and scientific challenges to religious faith prompted Victorians to seek both comfort and thrilling entertainment in the supernatural.

1. Christmas Eve Ghost Storytelling

In Victorian Britain, telling ghost stories was the centerpiece of Christmas Eve rather than Halloween. 
• Winter Solstice Roots (https://t.co/hbjuuTRLKb). Families gathered around roaring fires on the darkest nights of the year, drawing on ancient beliefs that the veil between the living and the dead grew thinnest at midwinter. 
• The Dickens Effect. Following the massive success of Charles Dickens's A Christmas Carol in 1843, periodicals and magazines published special Christmas annuals packed with supernatural tales. 
• Domestic Gothic Horror. Writers like J.S. Le Fanu, Elizabeth Gaskell, and M.R. James shifted ghost stories away from distant medieval castles and into familiar Victorian drawing rooms, libraries, and country estates.

2. Spiritualism and Parlor Séances

Beginning in the late 1840s, Spiritualism swept across Britain as both a serious religious movement and an evening parlor pastime.
• Communicating with the Dead. Friends and grieving families gathered around dark tables for séances, hoping to witness table-rapping, automatic writing, or voices channeled through a spirit medium. 
• Spirit Photography. Photographers used double-exposure techniques to produce "spirit portraits," placing translucent, ghostly figures of deceased relatives beside living sitters. 
• Theatrical Illusions. Popular stage shows used optical tricks like "Pepper's Ghost"—a pane of angled glass reflecting hidden actors—to project lifelike specters onto theater stages.

3. Elaborate Mourning and Death Rituals

High mortality rates and Queen Victoria's decades-long mourning for Prince Albert normalized visible, everyday reminders of the dead. 
• Strict Mourning Dress. Widows wore heavy black crepe, dull jet jewelry, and "weeping veils" for years, following strict social etiquette rules.
• Memento Mori. Families braided locks of a deceased loved one's hair into lockets and brooches, and commissioned post-mortem photographs of departed relatives posed as if asleep.
• Churchyard Superstitions. Victorians continued folk traditions of placing heavy wrought-iron cages (mortsafes) over graves and covering mirrors in a house after a death so the departing soul would not become trapped inside. 

4. Superstitions and Omens of Death

Everyday Victorian households observed dozens of folk omens believed to foretell a haunting or a death in the family:
• The Deathwatch Beetle. Hearing the rhythmic ticking of wood-boring beetles inside quiet wooden walls was taken as an omen that Death was counting down someone's final hours.
• Stopping the Clock. When someone died in a Victorian home, family members immediately stopped the parlor clock at the exact minute of death to prevent bad luck or a lingering spirit.
• Ringing Bells and Falling Pictures. A portrait falling off a wall without cause, a bird tapping at a windowpane, or a servant's bell ringing in an empty room was interpreted as a spectral warning.

Ys (pronounced like geese without the "g") is a famous Japanese action-adventure video game series about a young swordsman who explores mysterious lands, fights monsters in real time, and uncovers ancient magic. Unlike many traditional Japanese RPGs where you take turns selecting attacks from a menu, Ys is all about fast reflexes, dodging, and slicing enemies directly on screen.
Here is a simpler breakdown of what makes the series special:

1. The Story: One Hero, Many Adventures

• Adol the Adventurer: Almost every game follows the same hero, a brave red-haired swordsman named Adol Christin. He doesn't travel to save the world out of duty—he just loves exploring unknown places, which constantly lands him in the middle of big crises.
• Stand-Alone Chapters: Each numbered Ys game is like a different book from Adol’s life journals. Because each game takes place in a brand-new region with a new cast of characters, you do not need to play them in order to understand what is happening. (Think of it like Indiana Jones movies or The Legend of Zelda.)

2. What It Plays Like

• Fast, Arcade-Style Combat: You move around in real time, slashing enemies with a sword, dodging attacks, and unleashing flashy special skills. It is very easy to pick up and play, even if you are new to action games.
• Giant Boss Fights: Every game features massive, challenging bosses that require you to learn their attack patterns and find their weak spots.
• Famous Rock Music: The Ys series is legendary among gamers for its high-energy heavy metal and electric guitar soundtracks that play while you explore and fight.

3. The Best Place to Start

If you want to see what the series is all about today, most fans recommend starting with Ys VIII: Lacrimosa of DANA.
• In this game, Adol is shipwrecked on a cursed, uninhabited island.
• You explore the jungle, rescue other stranded passengers to build up a survivor village, and uncover the island's secrets. It gives you the complete Ys experience without needing any background knowledge.

In astrology, black iron is linked to the planet Saturn, especially in Indian (Vedic) astrology.

Why Saturn and Black Iron Go Together

Astrology connects every planet to specific colors and metals based on how they behave.
• Saturn's Personality: Saturn is the planet of hard work, strict rules, patience, and life lessons. It teaches through tough experiences rather than easy luck.
• The Metal Match: Black iron is heavy, dark, and tough. To make iron strong, a blacksmith has to put it through intense fire and hammer it into shape. Astrologers view this as a mirror of how Saturn tests people to make them stronger and wiser.

How People Use Black Iron

When someone is going through a streak of bad luck, delays, or heavy stress, an astrologer might say their Saturn is "unhappy" or out of balance. People use black iron to calm that energy down.
• Wearing It: People often wear a simple black iron ring on their middle finger (Saturn's finger) or a plain iron bracelet. Rings made from old, used horseshoes are especially popular because they are believed to have already absorbed plenty of hard work.
• Giving It Away: Donating iron objects—like simple cooking pans or tools—on a Saturday (Saturn's day of the week) is seen as a way to show humility and earn good karma.
• Protection: Because iron is tough and grounding, many traditions use small black iron charms to block bad luck, jealousy, or negative energy.

A Quick Difference Between Traditions

Depending on which style of astrology you look at, the rules change slightly:
• Indian (Vedic) Astrology: Black iron belongs strictly to Saturn.
• Western Astrology: Regular iron usually belongs to Mars (the planet of war, weapons, and action), while lead is given to Saturn because lead is heavy and slow.

Wearing a black iron ring is a popular remedy in Vedic astrology used to balance the heavy energy of Saturn (Shani). People wear it to help reduce delays, ease stress, and invite stability when Saturn is testing them.

Traditional Rules for Wearing It

If you decide to wear one according to astrological traditions, there are a few specific guidelines people usually follow:
• Which Finger: It is almost always worn on the middle finger. In palmistry and astrology, the middle finger is directly connected to Saturn.
• Which Hand: Traditionally, men wear it on their right hand, while women wear it on their left hand (though some modern practitioners base this on your dominant hand instead).
• The Material: Pure black iron—especially iron forged from a used black horseshoe (Kale Ghode Ki Naal)—is considered the most effective. A used horseshoe symbolizes hard work and endurance that has already been tested.
• Best Day and Time: It is usually put on for the first time on a Saturday evening after sunset, as Saturday is Saturn's day of the week.
• Cleansing First: Before putting it on, people commonly soak the ring in a mix of unboiled milk and clean water (or Ganga Jal) for a few minutes to purify it.

When Should You Avoid It?

In astrology, iron is seen as a strong, heavy metal that amplifies Saturn's traits. Because of this, astrologers advise caution in a few situations:
• Strong Saturn: If Saturn is already very strong or well-placed in your birth chart, adding iron might make you feel overly rigid, isolated, or weighed down by responsibilities.
• Clashing Planets: If you are already wearing rings or gemstones for the Sun (like Ruby), Moon (Pearl), or Mars (Red Coral), traditional astrologers advise against wearing iron alongside them, as those planets are considered rivals to Saturn.

Practical Care Tips

Because black iron is a raw metal, it reacts easily to moisture and skin oils.
• Preventing Rust: Take the ring off before washing your hands, showering, or swimming.
• Skin Staining: Raw iron can sometimes leave a harmless dark gray or greenish mark on your finger, especially if you sweat. Rubbing a tiny drop of coconut oil or clear nail polish on the inside of the band helps protect both the metal and your skin.

Jensen Huang's resignation — what it means for NVDA and the AI industry
The resignation — verified:
Thursday, November 12, around 8:48 AM ET, Nvidia announced Jensen Huang resigned as President, CEO and board member, effective immediately, ending a 33-year tenure. He co-founded the company in 1993.
Interim CEO: CFO Colette Kress (EVP + CFO since September 2013, keeping the CFO role); the permanent search is internal and external. Harvey C. Jones was appointed the company's first-ever Chair of the Board.
The 8-K: the board accepted the resignation on November 11, effective immediately; the company gave no reason. "Firing" is Rep. Moolenaar's word, not the fact — his own statement's title says "Resignation."
Market reaction: Wednesday's close of $173.73 → pre-market $157.54 (-9.32%, about $400 billion of market value erased) → Thursday's close $165.77 → Friday $162.85 (-2.01%). NVDA fell 12.75% on the week.
Analysts: Ives $225 (without Huang) vs $300 (with him); Stifel $315 → $205; BofA $350 → $280; William Blair cut to Market Perform.
Rotation: AMD +18.93% on the week (Friday -8.75% to $534.06), AVGO up about 19% on the week (Friday $347.01, -4.76%). The NVDA–AMD spread is about -$371. Red pen: AMD trades at 38.44x forward earnings vs NVDA at 13.72x; the scale gap is about 11–13x (NVDA's data-center quarter is about $75 billion, AMD's $6.7 billion).
Three structural breaks for the AI industry:
The founder premium is gone: "Jensen is Nvidia" no longer holds, and the market has to re-price succession uncertainty.
A succession vacuum: Kress is an interim CEO from finance, with no product or visionary pull. In your framework: "NVDA doesn't need an operator, it needs a visionary."
The scrutiny continues: the Senate and House will investigate the Trump administration's approval of Nvidia chip exports to China; Huang has agreed to testify before Congress on the Alice Huang matter before Thanksgiving (no date set). The Warren + Coons preservation letter requires confirmation by November 17.
Rumors and investigations (reported, not established):
The NYT reported an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, his direct report; Reuters reported an intimate relationship with a second employee (two sources, unnamed). Both are allegations, not findings.
The Alice Huang spy case: CNN reported that intelligence to date "does not prove" she spied for Beijing (not an exoneration); the FBI probe is ongoing, with no official finding. CNBC reported she owned stakes in Chinese businesses that provided computing power to Huawei (source reporting, not a finding).
Your rule has fired: the November 11 rule — liquidate NVDA holdings once the CEO is replaced — has fired. The $200 calendar spread (long Jun 17, 2027 $200 calls / short Dec 24, 2026 $200 calls, $12.18 debit) is confirmed held, with a maximum loss of $1,218 per spread. The next test: NVDA earnings Tuesday after the close, Kress's first print facing analysts — watch data-center demand, H200 sales to China, and guidance.
Earnings breakdown: CoreWeave (CRWV) — beat-and-raise, sold on leverage
Q3 (Nov 10, after the close): revenue $3.661 billion, +168% YoY, beating consensus of about $3.5 billion and the company's $3.4–$3.6 billion guide; GAAP EPS -$1.27, beating Zacks' -$1.45 (Finnhub shows -$0.95, a different basis); net loss $709 million.
Profits: adjusted operating income $379 million, beating the $200–$260 million guide; GAAP operating income $207 million. The Sankey: revenue $3.7B → gross profit $2.5B (68%) → operating profit $0.2B (6%) → interest $0.8B + tax and other $0.1B → net loss $0.7B.
Red pen: Q3 net interest expense of $846 million is more than 4x operating profit; Q4 interest is guided at $1.05–$1.15 billion; debt is $46.9 billion. R&D of $2.0 billion is 55% of revenue. 98% of revenue comes from committed contracts ($3.6B) — revenue quality is high; the problem is cost and leverage.
Guidance: backlog $132.5 billion (+138% YoY); FY26 revenue guided up to $13.0–$13.3 billion; capex $37–$39 billion; active power over 1.7 GW; operating cash flow $1.975 billion; cash $6.5 billion.
The stock: Nov 11 close $60.77 → Nov 12 $56.60 → Friday intraday $52.27 (-7.66%, low $49.24). A beat-and-raise sold off — that's the leverage story, not the revenue story.
The slide's numbers were checked against the official print; US $3.4B + rest of world $0.2B sums to $3.6B vs the $3.7B total — a $0.1B rounding difference.
Earnings breakdown: Nebius (NBIS) — a big beat, and the stock fell
Q3 (Nov 12, before the open): adjusted EPS $0.31, revenue $980.8 million; revenue +571% YoY (Q3 2025: $146.1 million) and +68% QoQ (Q2 2026: $582.3 million). Adjusted EBITDA $465.8 million.
Slide check: EPS consensus -$0.63 vs actual $0.31 (a 149% beat); revenue consensus $907.17 million vs actual $980.8 million (an 8% beat). The revenue consensus varies by vendor — the slide's $907.17 million matches MarketBeat, Finnhub's $925.68 million is the high outlier; the beat is large either way.
Red pen one: the slide's "EPS +178% YoY / +358% QoQ" uses the absolute-negative-base convention — the reality is a swing from loss to profit (YoY -$0.40 → +$0.31; QoQ -$0.12 → +$0.31). Don't say +178%.
Red pen two: FY26 revenue guidance was cut to the low end of the $3.0–$3.4 billion range (FactSet $3.35 billion); 2026 capex was raised to about $27 billion (from $20–$25 billion); 2027 capex is $40–$45 billion, far above the expected $28.77 billion; $7 billion-plus ARR was pushed from December to February; about $325 million of Q3 revenue was non-recurring.
Prepayments are the bright spot: Q3 new deals had prepayments covering over 100% of related capex (Q2: 50–60%); over 90% of Q3 contract value carries a prepayment (up about 20 points); deferred revenue on the balance sheet is $9.4 billion (from $1.6 billion at end-2025); payback on 1–3 year deals is 19 months (Q2: 22 months); 2027 prepayments are expected at $17–$20 billion (2026: $10 billion). Customers are paying to fund the build-out.
The stock: Nov 11 close $154.69 → Nov 12 $128.64 (-16.84%) → Friday intraday about $117 (-8.92%, low $109), about -24% in two days; one month -37.01%; 52-week high $299.86.
NBIS continued: 2027 revenue guidance is about 4x — but the market is pricing capex
Revenue trajectory: 2024 $92 million → 2025 $530 million → 2026 guide about $3.0 billion (low end of the range; analysts expect $3.37 billion) → 2027 guide $12–$13 billion, about 4x 2026 (analysts expect $11.98 billion). Q3 was $981 million, +571% YoY, beating the expected $908 million.
Quarterly outlook (VJN estimates): Q3 2026 about $0.9B, Q4 about $1.5B; 2027 Q1 about $2.2B, Q2 about $2.7B, Q3 about $3.2B, Q4 about $4.0B; 2028 Q1 about $4.6B, Q2 $5.2B. Everything after Q3 2026 is an estimate (e), not actuals.
Why a big beat still fell: revenue and EPS both beat big, but guidance was cut, capex jumped, ARR was delayed, and $325 million of revenue was non-recurring — the market is pricing the speed of the cash burn, not the speed of revenue. Prepayments covering 100%+ of capex are a guardrail, not a guarantee.
Against CRWV: both are "revenue exploding, interest and capex exploding faster" AI infrastructure stories; CRWV's interest is 4x its operating profit, and NBIS's capex guide is about 50% above expectations. This week the market chose to sell first and ask later.
Anthropic IPO — the price range is out; the seven giants are putting in $26 billion
Price range: $70–$78 (S-1/A No. 2, Nov 10); about 825 million shares offered, raising $57.75–$64.35 billion; on shares outstanding the valuation is about $916 billion–$1.02 trillion, midpoint about $968 billion — about equal to the May Series H mark of $965 billion.
Fully diluted: at $78, up to about $1.404 trillion (TechCrunch) — a different yardstick from the $1.02 trillion on shares outstanding; both numbers are real.
The $26B concurrent placement (Class N non-voting shares, at the IPO price): Alphabet $10 billion, NVIDIA $10 billion, AMD $2.5 billion, Broadcom $1 billion, Micron $1 billion, Microsoft $1 billion, TSMC $0.5 billion — exactly $26.0 billion in total. All seven buyers are also Anthropic's chip and cloud suppliers.
Timing: pricing reportedly Nov 18, first trade Nov 19 — unconfirmed; the filing carries no date. The founders keep 50.1% voting control through a single Class F share; the lock-up releases in stages (some non-founder insiders can sell 10% on day one).
Anthropic results: Q3 revenue $16.96 billion, compute ate 58%
Q3 2026: revenue $16.956 billion, +1,127% YoY, +47% QoQ (Q2 was +144% — growth is slowing); compute and infrastructure cost $9.863 billion, 58% of revenue; GAAP operating loss $567 million; adjusted operating income $2.463 billion, a 15% margin.
The Sankey: revenue $17.0B — consumption-based $13.2B (78%, API and app token usage), subscription $3.7B (22%, Claude fixed-fee plans); customers over $100K: 11,900+ (+1,153% YoY), net revenue retention 900%. Operating expenses $17.5B: compute $9.9B (58%), personnel $1.7B (10%), sales and marketing $2.4B (14%), other $3.6B (21%); operating loss $0.6B (-3% margin).
GAAP net loss of $23.29 billion is mostly a $21.9 billion non-cash note revaluation — not cash burned. Nine-month revenue is $33.24 billion, net loss $104.04 billion. Long-term commitments are about $900.9 billion (about $70.7 billion due within a year); the annualized run-rate at Oct 31 is about $81 billion; net proceeds are $84.6–$93.7 billion (including the placement).
Your position: you hold pre-IPO Anthropic shares (via Forge Global) and will not chase the IPO. On Nov 9, Claude Fable 5.2 + Mythos 5.2 launched ($8/$40 per million tokens, 20% cheaper than 5.1).
Against OpenAI: the same quarter, OpenAI had revenue of $10 billion and an adjusted operating loss of $10.9 billion (the loss exceeded revenue); Anthropic had revenue of $17 billion and an operating loss of $567 million. Both are burning money — Anthropic's unit economics are closer to breakeven.
Next week: NVDA and WMT earnings; the FOMC minutes are the key
NVDA earnings (Tuesday after the close):
Kress's first earnings as interim CEO, facing analysts. Watch three things: data-center demand, H200 sales to China, and guidance. The first print since the resignation — the market wants to know whether "NVDA without Jensen can still deliver." November 17 is also the date in the Warren + Coons preservation letter; the congressional probe is heating up.
WMT earnings (Thursday before the open):
Q3 FY27, released 6:00 AM CT Thursday, call at 7:00 AM CT (CEO John Furner + CFO John David Rainey). Consensus EPS $0.64 (Zacks, +3.2% YoY), revenue about $186.52 billion (Zacks) / $187.27 billion (TipRanks). Options imply about ±7%; last time (Aug 20) the stock moved just +0.10% the next day.

Two stories this week: inflation isn't cooling fast enough, and housing gave way first. Labor is still tight; long-end demand is weak.

The week's verdict: inflation is not out of control, but it is not cooling enough to breathe easy either — core is +0.3% for a third straight month and a December hike is fully priced; the long end is steepening on term premium plus weak auction demand, not on growth panic; labor is still tight while housing is the first to break under high rates. text:
Democratic Senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland announced Thursday that he will challenge longtime Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer for majority leader in the next Congress, according to the ASSOCIATED PRESS, NBC NEWS, and POLITICO.

Van Hollen said in a statement that “the American people called for change” and that “we need new leadership.” He added that the decision “is not about any one person — it’s about answering the call of the American people.”

The closed-door, secret-ballot election among Senate Democrats is expected in early December and will be the first contested race for the post in decades.

Van Hollen, 67, said in an interview that more than 10 senators have pledged to support him and described himself as the underdog. He has the backing of Senator Bernie Sanders and Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan.

Schumer, 75, who has led the caucus since 2017, responded that he has the votes to win and welcomes discussion about the caucus’s future. He cited the party’s gains of 55 seats and counting. Supporters including Senators Angus King and Catherine Cortez Masto have publicly backed him, pointing to his role in recruiting candidates, fundraising, and the midterm results.

Van Hollen has criticized Schumer’s ties to special interests and has said he is considering a presidential run. The challenge highlights divisions that have grown within the caucus, particularly among progressives seeking a change in direction after the midterms.

text:
DEMOCRATIC SENATOR ELISSA SLOTKIN COMPARES PRESIDENT TRUMP TO SADDAM HUSSEIN — AND ACCUSES HIM OF STEALING FROM THE AMERICAN PEOPLE:

Michigan Senator Elissa Slotkin has launched an extraordinary attack against President Donald Trump, comparing his alleged financial misconduct to that of one of the most brutal dictators in modern history.

Her statement?

“Saddam Hussein would spit out his tea at the amount of money Donald Trump has stolen from his own people.”

That's an explosive accusation from a sitting United States Senator.

And it deserves serious scrutiny.

Let's remember who Saddam Hussein actually was.

He ruled Iraq through a brutal authoritarian regime responsible for political executions, torture, mass repression, and the persecution of ethnic and religious minorities.

His government used chemical weapons against Kurdish civilians, invaded Kuwait, and violently suppressed political opposition.

These were documented atrocities committed by a dictatorship.

Comparing the president of the United States to Saddam Hussein is not an ordinary political criticism.

Slotkin is entitled to oppose Trump's policies.

She's entitled to criticize his business interests.

And she's entitled to demand investigations into potential conflicts of interest.

But accusing a president of stealing from the American people requires evidence of specific wrongdoing.

An increase in someone's wealth is not automatically proof of theft.

Trump's financial interests, cryptocurrency ventures, family businesses, and government-related transactions can all be examined under applicable laws and ethics requirements.

If Slotkin believes particular transactions involved criminal conduct, she should identify those transactions and explain which laws she believes were violated.

That's how serious allegations should be evaluated.

The American people deserve facts, not just the most inflammatory comparison a politician can come up with.

And there's a larger political context that makes her comments particularly significant.

Democrats are preparing to assume control of the House in January 2027.

Prominent members of the party have already discussed investigations, subpoenas, and potential impeachment proceedings involving Trump administration officials.

Slotkin has been among the Democrats calling for aggressive scrutiny of the administration.

The Trump White House has challenged accusations it considers politically motivated.

That sets up another potentially divisive confrontation between congressional Democrats and President Trump.

But political disagreements over policy and allegations of criminal wrongdoing are not interchangeable.

The president's immigration policies can be criticized without alleging theft.

His economic agenda can be challenged without comparing him to a dictator.

And his business interests can be investigated without presuming the outcome.

Accusations this serious should be established through evidence, not political rhetoric.

There's also an important fact about Trump's political history.

Democrats impeached him twice during his first presidency.

The Senate acquitted him both times.

He subsequently returned to the White House after winning the 2024 presidential election.

Those Senate acquittals do not resolve every separate allegation involving Trump, but they are part of the history of repeated political confrontations surrounding his presidency.

Now Democrats are preparing for another round of investigations, and Slotkin is making some of the most dramatic accusations yet.

The question is whether those investigations will produce substantiated findings or simply generate another cycle of partisan confrontation.

Congress has legitimate oversight responsibilities.

Public officials are accountable under the law.

But accountability requires distinguishing between documented facts, allegations, and political opinions.

That standard should apply to every administration.

Elissa Slotkin has compared Donald Trump's alleged financial misconduct to Saddam Hussein's dictatorship. That's an extraordinary accusation, and extraordinary accusations deserve specific evidence.

Trump's critics have every right to challenge his policies and investigate potential wrongdoing. But the American people also have every right to demand proof before accepting accusations of criminal conduct.

Do you think Slotkin's comparison goes too far, or is it justified by the evidence she's presented?

text:
Two weeks into the coding class he was teaching at Duke University in North Carolina this spring, Noah Gift told his students to throw out the course materials he’d given them. Instead of working with Python, one of the most popular entry-level programming languages, the students would now be using Rust, a language that was newer, more powerful, and much harder to learn.

Gift, a software developer with 25 years of experience, had only just learned Rust himself. But he was confident his students would be fine with the last-minute switch-up. That’s because they’d also each get a special new sidekick: an AI tool called Copilot, a turbocharged autocomplete for computer code, built on top of OpenAI’s latest large language models, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4.

Copilot is made by GitHub, a firm that runs an online software development platform used by more than 100 million programmers. The tool monitors every keystroke you make, predicts what you are trying to do on the fly, and offers up a nonstop stream of code snippets you could use to do it. Gift, who had been told about Copilot by someone he knew at GitHub’s parent company, Microsoft, saw its potential at once.

“There’s no way I could have learned Rust as quickly as I did without Copilot,” he says. “I basically had a supersmart assistant next to me that could answer my questions while I tried to level up. It was pretty obvious to me that we should start using it in class.”

Gift isn’t alone. Ask a room of computer science students or programmers if they use Copilot, and many now raise a hand. All the people interviewed for this article said they used Copilot themselves—even those who pointed out problems with the tool.

Like ChatGPT with education, Copilot is upending an entire profession by giving people new ways to perform old tasks. Packaged as a paid-for plug-in for Microsoft’s Visual Studio software (a kind of industry-standard multi-tool for writing, debugging, and deploying code), Copilot is the slickest version of this tech. But it’s not the only tool available to coders. In August, Meta released a free code-generation model called Code Llama, based on Llama 2, Meta’s answer to GPT-4. The same month, Stability AI—the firm behind the image-making model Stable Diffusion—put out StableCode. And, of course, there’s ChatGPT, which OpenAI has pitched from the start as a chatbot that can help write and debug code.

“It’s the first time that machine-learning models have been really useful for a lot of people,” says Gabriel Synnaeve, who led the team behind Code Llama at Meta. “It’s not just nerding out—it’s actually useful.”

With Microsoft and Google about to stir similar generative models into office software used by billions around the world (Microsoft has started using Copilot as a brand name across Office 365), it’s worth asking exactly what these tools do for programmers. How are they changing the basics of a decades-old job? Will they help programmers make more and better software? Or will they get bogged down in legal fights over IP and copyright? 

Cranking out code

On the surface, writing code involves typing statements and instructions in some programming language into a text file. This then gets translated into machine code that a computer can run—a level up from the 0s and 1s of binary. In practice, programmers also spend a lot of time googling, looking up workarounds for common problems or skimming online forums for faster ways to write an algorithm. Existing chunks of prewritten code then get repurposed, and new software often comes together like a collage. 

But these look-ups take time and let programmers out of the flow of converting thoughts into code, says Thomas Dohmke, GitHub’s CEO: “You’ve got a lot of tabs open, you’re planning a vacation, maybe you’re reading the news. At last you copy the text you need and go back to your code, but it’s 20 minutes later and you lost the flow.”

The key idea behind Copilot and other programs like it, sometimes called code assistants, is to put the information that programmers need right next to the code they are writing. The tool tracks the code and comments (descriptions or notes written in natural language) in the file that a programmer is working on, as well as other files that it links to or that have been edited in the same project, and sends all this text to the large language model behind Copilot as a prompt. (GitHub co-developed Copilot’s model, called Codex, with OpenAI. It is a large language model fine-tuned on code.) Copilot then predicts what the programmer is trying to do and suggests code to do it.

This round trip between code and Codex happens multiple times a second, the prompt updating as the programmer types. At any moment, the programmer can accept what Copilot suggests by hitting the tab key, or ignore it and carry on typing. 

The tab button seems to get hit a lot. A study of almost a million Copilot users published by GitHub and the consulting firm Keystone Strategy in June—a year after the tool’s general release—found that programmers accepted on average around 30% of its suggestions, according to GitHub’s user data. 

“In the last year Copilot has suggested—and had okayed by developers—more than a billion lines of code,” says Dohmke. “Out there, running inside computers, is code generated by a stochastic parrot.”

Copilot has changed the basic skills of coding. As with ChatGPT or image makers like Stable Diffusion, the tool’s output is often not exactly what’s wanted—but it can be close. “Maybe it’s correct, maybe it’s not—but it’s a good start,” says Arghavan Moradi Dakhel, a researcher at Polytechnique Montréal in Canada who studies the use of machine-learning tools in software development. Programming becomes prompting: rather than coming up with code from scratch, the work involves tweaking half-formed code and nudging a large language model to produce something more on point. 

But Copilot isn’t everywhere yet. Some firms, including Apple, have asked employees not to use it, wary of leaking IP and other private data to competitors. For Justin Gottschlich, CEO of Merly, a startup that uses AI to analyze code across large software projects, that will always be a deal-breaker: “If I’m Google or Intel and my IP is my source code, I’m never going to use it,” he says. “Why don’t I just send you all my trade secrets too? It’s just put-your-pants-on-before-you-leave-the-house kind of obvious.” Dohmke is aware this is a turn-off for key customers and says that the firm is working on a version of Copilot that businesses can run in-house, so that code isn’t sent to Microsoft’s servers.

Copilot is also at the center of a lawsuit filed by programmers unhappy that their code was used to train the models behind it without their consent. Microsoft has offered indemnity to users of its models who are wary of potential litigation. But the legal issues will take years to play out in the courts.

Dohmke is bullish, confident that the pros outweigh the cons: “We will adjust to whatever US, UK, or European lawmakers tell us to do,” he says. “But there is a middle balance here between protecting rights—and protecting privacy—and us as humanity making a step forward.” That’s the kind of fighting talk you’d expect from a CEO. But this is new, uncharted territory. If nothing else, GitHub is leading a brazen experiment that could pave the way for a wider range of AI-powered professional assistants. 

Code whisperer

GitHub started working on Copilot in June 2020, soon after OpenAI released GPT-3. Programmers have always been on the lookout for shortcuts and speedups. “It’s part of the DNA of being a software developer,” says Dohmke. “We wanted to solve this problem of boilerplate code—can we generate code that is no fun to write but takes up time?”

The first sign they were onto something came when they asked programmers at the company to submit coding tests that they might ask somebody at a job interview: “Here’s some code—finish it off.” GitHub gave these to an early version of the tool and let it try each test 150 times. Given that many attempts, they found that the tool could solve 92% of them. They tried again with 50,000 problems taken from GitHub’s online platform, and the tool solved just over half of them. “That gave us confidence that we could build what ultimately became Copilot,” says Dohmke.

In 2023, a team of GitHub and Microsoft researchers tested the impact of Copilot on programmers in a small study. They asked 95 people to build a web server (a non-trivial task, but one involving the kind of common, boilerplate code that Dohmke refers to) and gave half access to Copilot. Those using Copilot completed the task on average 55% faster. 

A powerful AI that replaces the need for googling is useful—but is it a game changer? Opinion is split.

“The way that I would think about it is that you have an experienced developer sitting next to you whispering recommendations,” says Marco Iansiti, a Keystone Strategy cofounder and a professor at Harvard Business School, where he studies digital transformation. “You used to have to look things up on your own, and now—whammo—here comes the suggestion automatically.”

Gottschlich, who has been working on automatic code generation for years, is less impressed. “To be frank, code assistants are fairly uninteresting in the larger scheme of things,” he says, referring to the new wave of tools based on large language models, like Copilot. “They are principally bound by what the human programmer is capable of doing. They’ll never likely at this stage be able to do something miraculous beyond what the human programmer is doing.”

Gottschlich, who claims that Merly’s tech finds bugs in code and fixes them by itself (but who doesn’t shed light on how that works), is thinking bigger. He sees AI one day taking on the management of vast and complex libraries of code, directing human engineers in how to maintain it. But he doesn’t think large language models are the right tech for that job.

Even so, small changes to a task that millions of people do all the time can add up fast. Iansiti, for example, makes a huge claim: he believes that the impact of Copilot—and tools like it—could add $1.5 trillion to the global economy by 2030. “It’s more of a back-of-the-envelope thing, not really an academic estimate, but it could be a lot larger than that as well,” he says. “There’s so much stuff that hinges on software. If you move the needle on how software development really works, it will have an infinite impact on the economy.”

For Iansiti, it’s not just about getting existing developers to produce more code. He argues that these tools will increase the demand for programmers because companies could get more code for less money. At the same time, there will be more coders because these tools lower the barrier to entry. “We’re going to see an expansion in who can contribute to software development,” he says.

Or as Idan Gazit, GitHub’s senior director of research, puts it: imagine if anyone who picked up a guitar could play a basic tune straight away. There would be a lot more guitar players and a lot more music.

Many agree that Copilot makes it easier to pick up programming—as Gift found. “Rust has got a reputation for being a very difficult language,” he says. “But I was pleasantly shocked at how well the students did and at the projects they built—how complex and useful they were.” Gift says they were able to build complete web apps with chatbots in them.

Not everyone was happy with Gift’s syllabus change, however. He says that one of his teaching assistants told new students not to use Copilot because it was a crutch that would stop them from learning properly. Gift accepts that Copilot is like training wheels that you might not want to take off. But he doesn’t think that’s a problem: “What are we trying to do? We’re trying to build complex systems.” And to do that, he argues, programmers should use whatever tools are available.

It is true that the history of computing has seen programmers rely on more and more layers of software between themselves and the machine code that computers can run. They have gone from punch cards and assembly code to programming languages like Python that are relatively easy to read and write. That’s possible because such languages get translated into machine code by software called compilers. “When I started coding in the ’80s and ’90s, you still had to know how a CPU worked,” says Dohmke. “Now when you write a web application, you almost never think about the CPU or the web server.”

Add in a long list of bug-catching and code-testing tools, and programmers are used to a large amount of automated support. In many ways, Copilot and others are just the latest wave. “I used Python for 25 years because it was written to be readable by humans,” says Gift. “In my opinion, that doesn’t matter anymore.” 

But he points out that Copilot isn’t a free pass. “Copilot reflects your ability,” he says. “It lifts everyone up a little bit, but if you’re a poor programmer you’ll still have weaknesses.”

Work to be done

A big problem with assessing the true impact of such tools is that most of the data is still anecdotal. GitHub’s study showed that programmers were accepting 30% of suggestions (“30% is out of this world in any kind of industry scenario,” says Dohmke), but it is not clear why the programmers accepted those suggestions and rejected others.

The same study also revealed that less experienced programmers accepted more suggestions and that programmers accepted more suggestions as they grew used to the tool—but, again, not why. “We need to go a lot deeper to understand what that means,” says Iansiti. “There’s work to be done to really get a sense of how the coding process itself is developing, and that work is all TBD.”

Most independent studies of tools like Copilot have focused on the correctness of the code that they suggest. Like all large language models, these tools can produce nonsense. With code it can be hard to tell—especially for less experienced users, who also seem to rely on Copilot the most.

Several teams of researchers in the last couple of years have found that Copilot can insert bugs or security flaws into code. GitHub has been busy improving the accuracy of Copilot’s suggestions. It claims that the latest version of the tool runs code through a second model trained to filter out common security bugs before making a suggestion to users.

But there are other quality issues beyond bugs, says Dakhel. She and her colleagues have found that Copilot can suggest code that is overly complex or doesn’t adhere to what professionals consider best practices, which is a problem because complex or unclear code is harder for other people to read, check, and extend.

The problem is that models are only as good as their training data. And Copilot’s models were trained on a vast library of code taken from GitHub’s online repository, which goes back 15 years. This code contains not only bugs but also security flaws that were not known about when the code was written.

Add to this the fact that inexperienced programmers use the tool more than experienced ones, and it could make more work for software development teams in the long run, says Dakhel. Expert programmers may have to spend more time double-checking the code put through by non-experts.

Dakhel now hopes to study the gap between expert and non-expert programmers more fully. Before Copilot was released, she and her colleagues were using machine learning to detect expert programmers by their code. But Copilot messed with her data because now it was harder to tell whether code had been written by an expert programmer or a less experienced one with AI help.

Now, having played around with Copilot herself, she plans to use her approach to study what kind of boost it gives. “I’m curious to know if junior developers using such a tool will be predicted to be expert developers or if it’s still detectable that they are junior developers,” she says. “It could be a way of measuring how big a level up these tools give people.”

Ultimately, we might not have to wait long before the jury is in. Software development is one of the most well documented and thoroughly measured of business activities. If Copilot works, it will get used. If it doesn’t, it won’t. In the meantime, these tools are getting better all the time.

Yet it is worth noting that programming—typing text onto a screen—is a small part of the overall job of software development. It involves managing multiple parts of a complex puzzle, including designing the code, testing it, and deploying it. Copilot, like many programs before it, can make parts of that job faster, but it won’t reinvent it completely.

“There’s always going to be programmers,” says Synnaeve. “They will get a lot of help, but in the end what matters is understanding which problems need solving. To do that really well and translate that into a program—that’s the job of programmers.”

Texas Scorecard: Democrat State Rep. John Bucy filed House Bill 387 to eliminate the death penalty in Texas. It would require life without parole for capital felonies committed by adults 18 and older, and life imprisonment for those under 18. The bill also strips death-penalty-specific procedures from the Code of Criminal Procedure.

It would apply to pending cases, appeals, and new prosecutions. Existing final convictions stay in place. Effective date would be September 1, 2027, or sooner with two-thirds approval.

This comes after Democrats flipped statewide offices, including the governor’s race. Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has said she personally opposes the death penalty. Texas has long reserved capital punishment for the worst offenders. Democrats are now prioritizing its removal while victims’ families still seek final justice.
