text:
TRUMP WANTS A VOTE NOW ON LOCKHEED'S $LMT 53 F-35S:

Lockheed Martin (LMT) at $596.04, -$8.05 / -1.33% on Friday.

Lockheed Martin stays on the Quality-Value Len5, a little less cheap than a week ago. It is still 6.7% under its election-day close, and aerospace and defense stocks as a group are nearly back to theirs. We were factually incorrect to call the $350 billion defense bill out of reach: President Donald Trump asked the Senate on Thursday to pass it before the Republican majority ends. John Thune, the Senate majority leader, has not committed to a vote. Congress is weighing short-term funding into April, past Lockheed's first forecast for 2027.

Lockheed is #42 on the Quality-Value Len5, from #44 in our post. Quality-Value wants a durable business at a price its own profit justifies, and Friday's close is about 19.5 times the profit Lockheed forecasts for 2026, up from 18.6 times a week earlier. Its $292 billion of signed work is unchanged. What would knock it off the Quality-Value Len5 is what we wrote a week ago: a first 2027 forecast in January that cuts profit because Washington is buying fewer jets, or the shares back above the March 2 closing high of $676.70 with the 2026 forecast unchanged. It is on none of the Momentum, Deep-Value and Special-Situations, Hypergrowth or Income Len5es. From the election-day close it is less than a third of the way down to October 7's $499, which we said would put it on the Deep-Value and Special-Situations Len5; a week ago it was about halfway.

Lockheed has won back two-fifths of its fall since the election. Since our post:
- The shares: +$28.96 / +5.1% from the $567.08 close we quoted.
- Monday to Wednesday: three gains in a row, to $610.05. Thursday and Friday: -2.3%.
- Since the November 3 close, on election day: -6.7%.
- iShares U.S. Aerospace & Defense ETF (ITA) at $71.51, -$0.22 / -0.31% on Friday. Since our post: +3.7%. Since its November 3 close: -0.8%.
We called the F-35 the reason Lockheed fell further than the fund. The fund's fall is nearly gone, and three-fifths of Lockheed's is still there.

We wrote that the vote put the party-line money out of reach, and we were factually incorrect on the timing. The Republican Congress, which can pass that bill without a Democrat, came back on November 9 and sits until January 3. At 12:24pm ET on Thursday, Trump called on Senate leaders to "IMMEDIATELY move on the 350 Billion Dollar Reconciliation Bill." The request that bill is meant to fund holds 53 of the 85 F-35s the Pentagon asked for in fiscal 2027. Lockheed traded near $606 when he posted and closed Friday at $596.04, and the fund fell over the same stretch. Thursday's fall came in the first half hour of trading, before the post.

Thune has made no decision on bringing the bill up. He told reporters there were "no decisions yet," The Hill reported on Friday, and said it comes down to "what you can get 50 votes for here and 218 in the House." Republicans can lose only three senators, Newsweek reported.

Washington's short-term funding expires December 11, and leaders in Congress are eyeing an extension into April, The Hill reported. It quoted Mike Rounds, a Republican senator from South Dakota, saying Democrats "would take out of appropriations" whatever Republicans put into the party-line bill. Appropriations, the yearly spending bills, pay for the 32 jets in the base budget.

Lockheed keeps its Quality-Value seat with 53 jets that have the President's backing and no vote count. A Senate vote on the party-line bill would be the first count, and December 11, when the short-term funding runs out, is the first deadline.

text:
$PCG  — The market might see a wildfire liability and litigation play. I see a potentially interesting regulated infrastructure investment, with a complicated balance sheet and a possible sum-of-the-parts opportunity.

I've spent quite a bit of time going through PG&E's filings, capital expenditure plans, regulatory framework, wildfire exposure and valuation. There are a few things I find interesting here.

Using the latest Q3 2026 filings, PCG generated approximately $25.8B in TTM revenue, $3.1B in net income and $7.8B in operating cash flow. Capital expenditures were approximately $12.8B, leaving negative $5B in FCF.

It also carries roughly $65B in debt.

I'm not going to pretend those are pretty numbers. But I also wouldn't automatically interpret negative FCF as deteriorating operations. Utilities are capital-intensive businesses, and PCG is in the middle of a substantial infrastructure investment cycle.

The important question is how much of that investment eventually enters rate base, what return the company actually earns, and how it finances the gap in the meantime. The financing costs are very real, even if the returns on those investments take years to materialize.

PG&E operates a regulated electric and gas infrastructure monopoly serving more than 16 million people across Northern and Central California. Its earnings opportunity is tied to rate-base growth and the returns it can earn on approved infrastructure investment.

The CPUC has authorized a 9.98% ROE for 2026–2028, with an overall authorized rate of return of 7.61%. Obviously, an authorized return isn't a guaranteed return. Regulatory approval, execution and timing still matter.

California is going to need a tremendous amount of investment in grid hardening, wildfire prevention, undergrounding, transmission and distribution infrastructure.

PG&E projects approximately $18.7B in wildfire mitigation expenditures for 2026–2028, including $12.4B in capital expenditures and $6.3B in operating expenses.

I think investors sometimes lump all compliance spending together and treat it as a cost. That's not quite right. Operating expenses are expenses. But qualifying capital investment, when prudently incurred and approved by regulators, can enter rate base and earn a return.

For perspective, if the entire $12.4B capital program eventually qualified for rate-base treatment, applying a 52% equity component and 9.98% authorized ROE implies roughly $644M in theoretical annual allowed equity returns at full deployment, or about $0.29 per share.

That's a gross investment illustration, not an earnings forecast or a calculation of net incremental rate-base growth. It doesn't account for regulatory lag, financing costs, depreciation, timing or potential disallowances. PG&E reported $3.43B in depreciation, amortization and decommissioning expense during the first nine months of 2026 alone. The actual earnings contribution depends on net rate-base additions, not simply the amount spent.

We've already seen regulators propose disallowing hundreds of millions of dollars in wildfire mitigation spending.

And there is another constraint that I think deserves more attention: customer affordability.

California already has some of the highest electricity costs in the country. The CPUC's November affordability report makes clear that wildfire-related costs are putting further pressure on household bills, particularly for lower-income customers.

This creates a difficult balancing act. Regulators need utilities to invest in safety and reliability, but they cannot indefinitely approve expensive projects and pass every cost to customers.

Undergrounding is a good example. It can reduce wildfire exposure, but it is expensive. The cost-benefit methodology and the CPUC's willingness to approve these projects will determine how much of the proposed investment can actually become recoverable rate base.

I wouldn't buy PCG on the assumption that California will somehow eliminate wildfire liability. That's unrealistic.

California's inverse condemnation framework remains a structural tail risk. A utility can face liability when its equipment causes property damage even without ordinary negligence. That makes wildfire exposure a fundamental part of the investment case, not simply a matter of whether management improves its safety procedures.

I do think the rules around subrogation, liability allocation and insurance recovery matter enormously to the company's long-term cost of capital.

SB 492 failed to advance in 2026, and I'm not assigning any benefit from hypothetical legislative reform to my base case. The broader discussion, however, isn't going away.

But something else from the Q3 earnings call caught my attention.

PG&E has approximately 4 million natural gas customers. Management explicitly acknowledged that these customers are effectively bearing sub-investment-grade borrowing costs because the gas business sits within a holding company exposed to electric wildfire liability.

That is a potentially important mismatch.

The gas business has a different operating risk profile from the electric utility's wildfire exposure. Yet the holding-company structure means the two businesses do not necessarily receive financing costs that reflect their individual risk profiles.

Management's strategic review is evaluating options that include corporate ring-fencing, asset sales and business separations. CEO Patti Poppe specifically discussed the possibility of a regulator-approved spin, sale or separation of the gas business.

I find this more interesting than a generic promise of cost savings.

If PG&E can isolate lower-wildfire-risk assets and allow them to access a more appropriate cost of capital, there may be value trapped inside the current corporate structure.

But I would not assume a separation automatically creates shareholder value. The regulator has to approve it, the debt must be allocated sensibly, and the remaining electric utility must retain a viable capital structure. A transaction that simply shifts financial obligations around without lowering the group's overall cost of capital would accomplish very little.

Management expects to provide a more definitive outcome from the strategic review by summer 2027.

PG&E Corporation's parent-level credit profile is not the same as that of its regulated operating utility. The parent carries an S&P rating of BB+ with a Stable outlook and a Fitch rating of BBB- with a Negative outlook. The operating utility has stronger investment-grade ratings.

I think this may be the most important part of the entire investment thesis because that distinction matters. 

The parent-level wildfire discount can affect financing economics across businesses that have limited direct exposure to wildfire liability.

Management estimates that its sub-investment-grade financing status since 2017 has cost customers approximately $4B in additional interest expense over the life of the debt. That is a cumulative estimate, not an annual expense, but it illustrates the economic cost of the current structure.

The strategic review has a foundational objective: achieving investment-grade credit ratings. Management continues to target a mid-teens FFO-to-debt ratio.

The company has also reduced its 2027 capital expenditure plan from approximately $13.4B to $11.4B, lowering near-term financing requirements by $2B.

I understand the logic. With negative FCF and substantial debt, PG&E cannot simply spend its way into a larger rate base without considering the cost of capital.

But I wouldn't automatically call this good news. Lower CapEx reduces financing requirements, but it also delays projects and potentially slows future rate-base growth. Management has withdrawn its previous 2028–2030 long-term capital and growth outlook while the strategic review continues.

The company has also targeted 2–4% reductions in nonfuel O&M expenses. I want to see those savings show up in actual earnings, rather than simply taking management's targets at face value.

There is, however, one encouraging financing detail from the latest earnings call.

Management said the equity financing required under its original $73B capital plan had already been addressed and that it does not expect additional equity issuance through 2030 under the strategic options currently being evaluated. CFO Carolyn Burke also explicitly stated that issuing equity at the current stock price was not an option.

That's meaningful. It changes how I think about the near-term dilution risk.

It doesn't eliminate every possibility of future dilution. A major wildfire event, material cost overruns or a deterioration in credit conditions could change the financing equation. But I would rather assess PCG using management's latest financing plan than continue assuming routine equity issuance.

For a company with this much investment ahead of it, I care about per-share earnings growth, not just growth in total net income.

A potential demand tailwind: data centers

There is another development worth watching.

PG&E has a 12.87 GW data center development pipeline. Of that, 3.88 GW is in final engineering, while management is targeting approximately 1.8 GW of potential data center demand online by 2030. The company has energized 174 MW since 2024.

These numbers should not be confused. The 12.87 GW is a development pipeline, not committed or energized capacity. The 1.8 GW is management's stated target for projects online by 2030.

Still, I find the economics interesting.

Management estimates that every additional 1 GW of properly priced data center load could reduce existing customers' electricity bills by 1% or more. Large-load customers can help spread the fixed costs of the grid across a broader customer base.

This could help address one of the biggest constraints facing California utilities: affordability.

If the projects actually connect, make meaningful financial commitments and pay rates that cover the incremental infrastructure costs, they could create a useful demand tailwind without relying entirely on higher bills for existing residential customers.

It is not a guaranteed benefit, but it gives PG&E another potential way to support infrastructure investment while addressing regulatory concerns.

At approximately $13.25, PCG trades at roughly 10.2x TTM GAAP earnings and 7.4x the midpoint of its 2027 core EPS guidance of $1.80. Price-to-book is approximately 0.84x.

Those multiples are making it more interesting.

I distinguish between what PG&E might eventually be worth if the strategic review succeeds and what I am willing to pay today for a 15% annualized return. Those are not the same thing. 

A successful turnaround could justify a materially higher valuation, but I don't want to pay upfront for regulatory reform, a potential gas separation or a credit-rating recovery that hasn't happened yet.

But I think it's important to understand why the market applies a discount. Investors aren't simply concerned about the next wildfire. They're also pricing in uncertainty around liability, financing costs, regulatory recovery and whether the company can turn its investment program into sustainable per-share earnings.

I would not automatically apply the 15x–17x forward P/E multiples seen across some regulated utility peers to PCG. The company's liability framework, parent-level credit profile and capital structure deserve a discount.

The question is how much of that discount can be removed if management executes the strategic review, improves credit metrics and demonstrates that new capital investment is producing sustainable earnings.

Why I'm interested?

I think there are three potential sources of value here.

First, the underlying regulated infrastructure business has an opportunity to grow its rate base through necessary investment in the California grid.

Second, the current holding-company structure may be imposing a financing penalty on businesses, particularly the gas business, that do not carry the same direct wildfire exposure. Ring-fencing or a regulator-approved separation could help unlock some of that value.

Third, a successful credit turnaround could lower financing costs and improve the economics of future investment. Data center load growth may provide an additional way to spread grid costs and support affordability.

None of these outcomes is guaranteed. They are also connected: a failed liability or restructuring effort could undermine the credit recovery, while affordability constraints could limit the rate-base opportunity.

The risks remain substantial: another major wildfire, regulatory disallowances, expensive financing, delayed projects and the possibility that capital investment doesn't translate into the returns investors expect.

I don't need wildfire risk to disappear. I need PG&E to become financially strong enough to manage it, and I need regulators to allow prudent investment to earn a reasonable return without making electricity unaffordable.

At approximately $13.25, I find the business interesting enough to consider a limited starter position. But I don't consider it a deep-value bargain, and I won't average down blindly. 

The real question is whether PG&E can separate the value of its infrastructure from the wildfire risk discount attached to its corporate structure — without simply transferring the financial burden to customers or existing shareholders.

That's the investment I'm trying to underwrite.

Onto the next one.

text:
Blue City Blues
After the elation of Election Day, reality checks on Democratic governance.

If Democrats can learn to govern as well as they campaign, America could be entering a new golden age. In last week’s elections Democrats won historic victories in places where their party has long been in the political wilderness. Dimming the optimism this week are reminders of the continuing dysfunction in areas where Democrats have long exercised control.

On Monday this column noted the latest evidence of consumer and taxpayer suffering in the solid blue states of California, New Jersey and New York. Today’s news carries disturbing reports from cities where Democrats have been dominating for decades.

In the Windy City, Democratic mayors have been in charge for nearly a century. Now Fran Spielman reports for the Chicago Sun-Times:

The abrupt resignation on Friday of Mayor Brandon Johnson’s third chief financial officer in a year could trigger another drop in Chicago’s already shaky bond rating and scare investors away from the city’s bonds.

Ashlee Gabrysch’s departure sent shock waves through City Hall and beyond — her resignation comes in the middle of a budget stalemate, after just three months as CFO. Even more damaging than Gabrysch’s sudden exit is what she said on her way out the door…

“As the City of Chicago’s Chief Financial Officer, there is nothing more important than my fiduciary duty to the City and its taxpayers. The Chief Financial Officer’s statements about city finances are not idle chatter: they are relied upon by investors, ratings agencies, City Council, and taxpayers. The CFO must act scrupulously to ensure they are always accurate and complete,” Gabrysch said in a statement released to the media.

“Throughout my career, I have remained committed to upholding the highest standards of financial integrity and transparency, and in my short time as Chief Financial Officer, I have faithfully discharged this duty. It has become apparent, however, that to continue in this role would be to compromise my integrity and professional obligations. I therefore have concluded that I must step down from my role, and hereby tender my resignation.”

Ms. Gabrysch hasn’t detailed the particulars that made the job incompatible with her integrity. Given the expensive history of Chicago governance and the fact that she is the third person to quit the job in a year, this column will go out on a limb and guess that the eventual disclosure is not going to make taxpayers happy.

Meanwhile on the left coast, in another jurisdiction where Democrats dominate, there is a continuing failure that probably doesn’t get enough attention. 

This lack of attention stems in part from a kind of embarrassment of riches when it comes to government transportation boondoggles. The state of California’s shockingly expensive and unproductive pursuit of high-speed rail has obscured how badly California municipalities are botching their low-speed rail projects.

Colleen Shalby reports for the Los Angeles Times:

Credit agency Fitch Ratings has dealt another blow to the troubled Skylink people mover train at Los Angeles International Airport, downgrading the project’s debt deeper into junk bond territory over the continued inability of the contractor and city’s airport department to complete the project…

The $3.3-billion train is the most-anticipated feature of the airport’s $30-billion overhaul. It was initially slated to open in 2023 — before the World Cup and the Super Bowl and long before the 2028 Olympics. It’s now three years behind schedule and more than $1 billion beyond its original construction budget. 

When it does open, the airport said it will shuttle travelers between terminals, parking lots, the LAX/Metro Transit Center and a new ride-hail lot.

What has to be infuriating for airline customers is that this is not some bold attempt to do what’s never been done. Ms. Shalby reports:

[Fitch analyst Seth Lehman] noted that the train is hardly a novel project as many major airports have one, making the delays at LAX all the more confounding.

“Each time there’s a path towards opening, there’s a setback,” he said.

text:
Singularity Watch, Day 30 — November 14, 2026

The FAA Grounds U.S. Flights and Microsoft 365 Fails Worldwide as Starship Reaches Orbit

Infrastructure: A Nationwide Ground Stop

The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports on November 13 after communication problems hit multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers. The Verge reported the stop was issued at 2:44 PM CST and lifted at 7:15 PM CST, more than four hours later. [1][2]

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the trouble began at 2:36 PM CST, when switches and routers "got overloaded with data" and gave inconsistent radar and communications data. He said radar and communications were never completely lost, and called for $50 billion to modernize the air traffic control system. [3]

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was "zero evidence" so far of a cyberattack or a rogue AI system, without ruling either out, and that patches applied to the existing system sparked the problem. Two airline officials told Reuters the affected network is overseen by L3Harris. [3][2]

By late evening nearly 10,000 flights had been canceled, according to Flightradar24 data cited by Reuters. Reuters called it the longest shutdown since September 11, 2001; the only other nationwide ground stop since then was a 90-minute halt in January 2023. [3]

Ryan quoted a post that asked whether the stop was connected to other recent infrastructure disruptions, and wrote at 6:11 PM CST: "We are now in a perpetual cyber war. Build your defensive agent swarms now." That is his view; officials had found no evidence of an attack. [4][3]

Infrastructure: Microsoft 365 Down Into a Second Day

A global outage of Microsoft 365 email, cloud and AI services that began midday on November 12 was still ongoing on the morning of November 13. Microsoft said servers were failing automated health checks and becoming unavailable, which overloaded the rest, and that it had no evidence of malicious activity. [5]

Some servers became unresponsive again once traffic returned, and Microsoft extended email timeout to 48 hours to preserve delayed mail. Ars Technica reported disruptions to hospitals, banks, courts and government IT in Japan, and Ciaran Martin, former head of the UK's National Cyber Security Centre, told NBC News it looks like one of the biggest outages of all time. [5]

Responding at 4:23 AM CST to a post arguing that AI is too unreliable for mission-critical services, Ryan wrote: "other way around. humans are unreliable and should never be in the loop for mission critical services." [6]

Eric S. Raymond proposed the term "hot-state dependency" for systems that depend on state that cannot be reconstructed after an interruption, and argued for replayable logs of every change. Ryan quoted his definition at 3:00 PM CST and added: "Our society is like this." [7]

Space: Starship Reaches Orbit

Starship Flight 15 lifted off from Starbase, Texas at 4:48 PM CST on November 13 in SpaceX's first attempt to recover both stages at the launch tower. Super Heavy Booster 22 diverted from its planned tower catch and exploded as it came down offshore in the Gulf. [8]

Ship 42 reached orbit and deployed 26 Version 3 Starlink satellites. If systems remain healthy, it is scheduled to return to the launch site for a tower catch about 22.5 hours after launch, around 3:20 PM CST on November 14. [8]

Before launch, Will DePue wrote that a double catch would be one of the most important moments in the history of rocketry, and a SpaceXSI employee who works on Grok Bot wrote that another team was attempting to recover an entire orbital rocket. Ryan surfaced both. [9]

Autonomy: The Cybercab Goes on Sale

Tesla's Robotaxi account announced at 5:27 PM CST that select customers are being invited to buy the Cybercab for personal use. The order page lists $29,990 before taxes, a $1,000 non-refundable deposit, a required $299 monthly Autonomy Subscription with one month included, and estimated delivery in December 2026 in Austin. [10][11]

The two-seat car has no steering wheel or pedals. Electrek reported that it operates only inside Tesla's Robotaxi service areas in five Texas cities and three Florida cities. [10]

Ryan responded twice: "$30k? That's it? How do I get on this list?" and "Add me to the list plz." [11]

Austin's mayor, Kirk Watson, said on November 10 that planners will study extending the city's light rail project about 3 miles to the airport, an analysis expected to take nine to 12 months. Ryan wrote at 10:39 AM CST: "Light rail comes to Austin just as self-driving taxis makes it obsolete." [12]

Compute: Nvidia After Huang

A statement from Singapore's Ministry of Home Affairs, dated October 31, recirculated on November 13. It says neither the Singapore Government nor its officials told the Wall Street Journal they were concerned about Alice Huang's ties to Jensen Huang, and that no investigations were conducted in respect of her. It also says investigations into the data center company Megaspeed are ongoing. [13][14]

Brad Gerstner of Altimeter Capital and Gavin Baker of Atreides Management sent a letter to Nvidia's board asking for "a slow, measured, and deliberate process" on future leadership that leaves all options open, "including the potential return of Jensen Huang." The letter says the company will be capably led in the interim by Colette Kress. Ryan surfaced it. [15]

Balaji Srinivasan urged Nvidia employees, shareholders, partners and customers to press the board to reinstate Huang. A Financial Times opinion piece called Huang's fall an indictment of founder mode; Ryan called the post "the ultimate indictment of traditional media." The FT article itself could not be read. [16][17]

Labs: OpenAI Folds Robotics Into General Models

Fortune reported on November 13 that OpenAI has disbanded its stand-alone robotics team, moving robotics research under Chief Research Officer Mark Chen and the applied robotics and hardware teams under President Greg Brockman. OpenAI said robotics remains core to its long-term vision. [18]

OpenAI told Fortune that its general-purpose frontier models, including GPT-6 Astra, have shown they can be applied directly to robotics. Fortune cited an Nvidia study in which an Astra-powered agent reached a 74.8% success rate on a simulated manipulation benchmark, against 51.0% for the best specialized robotic models on that leaderboard. [18]

Andrew Curran wrote that Anthropic reported a similar sudden jump in robotics capability with Fable 5.2, and OpenAI's David Schnurr said robotics at OpenAI is "alive and well," with 15 open roles. Ryan surfaced these posts. [19]

Labs: Anthropic's Compute Dilemma

In interview clips Ryan surfaced, Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei called compute "the deepest business dilemma that the company faces." He said revenue grew roughly 10x in each of 2024 and 2025, while compute has to be bought a year or two ahead. [20]

Amodei said the biggest reason to go public now goes back to these compute bets: more cash gives a bigger buffer between the low-compute and high-compute worlds, so the company can invest in biology, robotics, cybersecurity and knowledge work. [20]

Training: Four Bits From Pretraining Through RL

Thinking Machines Lab published on November 13 how it trained Inkling 2 Small with a native 4-bit NVFP4 forward pass in its expert layers, from the start of pretraining through the final reinforcement learning rollout, on Nvidia GB300 systems. The lab says it is the largest model it knows of trained that way. [21][22]

The recipe gave an 8% wall-clock speedup in pretraining and a 20% speedup in RL over full MXFP8 training, at a cost of about 2% in pretraining compute efficiency. Inkling 2 Small was pretrained in 68 hours on GB300 NVL72 racks, where a similar model took several weeks months earlier. [21]

Agents: Grok Bot Joins Meetings

Grok Bot announced at 1:11 PM CST that it can now join meetings to answer questions, take on work and track team decisions. Sam Sokolin said Grok Bot harness optimizations shipped this week give about 7% more usage per plan and up to about 15% more on routine runs. A separate post reported that SpaceXSI is working on an unannounced "Bot Factory" that chains bots in a fixed order. [23]

The Information reported, in an article that could not be read but was summarized by https://t.co/GPC7zcWbsm, that SpaceX's AI group laid off about 60 employees working on Grok Imagine, its image and video generator, leaving a handful to maintain it as the company prioritizes AI coding tools and Grok Bot. Ryan wrote: "Imagine is cool. But coding is far, far more valuable." [24][25]

Ryan also wrote, "Don't be locked into one harness or model. Use all of them. Own your own workflows," and praised a developer's self-hosted agent app, Seneca, which its author said will be released under the MIT license next week. He surfaced a creator's Grok Bot video editing workflow that runs five stages on its own. [26]

Security: Hardware Isolation and Open Weights

Apple Security Research published Secure Exclaves on November 12: protected runtimes that process camera and microphone data apart from the rest of the system, so the main operating system, apps and Apple cannot access it. Apple said it will keep hardening the system with AI-accelerated vulnerability research and expanded formal verification. Ryan surfaced the post. [27][28]

Transformer reported that more than 6,500 models tagged abliterated, uncensored or heretic were on Hugging Face in July, and that Hugging Face removed one model marketed for offensive cyber use. An uploader of such models responded that abliteration only removes refusals, and that their Qwen3.8 Flash-Next model had about 358,000 downloads in 30 days. [29][30]

CodeRabbit said its Deep Scans of 1,125 public repositories produced 1,215 high or critical findings, 75 of them already fixed. Ryan also surfaced a post citing 61 working bug reproductions on a benchmark, quoting the launch of Breken, which tests systems against synthetic users, agents and failing services. [31][32]

Engineering: Software That Repairs Itself

Ryan's one original post of the day, at 7:28 AM CST, read "self-healing software is real." It showed an agent report of a near miss in which two sessions updated the same checkout, and an issue it filed for one safe update command that gives no reset advice. [33]

Work: Leverage

In a morning exchange about developers who say they no longer like their jobs because of AI, Ryan wrote that AI "is leverage for your mind" and "far more powerful than hand coding," and that "the goal is to solve more problems better, faster, cheaper." He endorsed a reply saying that with a good codebase and verification loop, Opus 5.5 writes better code than its author. [34]

Ryan wrote that a bot "will be the primary user interface for a computer moving foward," and answered a post saying there is more to life than shipping with "No there isn't. Keep shipping." [35]

Lenny Rachitsky reported that 15% of open tech roles are now in the Bay Area, a record, while just 14% offer a remote option, the lowest on record. Ryan surfaced the post. [36]

Medicine and Commerce

Ryan surfaced an interview in which Isomorphic Labs president Max Jaderberg described using AI to choose 20 or 50 molecules to test instead of screening hundreds of thousands. He also surfaced a post reporting that Shopify fine-tuned Qwen3-32B for its commerce assistant and found it 2.2 times faster and 68% cheaper than the closed model it replaced. [37]

text:
You built a business before entering politics. You produced something people chose to buy. That gives me some hope that you understand the difference between creating value and organising an expensive conference about the possibility of creating value.

I am asking you to call out the arrogance, waste and theatrical self importance that have become so exhausting in public life. 

This criticism applies across political parties. The ANC, DA, EFF, MK and every other party should face the same scrutiny. ActionSA must be included. Political loyalty should never oblige a citizen to applaud nonsense.

We are forever “going forwards.”

Going forwards to where? The next conference venue? The next five star lunch? Another dinner at which everyone solemnly agrees that further engagement is required?

The country is apparently going forwards while the waistline goes sideways.

Implementation remains uncertain. Lunch arrives punctually.

“His Excellency.” “The Honourable Member.” “Distinguished delegates.” “Esteemed colleagues.”

What an extraordinary amount of verbal polishing these people require.

Excellence should be evident in the work. Honour should be evident in the conduct. Yet parliamentary proceedings have included physical confrontations and violence, documented in Parliament’s own records. The titles become a rather expensive joke when the distinguished gentlemen need separating.

And let us dispense with the fantasy that office confers a superior category of human existence. After his lavish lunch, His Excellency sits on the toilet like everyone else. His digestive system has never read the protocol manual.

The same titles accomplish even less in the grave. A funeral programme may list twenty distinctions; mortality does not offer an executive exemption.

What matters is what a person did for the living.

Yet the machinery of government can become remarkably energetic when arranging honours for the dead. A parliamentary reply reported in 2020 disclosed R105.6 million spent on fifteen official funerals between February 2018 and February 2020. Those are historical figures, but they illustrate the scale that ceremonial spending can reach.

Honour the dead with dignity and restraint. Then show comparable urgency towards the pensioner trying to remain in her home, the hungry child and the household waiting for clean water.

A grand funeral cannot compensate for a neglected life.

When officials indulge in avoidable luxury while people struggle for food and shelter, I regard that as a form of moral treason, a betrayal of the public trust. The people whose labour sustains government should never become an inconvenience between courses.

Then there is the jargon.

“Strategic alignment.” “Institutional strengthening.” “Stakeholder engagement.” “Catalytic interventions.” “Implementation modalities.” “Unlocking synergies.” “An integrated roadmap.”

One can almost hear the announcement:

“The Distinguished Executive Keystone Round Table Subcommittee on Strategic Pipeline Coordination has resolved to establish a Cabinet Steering Mechanism to facilitate preliminary stakeholder engagement concerning the implementation framework for the way forward.”

A magnificent sentence. Nobody has repaired the pipe.

By the time the deputy chairperson has finished thanking the chairperson for recognising the deputy chairperson, the caterers have achieved the only measurable delivery target.

We hear about Cabinets, chairs, benches and round tables. After the Phala Phala controversy over foreign currency reportedly concealed in a sofa, even the upholstery acquired national political significance. South Africans could be forgiven for wanting less attention paid to the furniture and more to the people outside the room.

When a photograph shows a hundred officials assembled in a conference venue, publish the full bill underneath it. Flights, hotels, transport, security, catering, consultants and staff time. Explain why each person attended and what the gathering accomplished.

If the cost runs into millions, say so. Then explain its value to someone choosing between groceries and electricity.

A group photograph proves that people arrived. It does not prove that they governed.

Put routine meetings online. Circulate documents. Record decisions. Allocate responsibility. Set deadlines. Anyone proposing an expensive gathering should explain why the work requires it.

For perspective, the 2026/27 national budget allocates approximately R2.46 billion to VIP Protection Services alone. Expenditure on protection requires justification, and ordinary people are entitled to demand equal seriousness about their safety.

Cape Town deserves the same scrutiny as every other administration.

Consider the pensioner who bought a modest house decades ago, paid the bond, maintained the property and expected some security in retirement. The neighbourhood becomes more expensive. The valuation increases. The pensioner has sold nothing, received no windfall and gained no additional monthly income.

A valuation notice cannot buy groceries.

Property rates based on market value are authorised under national legislation. But that does not settle the question of affordability. A home can become more valuable while its owner becomes less able to meet monthly extortion bills. It is a thieving scam. Authorized theft really. 

Cape Town residents are being driven to sell because of rising rates and neighbourhood costs. Reporting from Woodstock and Salt River documented such accounts in 2017; more recent reporting records homeowners warning that higher municipal bills could force them out. These concerns should be investigated and measured, rather than dismissed as resistance to paying.

A person does not have to be physically evicted to be forced out economically. A sale may look voluntary on a transfer document while being the only remaining escape from extortion bills the owner cannot meet.

That distinction matters to the family packing its belongings.

Relief should be accessible, predictable and processed promptly. An elderly person should not need the administrative stamina of a tender consultant to obtain assistance. Its all more extortion upon extortion. An army of parasites. People just want to be left alone in old age. 

Unpaid municipal "debt" can ultimately lead to legal proceedings and a court authorised sale of property. A primary residence requires judicial scrutiny, including consideration of alternatives, but the risk of losing it is real. Courts are not clean either. So many examples of crooked judges. 

Paying off the bank should not be followed by permanent anxiety about whether municipal demands will make remaining in the home impossible.

And how does the VP afford to live in multiple mansions and pay all these rates based on his salary? What business did he start?

Against that background, spending priorities deserve relentless examination. Cape Town reported budgets of approximately R9.39 million for a synthetic pitch in Site B and R9.68 million for the synthetic pitch installation phase at Delft. Who gets the tenders for all this plastic crap? Why not build libraries and computer centres instead? 

When residents struggle to remain in their homes, officials must be prepared to defend the priority given to plastic playing surfaces. Publish the contractors, beneficial owners, competing bids, final expenditure, maintenance obligations and actual use.

Compare that expenditure with computer centres, workshop equipment, libraries, agricultural training and repairs to existing facilities. Explain the benefits in terms residents can inspect.

A pensioner cannot pay a municipal account with a photograph of a councillor opening a football field.

There is also a concrete legal record to confront. On 30 April 2026, the Western Cape High Court declared three Cape Town charges unlawful and invalid: the citywide cleaning charge and fixed water and sewerage charges calculated through property value bands. The order took effect at the end of June. It concerned those particular charges, rather than the general legality of property rates.

Residents should not have to fund litigation to establish the limits of powers exercised by an administration they already pay for.

Now consider executive remuneration.

Cape Town’s audited 2024/25 statements disclose annual remuneration of approximately R4.745 million for the city manager, R3.888 million for the finance executive and R3.756 million for the corporate services executive. Divided by twelve, those totals are approximately R395,000, R324,000 and R313,000 a month, including bonuses, contributions and other disclosed items.

Those figures demand an exceptionally convincing account of value.

Before another pensioner is told to tighten her belt, let the administration demonstrate restraint in its own expenditure. The instruction loses some authority when delivered from a particularly comfortable chair.

The same standard belongs at national level. Publish verified qualifications, relevant experience, performance records and the reasons for appointments. Winning an election does not confer engineering knowledge. Party seniority does not establish financial competence.

Anyone who has studied government should be especially embarrassed to govern badly.

Where political wealth cannot be reconciled with legitimate income, investigate it independently. What business produced the money? What investment generated the return? What financed the properties? What interests are held through companies or associates?

Recover stolen money and prosecute proven corruption. Party membership must provide no protection.

These are questions about human decisions and accountability. We need no supernatural explanation for greed or indifference.

Taxation itself deserves a more honest moral discussion.

For a working person, money often represents hours of finite life. A shift completed, a field planted, a machine repaired, a patient treated or a product manufactured. Behind the accounting entry stands somebody’s effort.

When public money is wasted, some of that effort has been wasted with it.

The monetary system can create banknotes and electronic balances. It cannot create food, houses, skilled labour or additional years of human life merely by entering numbers into a computer. Money creation also has economic consequences, including inflation risks.

Every public expense should therefore face a plain question: what useful result justifies taking this portion of someone else’s working life?

A functioning water system can answer. An effective emergency service can answer. An unnecessary entourage and another ceremonial dinner deserve a much more hostile examination.

Young people need credible reasons to believe that decades of work and saving can produce security. They deserve affordable routes into housing, useful education and honest retirement arrangements.

That does not justify predicting that every pension will collapse. It demands protection of savings, transparent fees and risks, and serious attention to purchasing power.

The two pot system did not itself slash existing pensioners’ payments. It allows eligible active members access to a savings component while preserving another component for retirement. The concern is what happens when financial distress repeatedly drives people to consume money intended for later life.

A country should be ashamed when retirement becomes an exercise in deciding which essential bill can remain unpaid.

Meanwhile, ordinary people face unreliable water, sewage pollution, violent crime, gangs, extortion, unemployment, infrastructure theft, deteriorating roads, housing shortages and pressure on clinics and public transport.

In June 2026, Parliament reported that 47% of wastewater systems were in a critical state. That calls for trained people, maintained equipment and competent management. An executive luncheon cannot disinfect sewage.

Our cities should be safe, clean and governed. Drug trafficking requires intelligence, evidence, arrests, prosecution, asset recovery and action against corrupt protectors. Nationality should provide neither immunity nor a substitute for evidence.

The army has already been deployed in support of SAPS against gangsterism and illegal mining, with 2,200 personnel authorised from March 2026 to March 2027. The public should be shown what lasting results that deployment produces.

Secure the borders. Enforce lawful entry requirements. Prosecute officials who sell access. Set immigration policy against demonstrated capacity in employment, housing and services, while maintaining lawful asylum procedures.

Education should be the foundation of rebuilding that capacity.

I mean education for every child, of every race, in wealthy suburbs, townships, rural villages and informal settlements. Practical competence must never become a lesser track reserved for poor children.

Teach strong literacy, mathematics, science and digital skills. Work towards proficiency in three languages. Equip schools with workshops, computer centres, libraries and productive gardens.

By eighteen, learners should have encountered at least ten credible occupational pathways: crop production, plumbing, electrical installation, welding, carpentry, bricklaying, road construction, motor mechanics, refrigeration and electronics repair.

Give them useful foundations and clear routes into apprenticeships and specialised training. Where two years is sufficient, make it accessible. Where longer training or certification is required, provide a proper route.

Let children grow potatoes, mielies and vegetables. Teach soil, irrigation, harvesting, storage and costing. Give them supervised experience with tools, pumps, pipes, construction and electrical principles.

Literature can enrich a life. Practical competence helps sustain one. No learner should leave years of schooling unable to read confidently, calculate accurately or identify a realistic route into useful work.

The objective should be a generation capable of doing more than completing applications and waiting.

Mr Mashaba, I am asking you to confront the documented failures plainly. The financial statements, court judgments and public reports can be examined. The satire should never become an excuse for avoiding the substance.

Apply the same standard inside your own party.

Apartheid institutionalised racial oppression. Present leaders must answer for their own conduct. No political history, skin colour or party emblem confers permanent immunity from criticism.

People of every race have a common interest in opposing corruption, arrogance and the misuse of their labour and trust.

The country needs fundamental changes in appointments, spending, accountability and education. Another slogan will not suffice. Neither will another photograph of well fed officials applauding a declaration of their intention to become more concerned.

I regard that performance as clowning because it substitutes ceremony for competence and demands reverence for the substitution.

The tragedy is that people can lose years, savings and homes while the performance continues.

Honour the dead with restraint. Serve the living with urgency.

Let “excellent” describe the work and “honourable” describe the conduct.

And before the next committee goes forwards to lunch, require it to explain what it has actually done.

text:
LETTERS FROM STOCKHOLM
Nigeria Has the Talent. Why Do We Keep Recycling Failure?
By Kio Amachree

Nigeria is approaching a quarter of a billion people, yet we are continually asked to believe that our future depends on the same small circle of political veterans, power brokers and professional survivors. UNFPA put our population at 237.5 million in 2025. Among so many Nigerians, are we seriously expected to believe that this is the best leadership we can produce?
I refuse to believe it.

I know Nigerian men and women whose education, sophistication, experience and judgement would put much of our political establishment to shame. Friends and members of my own family have managed complex institutions, built businesses and earned international respect. Nigeria invested heavily in developing generations of capable people. Too many now serve the rest of the world while their own country remains trapped in the politics of patronage.

Nobody can repair Nigeria with a wave of the hand. But there are Nigerians who understand what competent government requires—and who would approach the responsibility with considerably more seriousness than the familiar faces demanding another opportunity.

My objection to the present assortment of presidential hopefuls is straightforward: too many offer the same old song and dance. New campaign colours, new alliances, new slogans—and the same exhausted political habits.

I have lived long enough, and known enough Nigerian leaders personally, to recognise the difference between public responsibility and naked ambition.

I grew up around members of the old northern establishment. General Hassan Usman Katsina taught me polo in 1968. Later, when I was at Eton, he visited to see how I was progressing with my studies.

He had more important official responsibilities than checking on a Nigerian schoolboy. Yet he understood that my education carried an obligation beyond personal advancement. In his eyes, a young Nigerian entering an institution associated with the British governing establishment was also representing his country.

Eton was founded in 1440 and has educated twenty British prime ministers. During my years there, its history already stretched back more than five centuries. For a newly independent African country, having its children enter such institutions carried considerable symbolic weight.

As I remember it, General Gowon and General Hassan Katsina wanted to ensure that the Amachree boy did not let Nigeria down.

I also remember the uproar when another Nigerian pupil left the school unexpectedly. General Hassan’s reaction, in my recollection, was fierce. He regarded the matter as an embarrassment to the country and summoned the boy’s father for a dressing-down at the Lagos Polo Club.

The message was unmistakable: opportunity came with responsibility.

I was also close to Umaru Shinkafi and knew other prominent northerners. These relationships gave me a view of an establishment that understood authority, preparation and the weight of national office.

That generation had its failures. Military government deserves scrutiny, and personal affection cannot erase history. But I remember individuals who believed that Nigeria’s reputation mattered and that those entrusted with opportunity had a duty to justify it.

Today, I too often see political survival presented as statesmanship.

Where is the presidential quality? Where is the seriousness? Where is the willingness to tell powerful friends that the public purse belongs to the public?

Ali Modu Sheriff’s place in Tinubu’s political operation illustrates my frustration with the endless recycling. Sheriff, a former governor of Borno, has been reported campaigning for Tinubu’s re-election. Nigerians are entitled to ask what this familiar alliance offers beyond the preservation of established political networks.

A photograph beside a president is no substitute for an account of a politician’s record.

Then there is the tribal poison.

As a man with a Yoruba mother and an Ijaw father, I find the ethnic policing of political opinion particularly absurd. Criticise Tinubu and some supporters immediately decide that you must be Igbo—as though an Igbo identity were an accusation and a Yoruba identity required obedience.

I have received vile insults directed at my late parents. I have received threats from people presenting themselves as Yoruba defenders of Tinubu. Some messages are so repulsive that I will not reproduce them.

Those responsible must answer for their conduct. They cannot claim to speak for an entire people, and I will not surrender my mother’s heritage to political bullies.

But I will say this plainly: leaders who benefit from ethnic intimidation have a responsibility to confront it unequivocally.

The intimidation of Igbo and other non-Yoruba voters in Lagos is documented. The United States’ human-rights reporting on the 2023 elections described threats against ethnic Igbo voters and the obstruction of non-Yoruba voters at polling stations. Human Rights Watch likewise recorded election violence and failures by security personnel to protect voters.

This is a national disgrace.

No Nigerian should have to establish an ancestral claim to a city before exercising a constitutional right there. No political party owns Lagos. No ethnic group owns the presidency. Citizenship must mean something wherever a Nigerian chooses to live.

My standards also apply to the opposition.

I have been abused by supporters of Peter Obi because I question what I regard as his excessively cautious approach to entrenched power. Supporting an opposition candidate does not require surrendering one’s judgement.

Obi must explain how he intends to confront the machinery of corruption. Nigerians need more than a reassuring personality. We need an operational plan: independent investigations, transparent procurement, protected witnesses, credible prosecutions and consequences that reach powerful people.

The reported attack surrounding the ADC gathering in Benin City in February 2026 underlines the danger of political intimidation. Police confirmed an attack on the party secretariat and reported damage at John Odigie-Oyegun’s residence; Obi’s representatives described gunmen following the politicians. Responsibility must be established through investigation, but the need for protection and accountability is already clear.

A reforming president must be relentless within the law. Courage must translate into institutions strong enough to confront people accustomed to escaping consequences.

Consider Gilbert Chagoury.

His business interests and proximity to successive Nigerian governments deserve sustained scrutiny. Bloomberg reported that the Lagos–Calabar coastal highway, then estimated at $13 billion, was awarded to Hitech, a company owned by Chagoury, a longstanding Tinubu ally.

Then came the GCON, Nigeria’s second-highest national honour, reported in January 2026. Premium Times also recounted Chagoury’s 2000 Swiss conviction for money laundering and aiding a criminal organisation.

What message does this send about the standards Nigeria rewards?

The relevant questions concern access, competition, public value and accountability. Publish the contracts. Explain the procurement decisions. Disclose relevant ownership interests. Demonstrate that the public received value for money.

I want to hear that demand clearly from anyone asking to become president, including Peter Obi.

And to those who behave as though office guarantees lifelong immunity, I suggest studying what has happened elsewhere.

Isabel dos Santos once appeared almost inseparable from Angola’s ruling establishment. A British court nevertheless imposed a worldwide freezing order covering up to £580 million of her assets, and her appeal was dismissed in September 2024. Britain subsequently imposed an asset freeze and travel ban under its anti-corruption sanctions regime. She disputes allegations of wrongdoing.

A freezing order is distinct from confiscation or a criminal conviction. But its practical lesson is clear: political influence at home does not guarantee unrestricted access to wealth abroad.

Charles Taylor offers a different example involving international crimes. The former Liberian president was convicted by the Special Court for Sierra Leone and sentenced to fifty years’ imprisonment. His former office did not prevent his trial.

These cases involve different laws and circumstances. Neither makes the arrest of any Nigerian politician inevitable. They do demonstrate why powerful people should be cautious about assuming that accountability can always be postponed until it disappears.

To Tinubu, Wike, David Umahi, the Senate leadership and every other holder of public authority, my message is simple: exercise power as though your decisions may one day be examined independently.

Contracts leave records. Financial transfers leave records. Public statements survive their speakers’ convenience.

I will continue watching the Washington litigation concerning records associated with the investigation in which Tinubu was named. Judge Beryl Howell’s October 30, 2026 opinion concerns access to FBI and DEA investigative material under freedom-of-information law. It is a disclosure case, rather than a criminal conviction, and its significance should be assessed through the actual court record. Nigerians deserve access to whatever the law requires to be disclosed.

We do not need invented intelligence dossiers to demand accountability. The documented questions are serious enough.

And we certainly do not lack examples of Nigerian ability.

My cousin Adebayo Ogunlesi helped build Global Infrastructure Partners into a business acquired by BlackRock in a transaction announced at approximately $12.5 billion and completed in October 2024. He subsequently joined BlackRock’s board and was appointed to OpenAI’s board in January 2025.

Here is a Nigerian whose judgement has been entrusted with major international responsibilities.

Business success alone does not establish fitness for the presidency. But Ogunlesi’s career exposes the absurdity of pretending that Nigeria lacks people capable of operating at the highest level.

We produce them. We educate them. We export them.

Then our political system too often rewards the people most skilled at controlling delegates, assembling patronage networks and financing the next campaign.

Why should Nigerians accept this?

I will support a candidate who makes clear commitments to the Nigerian people: open public contracting, independent law enforcement, credible elections, protection against political violence, and appointments based on competence.

That candidate must also explain how those commitments will survive pressure from financiers, party elders and personal friends.

I want to know what happens when the investigation reaches your ally. What happens when the contract belongs to your sponsor? What happens when the thug threatening voters wears your party’s colours?

Your answer to those questions tells me more than a hundred campaign speeches.

I have defended Nigerian unity because I believe our diversity can be a source of strength. But unity requires a functioning bargain between citizens and the state.

People cannot be asked indefinitely to endure insecurity, humiliation and deprivation while being lectured about the sanctity of a national arrangement that fails to protect them.

Another decade of this behaviour would deepen the damage to the Nigerian idea itself.

Those of us who believe in the country should be the most demanding of its leaders. Our commitment deserves a government that makes belonging worthwhile.

Nigeria has the people. Nigeria has the ability. Nigeria has citizens who understand service and responsibility.

The political establishment must stop treating those citizens as spectators while the same exhausted actors divide the stage.

I am tired of being offered another version of failure and told to call it hope.

Kio Amachree
Letters from Stockholm — The Kio Solution

text:
Chuck Noll Built Winners Before He Built Champions

Chuck Noll didn’t arrive in Pittsburgh to win headlines. He arrived to build something that would last.

When he took over the Steelers in 1969, the franchise was one of the league’s worst. He went 1-13 in his first season. By most standards, he should’ve been under pressure. Instead, he stayed committed to an idea that ran counter to the NFL’s impatience: winning follows people, not the other way around.

Noll believed you had to build winners before you could build champions. Talent mattered, but character and reliability mattered more. That belief shaped the draft boards and the locker room.
He didn’t coach with volume or theatrics. He treated players like adults and expected the same in return. Mean Joe Greene could be Mean Joe. Jack Lambert could be intense. Terry Bradshaw could grow at his own pace. As long as they did their jobs, Noll let them be themselves. The team always came first.

The early years were hard. But he drafted, developed, taught, and waited. The result was one of the most complete rosters the league has ever seen and four Super Bowls in six seasons. The titles weren’t the point. They were the proof.

What Noll created wasn’t just a dynasty. It was a self-sustaining culture. Players owned the standard. Success became normal.

In today’s NFL, where noise often substitutes for leadership, Chuck Noll’s approach still looks almost radical. He showed that you don’t build champions by chasing wins. You build them by first building winners.

text:
This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.

Many people in AI will be familiar with the story of the Mechanical Turk. It was a chess-playing machine built in 1770, and it was so good its opponents were tricked into believing it was supernaturally powerful. In reality, the machine had space for a human to hide in it and control it. The hoax went on for 84 years. That’s three generations! 

History is rich with examples of people trying to breathe life into inanimate objects, and of people selling hacks and tricks as “magic.” But this very human desire to believe in consciousness in machines has never matched up with reality. 

Creating consciousness in artificial intelligence systems is the dream of many technologists. Large language models are the latest example of our quest for clever machines, and some people (contentiously) claim to have seen glimmers of consciousness in conversations with them. The point is: machine consciousness is a hotly debated topic. Plenty of experts say it is doomed to remain science fiction forever, but others argue it’s right around the corner.

For the latest edition of MIT Technology Review, neuroscientist Grace Huckins explores what consciousness research in humans can teach us about AI, and the moral problems that AI consciousness would raise. Read more here.

We don’t fully understand human consciousness, but neuroscientists do have some clues about how it’s manifested in the brain, Grace writes. To state the obvious, AI systems don’t have brains, so it’s impossible to use traditional methods of measuring brain activity for signs of life. But neuroscientists have various different theories about what consciousness in AI systems might look like. Some treat it as a feature of the brain’s “software,” while others tie it more squarely to physical hardware.

There have even been attempts to create tests for AI consciousness. Susan Schneider, director of the Center for the Future Mind at Florida Atlantic University, and Princeton physicist Edwin Turner have developed one, which requires an AI agent to be isolated from any information about consciousness it could’ve picked up during its training before it’s tested. This step is important so that it can’t just parrot human statements it’s picked up about consciousness during training, as a large language model would.  

The tester then asks the AI questions it should only be able to answer if it is itself conscious. Can it understand the plot of the movie Freaky Friday, where a mother and daughter switch bodies, their consciousnesses dissociated from their physical selves? Can it grasp the concept of dreaming—or even report dreaming itself? Can it conceive of reincarnation or an afterlife?

Of course, this test is not foolproof. It requires its subject to be able to use language, so babies and animals—manifestly conscious beings—would not pass the test. And language-based AI models will have been exposed to the concept of consciousness in the vast amount of internet data they have been trained on. 

So how will we really know if an AI system is conscious? A group of neuroscientists, philosophers, and AI researchers, including Turing Prize winner Yoshua Bengio, have put out a white paper that proposes practical ways to detect AI consciousness based on a variety of theories from different fields. They propose a sort of report card for different markers, such as flexibly pursuing goals and interacting with an external environment, that would indicate AI consciousness—if the theories hold true. None of today’s systems tick any boxes, and it’s unclear if they ever will. 

Here is what we do know. Large language models are extremely good at predicting what the next word in a sentence should be. They are also very good at making connections between things—sometimes in ways that surprise us and make it easy to believe in the illusion that these computer programs might have sparks of something else. But we know remarkably little about AI language models’ inner workings. Until we know more about exactly how and why these systems come to the conclusions they do, it’s hard to say that the models’ outcomes are not just fancy math. 

Deeper Learning

How AI could supercharge battery research

We need better batteries if electric vehicles are going to achieve their potential of nudging fossil-fuel-powered cars off the roads. The problem is that there are a million different potential materials, and combinations of materials, we could use to make these batteries. It’s very labor-intensive and expensive to do rounds and rounds of trial and error. 

Enter AI: Startup Aionics is using AI tools to help researchers find better battery chemistries faster. It uses machine learning to sort through the wide range of material options and suggest combinations. Generative AI can also help researchers design new materials more quickly. Read more from Casey Crownhart in her weekly newsletter, The Spark, on the tech that could solve the climate crisis.

Bits and Bytes

Big Tech struggles to turn AI hype into profits
Microsoft has reportedly lost money on one of its first generative AI products. And it’s not alone: the other tech giants are equally struggling to find a way to capitalize on their massive investment in generative AI, which is eye-wateringly expensive to train and run. (The Wall Street Journal) 

How AI reduces the world to stereotypes
Rest of World analyzed 3,000 AI-generated images of different countries and cultures, and found they portray the world in a deeply stereotypical way. No surprises there, but this visual piece neatly shows just how deeply ingrained biases are in AI systems. (Rest of World) 

Even Google insiders are questioning the usefulness of the Bard chatbot
Glad to know it’s not just me! In leaked messages from an official invite-only Discord chat, Google product managers and designers share their skepticism about the utility of the company’s AI chatbot Bard, considering that the system makes things up. Google insiders seem to think it is best for creative uses, brainstorming, or coding—and even then, it needs lots of supervision. (Bloomberg)

The US is mulling escalating its AI tech blockade on China
Anxious about the prospect of China gaining AI supremacy, the UA has been limiting its access to the computer chips needed to power AI. The US is now considering escalating its blockade and restricting China’s access to a broad category of general-purpose AI programs, not just physical parts. (The Atlantic) 

How a billionaire-backed network of AI advisors took over Washington
The little-known Horizon Institute for Public Service, a nonprofit created in 2022, is funding salaries of people working in key Senate offices, agencies, and think tanks. The group is pushing to put the existential risk posed by AI at the top of Washington’s agenda, which could benefit AI companies with ties to the network. 
(Politico)

Google offers to pay its customers’ legal feel in generative AI lawsuits
Google has joined Microsoft and Getty Images in promising to cough up legal fees if its customers get sued over the outputs of its generative AI models or the training data they use. This is a smart move from Big Tech, as it could help persuade organizations that are hesitating to adopt these companies’ AI tools until there is more legal clarity over copyright and AI. (Google)

My first marriage lasted less than five years. I raised my daughter on my own. When she moved out, I bought a tiny rice cooker and made breakfast in it for a week straight because I liked that it could make just enough for me.

On our second date, my new husband noticed that I’d stopped eating because my food was too spicy. He offered to switch plates. I remember how good it felt to have someone notice.

Living together, I started noticing things too. The way he shut a cupboard. How long he took to answer. One Sunday we’d planned to go to a diner. I put on my coat and asked if he was ready.

“If you’re in such a hurry, go by yourself.”

I took my coat off. I was already thinking about what the house would feel like when I came back.

My daughter reminded me of the last time she’d visited. My husband had gone to bed. She made a joke and I shushed her.

“At your old place, I could show up at eleven and you’d put a pot on.”

text:
Britain, Russia and the Dangerous Art of Waking Up Too Late

After four and a half years of war in Ukraine, Defence Secretary @wesstreeting discovers the virtues of talking to Moscow. But what of Britain's own neglected defences - and the price of a foreign policy that has too often confused military commitment with military preparedness?

There is something peculiarly British about discovering the wisdom of diplomacy only after spending several years helping to supply the weapons of war. It is rather like remembering the importance of the fire brigade after the house has caught alight - and then congratulating oneself for discovering the telephone.

And so, we come to Mr. Wes Streeting, His Majesty's Secretary of State for Defence, who has informed the Financial Times @FT that Britain and Russia ought to establish fresh channels of communication, particularly between their respective armed forces, to avoid what he describes as the danger of miscalculation. ¹

Well, one can hardly disagree.

Indeed, I would go considerably further. Such communication is not merely desirable; it is an elementary requirement of responsible statecraft, particularly when two nuclear-armed powers find themselves confronting one another across an increasingly dangerous European security landscape.

What is remarkable is not that Mr. Streeting has finally arrived at this conclusion, but that it has taken so long for the British Government to recognize the obvious.

In explaining the dangers posed by Moscow, Mr. Streeting declared:

"We have seen over the course of this year numerous examples of what some people call hybrid threats, and I prefer to call state-sponsored terrorism."¹

Strong words, certainly. But strong words are no substitute for a coherent national defence policy.

One must wonder what Mr. Streeting thinks he and, indeed, His Majesty's Government  (HMG) have been doing while committing substantial sums of British taxpayers' money, military equipment and political capital to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's war effort over the past four and a half years. ²

Russia's invasion of #Ukraine in February 2022 was an act of aggression, and Ukraine is entitled to defend itself. That much should be beyond serious dispute. But supporting Ukraine does not absolve Westminster of its first and overriding responsibility - the defence of the United Kingdom and its people.

And here lies the uncomfortable question that Mr. Streeting and his colleagues would rather not have asked.

What has become of Britain's own ability to defend itself?

For years, successive governments have presided over the contraction of the British Army, persistent personnel shortages, procurement difficulties and the enormous financial pressures confronting the Royal Navy and Royal Air Force. ³

The #Army has struggled to retain sufficient manpower. The #Navy must balance extensive operational commitments against the availability of ships, submarines and crews. The #RAF, meanwhile, faces its own challenges in sustaining personnel, aircraft availability and the capabilities required of a modern fighting force. ³ ⁴

None of these problems began with the war in Ukraine, nor can they all be attributed to assistance given to Kyiv. They are the cumulative consequences of political decisions made in Westminster over many years, by governments of more than one political persuasion.

Yet the contradictions are becoming impossible to overlook.

Britain has been prepared to make substantial military commitments abroad while struggling to ensure that its own armed forces possess the personnel, equipment, ammunition stocks and industrial capacity necessary to sustain a major conflict. ² ³

It is one thing to proclaim Britain's determination to confront #Russian aggression. It is quite another to possess the military strength to make that determination credible.

The distinction is not academic. It is the difference between deterrence and wishful thinking.

And if the events of the past four and a half years have taught us anything, it is surely that wars do not obey the confident predictions of politicians, nor do they end merely because ministers insist that the right side must prevail.

Mr. Streeting is therefore right to seek renewed military communication with Moscow. It is long overdue, and it should be welcomed.

But diplomacy cannot be treated as an admission of weakness, any more than military assistance to #Ukraine should be regarded as proof of national strength.

The purpose of maintaining contact with an adversary is not to approve of his actions. It is to prevent an accident, misunderstanding, or reckless military encounter from turning an already dangerous confrontation into something infinitely worse.

During the Cold War, when the world lived beneath the permanent shadow of nuclear annihilation, Washington and Moscow understood that communication between enemies was sometimes more important than conversation between friends.

The alternative was to leave the fate of millions to chance, confusion or the judgement of a frightened military commander.

That is precisely the danger Mr. Streeting now acknowledges. ¹

But there is an even larger question, and it concerns not #Moscow, #Kyiv or #Brussels, but #London.

When is His Majesty's Government (HMG) going to wake up to the reality that Britain's national security cannot be maintained by grand declarations, overseas commitments and an increasingly strained military establishment?

A country that aspires to exercise influence over the course of a European war must first possess the means to defend its own territory, safeguard its maritime approaches, protect its airspace and sustain its armed forces should the unthinkable become reality.

Our soldiers, sailors and airmen deserve better than political rhetoric unsupported by adequate resources.

And the British public deserves something more substantial than a government that warns of the approach of war while continuing to wrestle with the consequences of decades of inadequate defence planning. ⁵

Mr. Streeting's proposal is sensible. I welcome it without reservation.

But the Defence Secretary should understand that opening a channel to #Moscow is only one part of his responsibility. The other, and arguably the more urgent, is ensuring that #Britain possesses armed forces sufficiently strong, properly equipped and adequately funded to make both diplomacy and deterrence effective.

For diplomacy without credible defence risks becoming supplication, while military posturing without diplomacy risks becoming catastrophe.

Britain needs neither.

It needs prudence, strength, restraint and a government capable of distinguishing between the defence of the national interest and the pursuit of international applause.

And perhaps, before the next great European crisis arrives at our doorstep, somebody in #Whitehall might finally remember an elementary truth:

The first duty of His Majesty's Government (#HMG) is not to defend Zelenskyy's war machine, nor its own reputation for doing so, but to defend the people of Britain at home.

That, Mr. Streeting, is where national security begins.
