Why the US Treasurys 57.2 Billion Dollar Bill Issuance Weighed on Semiconductors and Bitcoin This Week

Behind the simultaneous pullback in semiconductor stocks and Bitcoin over recent weeks lies a mechanical drain on market liquidity driven by heavy US Treasury bill issuance. According to Wall Street liquidity tracking data, the US Treasury settled a combined 57.2 billion dollars in net new Treasury bills across just two sessions this week, pulling 34.2 billion dollars out of the market on Tuesday November 10 and another 23.0 billion dollars on Thursday November 12. When banks and money market funds wire cash to settle net new government debt, dollar liquidity is drained directly out of private financial markets and locked inside the Treasury General Account TGA, leaving far less dry powder for risk assets.

In fact, the current wave of net Treasury bill issuance that began on October 1 aligns almost to the day with the correction in tech equities and crypto.

Since the Treasury resumed net positive bill issuance at the start of October to rebuild its cash balance, the Nasdaq 100 has dropped more than 10%, the flagship VanEck Semiconductor ETF SMH has fallen over 20%, and Bitcoin has retreated from the 85,000 dollar range toward the 73,000 dollar level. Because short term Treasury bills offer risk free yields near 5% with zero price volatility, weeks with massive auction settlements consistently prompt institutional desks to trim high beta semiconductor stocks and non yielding crypto holdings to absorb the incoming supply of government paper.

A look at daily market performance over the past year shows just how heavily these Treasury settlement days dictate asset returns.

Across the 70 trading sessions over the past 12 months that featured net positive Treasury bill settlements, the semiconductor ETF SMH generated a cumulative return of just 2.3%. Across the remaining 182 trading days where there was no net bill drain or where net redemptions returned cash to the system, SMH surged a cumulative 37.8%. Regardless of how strong corporate earnings are, high beta assets struggle to advance on days when the government is vacuuming cash out of the financial plumbing, while virtually all of the markets gains occur once that drain pauses.

The encouraging detail for investors is that this weeks 57.2 billion dollar settlement marks the peak of the current issuance wave.

According to Treasury borrowing schedules, the cycle is set to flip back toward net bill redemptions starting in late November and running through December, which will push cash out of the Treasury account and back into private money markets. Ultimately, the frustrating six week slide across semiconductors and Bitcoin reflects a temporary dollar liquidity squeeze rather than broken fundamentals, setting the stage for a sharp relief recovery once the Treasury cash drain reverses heading into December.

This story is from The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.

It’s done. It’s over. Two and a half years after it was first introduced—after months of lobbying and political arm-wrestling, plus grueling final negotiations that took nearly 40 hours—EU lawmakers have reached a deal over the AI Act. It will be the world’s first sweeping AI law. 

The AI Act was conceived as a landmark bill that would mitigate harm in areas where using AI poses the biggest risk to fundamental rights, such as health care, education, border surveillance, and public services, as well as banning uses that pose an “unacceptable risk.” 

“High risk” AI systems will have to adhere to strict rules that require risk-mitigation systems, high-quality data sets, better documentation, and human oversight, for example. The vast majority of AI uses, such as recommender systems and spam filters, will get a free pass. 

The AI Act is a major deal in that it will introduce important rules and enforcement mechanisms to a hugely influential sector that is currently a Wild West. 

Here are MIT Technology Review’s key takeaways: 

1. The AI Act ushers in important, binding rules on transparency and ethics

Tech companies love to talk about how committed they are to AI ethics. But when it comes to concrete measures, the conversation dries up. And anyway, actions speak louder than words. Responsible AI teams are often the first to see cuts during layoffs, and in truth, tech companies can decide to change their AI ethics policies at any time. OpenAI, for example, started off as an “open” AI research lab before closing up public access to its research to protect its competitive advantage, just like every other AI startup. 

The AI Act will change that. The regulation imposes legally binding rules requiring tech companies to notify people when they are interacting with a chatbot or with biometric categorization or emotion recognition systems. It’ll also require them to label deepfakes and AI-generated content, and design systems in such a way that AI-generated media can be detected. This is a step beyond the voluntary commitments that leading AI companies made to the White House to simply develop AI provenance tools, such as watermarking. 

The bill will also require all organizations that offer essential services, such as insurance and banking, to conduct an impact assessment on how using AI systems will affect people’s fundamental rights. 

2. AI companies still have a lot of wiggle room

When the AI Act was first introduced, in 2021, people were still talking about the metaverse. (Can you imagine!) 

Fast-forward to now, and in a post-ChatGPT world, lawmakers felt they had to take so-called foundation models—powerful AI models that can be used for many different purposes—into account in the regulation. This sparked intense debate over what sorts of models should be regulated, and whether regulation would kill innovation. 

The AI Act will require foundation models and AI systems built on top of them to draw up better documentation, comply with EU copyright law, and share more information about what data the model was trained on. For the most powerful models, there are extra requirements. Tech companies will have to share how secure and energy efficient their AI models are, for example. 

But here’s the catch: The compromise lawmakers found was to apply a stricter set of rules to only the most powerful AI models, as categorized by the computing power needed to train them. And it will be up to companies to assess whether they fall under stricter rules. 

A European Commission official would not confirm whether the current cutoff would capture powerful models such as OpenAI’s GPT-4 or Google’s Gemini, because only the companies themselves know how much computing power was used to train their models. The official did say that as the technology develops, the EU could change the way it measures how powerful AI models are. 

3. The EU will become the world’s premier AI police

The AI Act will set up a new European AI Office to coordinate compliance, implementation, and enforcement. It will be the first body globally to enforce binding rules on AI, and the EU hopes this will help it become the world’s go-to tech regulator. The AI Act’s governance mechanism also includes a scientific panel of independent experts to offer guidance on the systemic risks AI poses, and how to classify and test models. 

The fines for noncompliance are steep: from 1.5% to 7% of a firm’s global sales turnover, depending on the severity of the offense and size of the company. 

Europe will also become the one of the first places in the world where citizens will be able to launch complaints about AI systems and receive explanations about how AI systems came to the conclusions that affect them. 

By becoming the first to formalize rules around AI, the EU retains its first-mover advantage. Much like the GDPR, the AI Act could become a global standard. Companies elsewhere that want to do business in the world’s second-largest economy will have to comply with the law. The EU’s rules also go a step further than ones introduced by the US, such as the White House executive order, because they are binding. 

4. National security always wins

Some AI uses are now completely banned in the EU: biometric categorization systems that use sensitive characteristics; untargeted scraping of facial images from the internet or CCTV footage to create facial recognition databases like Clearview AI; emotion recognition at work or in schools; social scoring; AI systems that manipulate human behavior; and AI that is used to exploit people’s vulnerabilities. 

Predictive policing is also banned, unless it is used with “clear human assessment and objective facts, which basically do not simply leave the decision of going after a certain individual in a criminal investigation only because an algorithm says so,” according to an EU Commission official.

However, the AI Act does not apply to AI systems that have been developed exclusively for military and defense uses. 

One of the bloodiest fights over the AI Act has always been how to regulate police use of biometric systems in public places, which many fear could lead to mass surveillance. While the European Parliament pushed for a near-total ban on the technology, some EU countries, such as France, have resisted this fiercely. They want to use it to fight crime and terrorism. 

European police forces will only be able to use biometric identification systems in public places if they get court approval first, and only for 16 different specific crimes, such as terrorism, human trafficking, sexual exploitation of children, and drug trafficking. Law enforcement authorities may also use high-risk AI systems that don’t pass European standards in “exceptional circumstances relating to public security.” 

5. What next? 

It might take weeks or even months before we see the final wording of the bill. The text still needs to go through technical tinkering, and has to be approved by European countries and the EU Parliament before it officially enters into law. 

Once it is in force, tech companies have two years to implement the rules. The bans on AI uses will apply after six months, and companies developing foundation models will have to comply with the law within one year.

HAND COVERS BRUISE

To understand why I am here to tell you this story and so you can be more assured to trust it is because I have myself been in Zuckerberg's shoes on the opposite side of scapegoating's economics. I created a lot of value from being a system administrator, but I had no finesse in spotting the scapegoating. Often, I was fired or felt the need to quit. 

This gave me free time and reason to keep my solitude out preservation and investigate much of the world. I have been able to successfully avoid oath or any legal obligation to be made quiet. I saw that the world was becoming a game and I simply refused to join it. Being made well aware that I could not expect or demand others to do the same and that this path would be one I would suffer its poverty and tyranny from my choosing in doing so my right to free speech has been made inalienable in the most literal way possible. 

I also volunteered for theater and helped in backstage work that led to me having a career in show and presentation. I got a glimpse behind the curtain in the simplest form of it because I was willing to maintain its stage. 

This meant from 2001 tell now I had a front row seat to the internet in its transformation and can reference for you the audience on the outside of all of this what is going on.

The irony to and I would say is God's grace, I was simultaneously on the inside of it. Working in DC for the Cato Institute in 2011 and for Amazon Web Services in 2011 to 2012 and other places where I took a look behind the curtain. 

Doing all of this before and after living in Richland, WA right next to Hanford and seeing firsthand the kind of discord and despair bureaucracy and its most sacred ritual, The Manhattan Project, brought with its most ultimate idol the nuclear bomb. Despite the global communities' best intentions to overcome the consequences of World War 2, I saw from this little town how the concern to be nice was making us not kind and would make obsolete this effort, despite anyone's intentions. The math simply didn't add up. 

This has stuck with me in everything I do from IT to right this very moment.

Being nice is telling people what they want to hear.

Being kind is telling people what they need to hear.

I am able to say all of this because I was able to find a way to speak to it when I was in DC in 2011 and during Obama's reign. Like Zuckerberg I did IT during his heel flip, but unlike him I saw this from within the beast's nature and I also come to do my most important work which was share the piece pipe and make friends with the world.

I stayed at the International Student House in DC. This was one of the best jobs I ever had. Everyone there was there to learn or to be diplomatic and, in some cases, literally studying to resolve conflicts and bridge understanding. Out of 130 students or so I was one of a handful Americans. I was there to help teach and look out for the others to know basic American tenets of culture. And I was more than willing to hear what their tenets were and know their culture to get this accomplished. 

I also did night shifts guarding the front and making sure people found their way home or had directions to where they were going. While I did these shifts, I was studying to build a website for teaching and to monetize it in a way that it was self-perpetual in generating value and didn't become an administration of knowledge. I used movies, music and stories and any theory that would help me come to this point of understanding and be able to deliver it.

My insistence on discouraging a administration of knowledge I learned from watching the movie The 5th Estate. I was inspired by two movies to in sketching out this educational platform and that I would watch when working on this project which was The Pirates of Silicon Valley and The Social Network.

I really took inspiration from Steve Jobs and Mark Zuckerberg specifically because of the profound change their inventions made. Knowing what they did I needed to understand so I could do the same. Then while in DC and doing IT for the Cato Institute, I came to really appreciate Thiel and Musk with PayPal and Craig Newmark for Craigslist seeing proof of concept the inherent peace-making nature of trade.

I was already a fan of Ron Paul, The Golden Rule, and read much of what was to be offered by the Mises Institute, but this time in DC I needed to put proof to concept and practice my method I developed to solve any complex problem, regardless of language or ignorance. That with determination and the willingness to be open to someone's willingness to do better, we together could make better and that this was the true nature and value of profit, it's peace. 

Then with this education platform we could teach making incentive to people's willingness to share and produce knowledge and provide understanding rather than discourage it.

The others who stayed at ISH in DC found it amusing and charming my admiration of Zuckerberg and others and how much I repeatedly watched the movies. I admit I was a little obsessed, but I didn't care it was my goofball thing and everyone there had one just by the nature of what we were there to do. We gave each other the greatest license to make mistakes the world probably had ever seen because we were literally from all corners of it. I also reiterated to them how important this movie was to understand scapegoating.

I knew what I was going to create was going to be seen as a threat from some nebulous force that finds value in keeping the world in the shadows and the more I could understand diplomacy, trade and the means to make peace the easier this would be to facilitate and dodge the scapegoating so many other tech geniuses would inevitably face.

What I can confidently say, with all of this time in DC I was looking at something that I know had value, despite it's ugliness, that I needed to know more of to make peace against the conflict it created. I did this because it would help me in some way to help the world teach itself and me the ability to craft it's platform.

I also loved my time at ISH DC because one thing all these guys had no shame of and totally made no judgement of, as it is so common nowadays, was smoking cigarettes. I would spend hours and hours conversating with people passing the peace pipe. Most of all I befriended a group of men my age and one was the son to the diplomat of India. EJ or DJ? He was good friend and his story was to me in my journey in this what Slum Dog Millionaire was to others to help you understand. 

Their friendship I found enduring through living in the belly of beast as the kind of cyber-anarchist I was in that moment. While I spent most of my day having be the adult so many others expected, with these men company, we found the means to understand and we literally came from all corners of the globe and experience each the most extreme forms of the male experience, for good or bad. It was quite incredible. 

Another man who was named Ahmed (I believe, I might be wrong I am often awful with remembering names at times) This wonderful and generous man was a middle age Iranian Nuclear scientist. I found him so fascinating coming from Hanford and knowing that he experienced a bureaucratic culture I was familiar with in the oldest country and oldest culture in the world. And for me I did so in one the newest. The poetic symmetry and opportunity I found too awesome to ignore. I often joked with him that him and I could solve a way to make peace of nuclear war because of the irony and symmetry of it all. Something I know is now something more than that, a miracle.

My respect for this man and what he had for me turned into a gift when at 2am, and after I randomly decided to stay at work to do inventory, I see Ahmed in the Metro station. I was rushing to try to catch the last train. And I could hear someone yelling in Farsi. I had been around the different languages I was able to tell whoever they were they were Persian or Iranian or at least they were a native speaker. 

What I saw was a crowd of the world's most intelligent bureaucrats look with worry and anguish acting as if this innocent man was a threat. Knowing that if I did not embrace him with my strength and my clear English others would possibly hurt him. I pushed my way through the crowd and acknowledge him by his name which he lit up with happiness to see a good friend. The crowd paused and took a breather. It realized there was no threat and I was able to guide him home and make sure he stayed safe. 

I often have joked over the years that this event would be proof to any intelligence agency my willing to make peace, and I learned it at the very home where the industry of peacemaking finds its most industrious. 

I am explaining all of this to highlight the miracle that I see has taken place. This past six months I have been slowly made aware of all of this and why I must be the one to tell you. My efforts to learn how to make this platform of education to make peace has become something far greater than I knew I could do. It is for this reason to Zuckerberg and others knew they could trust me with this.

Another aspect of this is because of numerous things I have learned from my dad and his families time in Freemasonry. I never initiated. Not because I didn't like Freemasonry, I mean it provided so much for me. It was simply an administration of knowledge. Its motto my dad told me was to make "Good men better." and I thought then why all the secrecy just do it. You can teach it with the G symbol alone:

Be generous as much as you can without it making you less. 

What I did not appreciate then is I never took an oath and never made to keep secret what info I absorbed from being around so many Freemasons, I learned a lot without ever joining.

I did this while simultaneously not at all aware I was the direct descendent of its most important and sacred lodge and family. I had learned two things I learned that I spoke openly of in DC that I repeated without knowing how true or false they were, but just that it made sense. 
Little did I know these two things may have been highly kept secrets, and I just said it without taking any opportunity to keep it private and profit from it. 

I was generous with the truth as I knew it and was hanging out with the world's soon to be diplomats. Being generous with knowledge is ultimately how peace is made. I was never briefed or told what I learned need to be made secret because I never was obligated to. I simply absorbed it and stayed as independent as possible. I also made it a motto to try to just admit the truth to mistake or "bad" things I did, by simply taking ownership then being open to any opportunity to make up for it.

I must fully admit that I really had no idea how true either of these things were, but I didn't have a reason to doubt their source or the intention behind it being told to me. I had no reason to doubt it, the truth flies effortlessly and it felt the same. My father and his dearest friend a `Iranian national and one of the world's leading CPU architects. I was a child when I heard both and the two that told me I trusted it when it was said.

These two things that I have garnered to be very consequential in their utterance for the source of their mystery and that I spoke truth to not knowing of where it may lead without knowing how secret it was or that it was even a secret:

All CPUs in the world are not based off random encryption, because this takes place in a vacuum. This means fundamentally every encryption can be bypassed.

The other secret Iran was named to appease or because of Hitler. I have since learned Hitler taking hostage of the Aryian story and Iran changing it's name may have been independent.

But this kind of thing, having to work with Hitler has been so unfairly used against people who made honest mistakes. 

This story I found a great way to show how a brand can be imbued with shame, even if it's the legacy and majestic culture of the world's most enduring and oldest country, Persia or Iran. For me just accepting both and moving on helps to resolve whatever shame making honest mistakes can cause.

The other of all encryptions being made obsolete I used as a reminder to try to keep myself out of trouble as much as I could knowing a day would come that I would be very thankful I did. I also felt it necessary to tell others so they could try to do the same.

These two facts I had repeated to my Iranian friend, to others and to anyone that would listen while in DC. I also knew how important it was from these two things to be pious and to not be blackmailed in this Brave New World. That ultimately was why I found value in saying it.

What I have come to now realize and why I am the one saying all of this is I may have contributed both to the crisis Obama, Epstein, Netanyahu and The Cabal created while also the means to its resolution. Epstein had with the UN used diplomatic immunity and charitable giving as a means to gain people's trust in order to scam them.

As I have told some people I know I have the pieces and the generosity to give them, I just don't have the intelligence to know what this jigsaw puzzle looked like. 

These are the bruises I carry, and I say them to simply show my hand and make a handshake to know peace. I show my hand because it is the oldest gesture in human history to signal good will and intention.

It is why I titled this section "Hand Covers Bruise" and the nature of why I am here it's most simple form. It comes from a song from the movie about Zuckerberg I obsessively watched while living with the world's diplomats. It also describes what Epstein does and The Cabal did to all of us.

I know from my time doing tech support and people's naivety around this time, Obama, Epstein, Clintons and Soros & The Cabal had to have showed their hand and corruption through the chats and groups. To what extent and what exactly I can't say. Just know on average only 10% of users make content visible to everyone else. The majority of a social media website's data is in groups and private messages.

What is also clear to me though is Zuckerberg had a very different tone soon after Obama entered office. And like Elon Musk and Elizabeth Holmes, Zuckerberg went from being a darling to getting scapegoated for others failures. 

Zuckerberg especially I have sympathy for because the Social Network movie showed me how many were just wanting an excuse to speak from their envy. I was a tech nerd just like Zuckerberg, sysadmin rather than a programmer, but I respected his craft. Many watched that movie and got their excuse they want to be bigoted of him. I found inspiration to invent and create. You didn't need college to find self-mastery or develop a craft.

The about face so many had with Zuckerberg and it mostly coming from the Obama admin and then encouraged to the bully pulpit, I am certain was a Cabal psyop that found its origins on Reddit and it was because they made fools of themselves and Zuckerberg was the one that broke the news. 

Simply, this happens to tech guys all the time. 

We also saw this about face towards Trump. He went from being the example liberals and the left would point out as an honest billionaire only to become a sworn enemy because he rightfully questioned Obama's origins. None of them held it against Hillary Clinton though and her campaign was more boisterous about it during the primary than anyone else. 

Then this topic was unfairly used to paint conservatives as racist. What was profoundly stupid about this was the same questions of origins and legitimacy was made about McCain because he was born in the "zone" of the Panama Canal. 

This scapegoating is why I know Obama was the most decisive and arrogant president we have had. He did everything to encourage bigotry. I only had a slight hope for him because Zuckerberg campaigned with him.  That vanished very quickly just like it did for Zuckerberg.

What I discovered was that Zuckerberg got his slice of justice though and it was righteous as much as it was hilarious.

As time went on Zuckerberg faced more and more pressure to launch Facebook's IPO. Anyone who knows how this works knows this results in a dramatic sea change for the founder because they are compelled to delegate their ownership and control over their own creation. Zuckerberg insisted an IPO was not necessary. 

CFO David Ebersman was brought into the company to help it scale and with Michael Grimes and Sheryl Sandberg (who worked in the Clinton admin) forced the company into IPO because of a ridiculous SEC rule. Facebook was forced into launching an IPO because they had exceeded 500 shareholders and Zuckerberg was shoved aside. Likely because they discovered he caught them in their corruption and they assumed to be invincible then tried to use the IPO launch to take Facebook away from Zuckerberg.

Zuckerberg got the last laugh though and it was righteous. For those responsible and the underwriters involved (Morgan Stanley, JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs) forget the most important rule in the information age:

Don't fuck with your IT guy.

On May 18, 2012, Facebook launched its IPO and it was expected to be the biggest IPO launch in history. It was the hottest stocks to buy, and everyone wanted a cut especially the Obama admin, those who caused the Great Recession and Jeffrey Epstein. It was nothing short of a disaster.

Right on the dot at 11:11 a.m. the NASDAQ experienced a glitch that froze orders for nearly 30 minutes. Hundreds of millions of dollars were lost, a SEC investigation occurred, dozens of lawsuits filed, threats by the federal government, etc. NASDAQ and the underwriters had their credibility tarnished. 

The stock price was way above what most people expected. Ebersman and Grimes bit off more than they could chew and had no reason to doubt this would be their moment to hit the big time. Knight Capital vehemently blamed NASDAQ and wouldn't stop pointing the finger.

Then on August 1st, 2012, at 11:11 a.m. a glitch hit Knight Capital's system and this one cost them almost the entire business to the tune of ~$550 million. 

Zuckerberg gave them their just deserts, hacked the systems and elegantly did a simple change in both cases to have it become a giant vacuum sucking everyone's greed out with it. The most hilarious part is despite their threats; nobody could do anything to retaliate. They showed their corruption on his platform. He had the proof, and they knew it. They had to eat his boot.

The cherry on top? Zuckerberg and few others sold a portion of shares at their offering price right before the IPO launched. Those who bought them were the underwriters, Epstein and the usual suspects of the Great Recession. 

Zuckerberg ended up walking away being the one making the most money after he sold 30.2 million shares and made $1.15 billion. Most of it went to taxes, but he did this because while everyone's hair was on fire and trying to sell and recover, he retained his majority voting control and got sweet sweet justice. 

In my research of the details of this I realized Epstein was most definitely involved and suffered because there is absolutely nothing documented you can find about the Facebook IPO and Epstein. Nothing. There is no way a man like Epstein would miss out on the biggest IPO launch in history and with so many of his friends buying in to.

Most emails involving Facebook and Zuckerberg in the Epstein files is him being desperate to get Zuckerberg's attention and it happens years after this event. Epstein was friends with Lawrence Summers was working at Harvard while Zuckerberg was there and created Facebook. 

Epstein constantly was asking for introductions with founders and geniuses, there is no way he didn't seek to invest into Facebook. My guess is this information was suppressed because what Zuckerberg did was too embarrassing to leave out there for Epstein. Zuckerberg simply ignored him and it drove Epstein insane. The irony being Zuckerberg made a platform for people to connect, couldn't he just, message him?

As some reading this may already know, the day Facebook launched on February 4th, 2004 was the same day a program called LifeLog shutdown at DARPA. There is no direct evidence showing that Lifelog lead into Facebook, but the fact it was the SAME DAY and they function the same is telling.

Peter Thiel was the first big investor, and he isn't shy to invest in companies that work with intelligence agencies. What is interesting to note is that unlike most tech companies that do have intelligence agency involvement, In-Q-Tel was not an investor into Facebook.

What is also worthy to note is that Zuckerberg once said in an interview he made Facebook after reading a book by Sigmund Freud. I have not been able to find this article since I read it years ago, but it made me realize that there is a psychological component to Facebook's design. 

Freud once said that he believes humanity would eventually become telepathic where they wouldn't need language and just speak in acronyms because he was a Marxist. At some point history would no longer be a thing because all wants, needs, pain, etc. would be satisfied and history he believed was a record of mankind's suffering. Anybody with individuality left would kill themselves because they were too arrogant for society.

When I first heard this, it sounded insane to me, but I also was made aware of how many others just took it to be true. 

What Zuckerberg probably realized was, and what Freud failed to understand, was that "connecting the dots" and "connecting with people" are functionally two separate things.

Connecting dots is being intelligent. 
Connecting with people is being genuine

He was at Harvard with the most intelligent people in the world, but they were not the most genuine. Eventually people's intelligence would make them forget to be generous because they thought it was weak. Language deteriorates because people forget to be generous and genuine.

Once they do this meaning for them becomes "mean" aka hurtful. Truth hurts yes, but meaning doesn't unless you assume it does.

He made Facebook to generate meaning by facilitating genuine connection that he wasn't finding at Harvard.

text:
This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.

Every year, some 22,000 Americans a year are killed as a result of serious medical errors in hospitals, many of them on operating tables. There have been cases where surgeons have left surgical sponges inside patients’ bodies or performed the wrong procedure altogether.

Teodor Grantcharov, a professor of surgery at Stanford, thinks he has found a tool to make surgery safer and minimize human error: AI-powered “black boxes” in operating theaters that work in a similar way to an airplane’s black box. These devices, built by Grantcharov’s company Surgical Safety Technologies, record everything in the operating room via panoramic cameras, microphones in the ceiling, and anesthesia monitors before using artificial intelligence to help surgeons make sense of the data. They capture the entire operating room as a whole, from the number of times the door is opened to how many non-case-related conversations occur during an operation.

These black boxes are in use in almost 40 institutions in the US, Canada, and Western Europe, from Mount Sinai to Duke to the Mayo Clinic. But are hospitals on the cusp of a new era of safety—or creating an environment of confusion and paranoia? Read the full story by Simar Bajaj here. 

This resonated with me as a story with broader implications. Organizations in all sectors are thinking about how to adopt AI to make things safer or more efficient. What this example from hospitals shows is that the situation is not always clear cut, and there are many pitfalls you need to avoid. 

Here are three lessons about AI adoption that I learned from this story: 

1. Privacy is important, but not always guaranteed. Grantcharov realized very quickly that the only way to get surgeons to use the black box was to make them feel protected from possible repercussions. He has designed the system to record actions but hide the identities of both patients and staff, even deleting all recordings within 30 days. His idea is that no individual should be punished for making a mistake. 

The black boxes render each person in the recording anonymous; an algorithm distorts people’s voices and blurs out their faces, transforming them into shadowy, noir-like figures. So even if you know what happened, you can’t use it against an individual. 

But this process is not perfect. Before 30-day-old recordings are automatically deleted, hospital administrators can still see the operating room number, the time of the operation, and the patient’s medical record number, so even if personnel are technically de-identified, they aren’t truly anonymous. The result is a sense that “Big Brother is watching,” says Christopher Mantyh, vice chair of clinical operations at Duke University Hospital, which has black boxes in seven operating rooms.

2. You can’t adopt new technologies without winning people over first. People are often justifiably suspicious of the new tools, and the system’s flaws when it comes to privacy are part of why staff have been hesitant to embrace it. Many doctors and nurses actively boycotted the new surveillance tools. In one hospital, the cameras were sabotaged by being turned around or deliberately unplugged. Some surgeons and staff refused to work in rooms where they were in place.

At the hospital where some of the cameras were initially sabotaged, it took up to six months for surgeons to get used to them. But things went much more smoothly once staff understood the guardrails around the technology. They started trusting it more after one-on-one conversations in which bosses explained how the data was automatically de-identified and deleted.

3. More data doesn’t always lead to solutions. You shouldn’t adopt new technologies for the sake of adopting new technologies, if they are not actually useful. But to determine whether AI technologies work for you, you need to ask some hard questions. Some hospitals have reported small improvements based on black-box data. Doctors at Duke University Hospital use the data to check how often antibiotics are given on time, and they report turning to this data to help decrease the amount of time operating rooms sit empty between cases. 

But getting buy-in from some hospitals has been difficult, because there haven’t yet been any large, peer-reviewed studies showing how black boxes actually help to reduce patient complications and save lives. Mount Sinai’s chief of general surgery, Celia Divino, says that too much data can be paralyzing. “How do you interpret it? What do you do with it?” she asks. “This is always a disease.”

Read the full story by Simar Bajaj here. 

Now read the rest of The Algorithm

Deeper Learning

How a simple circuit could offer an alternative to energy-intensive GPUs

On a table in his lab at the University of Pennsylvania, physicist Sam Dillavou has connected an array of breadboards via a web of brightly colored wires. The setup looks like a DIY home electronics project—and not a particularly elegant one. But this unassuming assembly, which contains 32 variable resistors, can learn to sort data like a machine-learning model. The hope is that the prototype will offer a low-power alternative to the energy-guzzling graphical processing unit chips widely used in machine learning. 

Why this matters: AI chips are expensive, and there aren’t enough of them to meet the current demand fueled by the AI boom. Training a large language model takes the same amount of energy as the annual consumption of more than a hundred US homes, and generating an image with generative AI uses as much energy as charging your phone. Dillavou and his colleagues built this circuit as an exploratory effort to find better computing designs. Read more from Sophia Chen here.

Bits and Bytes

Propagandists are using AI too—and companies need to be open about it
OpenAI has reported on influence operations that use its AI tools. Such reporting, alongside data sharing, should become the industry norm, argue Josh A. Goldstein and Renée DiResta. (MIT Technology Review) 

Digital twins are helping scientists run the world’s most complex experiments
Engineers use the high-fidelity models to monitor operations, plan fixes, and troubleshoot problems. Digital twins can also use artificial intelligence and machine learning to help make sense of vast amounts of data. (MIT Technology Review) 

Silicon Valley is in an uproar over California’s proposed AI safety bill
The bill would force companies to create a “kill switch” to turn off powerful AI models, guarantee they will not build systems with “hazardous capabilities such as creating bioweapons,” and report their safety testing. Tech companies argue that this would “hinder innovation” and kill open-source development in California. The tech sector loathes regulation, so expect this bill to face a lobbying storm. (FT) 

OpenAI offers a peek inside the guts of ChatGPT
The company released a new research paper identifying how the AI model that powers ChatGPT works and how it stores certain concepts. The paper was written by the company’s now-defunct superalignment team, which was disbanded after its leaders, including OpenAI cofounder Ilya Sutskever, left the company. OpenAI has faced criticism from former employees who argue that the company is rushing to build AI and ignoring the risks.  (Wired) 

The AI search engine Perplexity is directly ripping off content from news outlets
The buzzy startup, which has been touted as a challenger to Google Search, has republished parts of exclusive stories from multiple publications, including Forbes and Bloomberg, with inadequate attribution. It’s an ominous sign of what could be coming for news media. (Forbes) 

It looked like a reliable news site. It was an AI chop shop.
A wild story about how a site called BNN Breaking, which had amassed millions of readers, an international team of journalists, and a publishing deal with Microsoft, was actually just regurgitating AI-generated content riddled with errors. (NYT)

text:
Dangerous. Unpredictable. Always wild.

Three words, and anyone who has spent real time around bears would sign their name under every one of them.

So here is the question I can't put down: what do you call a relationship where a person has spent years within arm's reach of an animal like that, and the animal is still, unmistakably, an animal nobody can predict?

Not tamed. Nobody serious uses that word. Not safe. Nobody serious uses that one either. The line that came with this video is clearly an unfinished sentence, and I think the unfinished part is the whole story. "You can be around them for years" is a sentence with a second half. Sentences like that always have one. The only question is whether the second half is a warning, a confession, or a kind of wonder.

I'm not going to tell you which. I'm going to tell you why it matters, because this is the kind of clip you finish in less time than it takes to read a paragraph, and then it keeps working on you for hours.

Let's start with the word that does the most work: wild.

Most of us use "wild" as a mood. A wild party, a wild guess, a wild night. In the language of people who actually work with large animals, it's closer to a technical claim. It means the animal's decisions are not made for your benefit. It means the part of its mind that decides what to do next was built over an enormous stretch of time for a world that has no interest in your plans. It means that no amount of familiarity gives you a contract.

A dog has been shaped by thousands of years of living beside people. A bear has not. A bear is the same animal your great-grandparents would have crossed a valley to avoid, with the same equipment, the same appetite, the same patience, and the same capacity for sudden, total commitment to a decision you never saw it make.

That is what "always wild" means. Always. Not wild until it knows you. Not wild until it likes you. Always.

And yet.

There is a particular kind of silence that happens when someone who understands every word of that sentence chooses to stay anyway.

I want to be careful here, because there are two lazy ways to react to a video like this, and both of them are wrong.

The first is the soft way: look how sweet, look how gentle, animals just need love. That reaction erases the danger, and the danger is the reason the moment means anything. If a bear were a large, furry house pet, there would be nothing to talk about. The weight of the moment comes entirely from the fact that it isn't one.

The second is the hard way: reckless, irresponsible, a tragedy waiting to happen. That reaction erases the years. It treats a long, patient, daily practice as if it were a stunt filmed by someone who wandered up five minutes earlier. Whatever you think about whether anyone should be doing this, the one thing the title tells you for certain is that this was not a five-minute decision.

Years. That's the word I keep returning to.

Think about what years do to a human being who spends them near something that could end his life without malice, without warning, and without a second thought. Most jobs wear us down into routine. Routine is comfortable. Routine is how people stop checking the ladder, skip the second lock, answer the phone while driving. In most work, familiarity makes us more careless.

With a bear, familiarity has to do the opposite. It has to make you more exact. The longer you're around the animal, the more precisely you have to know when it is tired, when it is bored, when it is curious, when something in the air changed three minutes ago and you haven't noticed yet. Years near a bear don't produce comfort. If they're done right, they produce a kind of attention that most of us will never need in our entire lives.

So when you watch someone who looks completely at ease, it's worth asking what that ease is made of. Is it the ease of someone who has stopped paying attention? Or the ease of someone who has paid so much attention, for so long, that it has become a language he no longer has to translate?

Those two things look identical from a distance. They are not even close to the same thing.

Let's talk about what you're actually dealing with when you share space with a brown bear, because the numbers are the part people underestimate.

An adult brown bear can weigh several hundred pounds, and larger ones go well beyond that. Over a short distance it can outrun any human who has ever lived, and it does it without looking like it's trying. It doesn't need to be fast for long. It only needs to be fast once.

Its sense of smell is in a different category from ours. We walk through a world that is mostly visual. A bear walks through a world that is mostly chemical, a layered map of who passed here, what was eaten here, what is hidden under that log, what is happening on the other side of the ridge. When you stand next to one, you are not just being looked at. You are being read, thoroughly, in a language you don't speak.

And then there are the hands. Not hands exactly, but you know what I mean. Paws that can turn over a rock the size of a suitcase, and yet can also be careful enough to pick one berry off a branch. That range, from enormous force to near-delicate control, is one of the most unsettling and most beautiful things about the animal. The same body that could do almost anything chooses, most of the time, to do something small.

Keep that sentence in mind. The same body that could do almost anything chooses, most of the time, to do something small.

That is the entire emotional engine of a video like this.

Not the bear. Not the man. The space between what could happen and what is happening.

People who study large predators will tell you that most encounters between humans and bears end quietly, with nothing at all. The bear notices, decides you are neither food nor threat, and goes back to its day. That's the usual outcome. It is also the reason the rare exception is so heavy, and the reason experienced people never confuse "usually" with "always."

"Usually" is a lovely word until the one time it isn't.

Which brings me back to the title and its three adjectives. Notice the order. Dangerous first. Unpredictable second. Wild last.

Dangerous is about capability. Unpredictable is about knowledge, specifically how little we have of what's going on inside. Wild is about origin, about what the animal is at its root regardless of what any of us do.

Each one removes a different kind of comfort. Dangerous removes the comfort of size, because you can't dismiss the thing as harmless. Unpredictable removes the comfort of experience, because you can't claim to have it figured out. Wild removes the comfort of hope, because you can't tell yourself that enough time will change what it is.

Whoever wrote that line had thought about all three. That's what makes the second half of the sentence so interesting. A person doesn't list three reasons to be afraid unless he is about to say something that cuts against them.

Here's a thing I find myself thinking about when I see people and large animals together.

We tend to describe closeness as a ladder. Strangers, then acquaintances, then friends, then family. Each rung means more trust, more certainty, more safety. We assume that the closer you get, the less there is to fear.

With wild animals that ladder is broken. The closer you get, the more you know, and the more you know, the more clearly you see exactly what you don't. The expert in the room is rarely the most relaxed one. The expert is the one who can describe, in specific detail, every way this could go wrong, and who holds all of that in mind while sitting very still.

That's not fear. It's something more disciplined than fear. Fear reacts. This waits.

If you want to understand why the most experienced people around big animals are often the quietest, that's it. Their calm is not the absence of knowledge. It's the accumulation of it.

I'll say it plainly, since the internet loves to turn anything into a challenge: this is not an invitation. Nothing about this video is a demonstration of what an ordinary person can or should do. The whole point of the title is that the opposite is true. If the thing were safe, nobody would need to say it was dangerous.

What you're looking at is the end of a very long road that most people would never choose to start walking. You don't get to skip to the end of it. Nobody does.

So what could possibly be the second half of that sentence?

I've been turning it over, and I think there are only a few honest endings.

One is the cautionary ending: "...and it takes one second to forget what they are." This is the ending that lives in every wildlife handler's head. It's the one that explains why people with decades of experience still keep a barrier, a protocol, a second person, a plan. It's not pessimism. It's respect with its eyes open.

Another is the confessional ending: "...and you still never fully know them." That is a stranger and more intimate thing to admit. It says that years of shared mornings don't add up to understanding. It says there's a permanent room in the other mind that you will never enter, and that this isn't a failure of effort. It's simply the nature of the thing.

And a third is the one that makes people's throats tighten: "...and still, some days, it chooses to stay close."

Notice how that third ending sits inside the first two without cancelling either of them. It doesn't say the bear became safe. It says the bear, being exactly as capable and exactly as unreadable as before, did something gentle anyway. The danger doesn't leave. The gentleness doesn't lie. Both are true at the same time, in the same place, and you are asked to hold them both.

Most of life doesn't ask that of us. Most of the time we're allowed to sort things into good and bad, safe and unsafe, trustworthy and not. This is a rare case where the sorting fails, and the failure is the point.

I think that's why we can't look away from scenes like this. We're not watching an animal and a man. We're watching two incompatible truths sitting side by side without either one having to give way.

Let me get at the word "trust," because it's the one everybody will reach for in the comments, and I want to complicate it before it gets flattened into something cute.

When we say a person trusts an animal, or an animal trusts a person, we usually mean something warm. A feeling. A bond. A look in the eyes that we read as affection.

But the working definition, the one that people with real experience use, is colder and more interesting. Trust, between a human and a large animal, is mostly about predictability in a specific context. Over time, the animal learns that a certain person arrives at certain times, moves in certain ways, smells a certain way, makes certain sounds, and has never once been connected to anything bad. The person, in turn, learns the animal's signals, the small tells of mood and intent, the difference between a relaxed jaw and a tense one, between a slow turn of the head and a sudden one.

Neither of them is "deciding to be friends." Each of them has built an extremely detailed model of the other, and the model says: this is fine. This has been fine for a long time.

Which is exactly why the word "years" in the title matters so much, and exactly why it can't be the whole sentence. A model is only a model. It's built from the past. It has no way of promising the next minute.

That is the most human part of the whole thing, actually. All of us live inside models of the people we love. We assume we know how they'll react, what they'll say, what they'd never do. And every so often the model is wrong, and we discover that the person next to us has an interior we've never seen.

The difference is that with a bear, everyone involved knows it. There is no illusion to be shattered, because nobody serious ever signed up for the illusion.

There's another layer here that I think gets skipped, and it's the question of who is looking.

Every video like this has a second subject, and it's us.

Why does a clip about a man and a bear stop thumbs in mid-scroll? It isn't only the animal. It's that we are fascinated by people who have crossed a line we haven't. We want to know what it's like on the other side, and we want to know it from a safe distance, through a glass screen, with the volume on and nothing at stake.

That is a strange pleasure. We borrow someone else's proximity to danger and feel something real, without paying anything for it. It's the same thing that fills theaters for thrillers and mountains of books about expeditions that nearly ended badly. We want the vertigo without the fall.

But there's a more generous reading of the same impulse. Maybe what draws us isn't the danger at all. Maybe it's the sense that somewhere, someone has found a way to be near something powerful without needing to dominate it. That's rare. Most of our history with large animals is a history of one of two things: fear or control. Run from it, or put it in a box. A relationship built on neither is hard to imagine, and harder to watch without feeling a small, quiet pull.

I'm not sure which of those two motives is the true one. I suspect both are, in different proportions for each of us.

Now for the part that makes people argue.

Any time a person and a large wild animal appear together like this, the comments split into two armies within about ninety seconds.

One army says: this is beautiful, this is a rare bond, people who understand animals are a gift.

The other says: this is exploitation, wild animals belong in the wild, nothing about this is natural, and the person is either lucky or foolish.

I don't think either side is stupid. I think both are holding a real piece of a larger question, and the larger question is worth sitting with instead of winning.

Here is how I'd put it. What do we owe an animal that is in our care? What do we owe an animal that will never be able to go back to what it was? Where does protection end and ownership begin? And at what point does admiration for an animal turn into a demand that it perform our idea of closeness?

I can't answer those from a single short video, and neither can anyone else, no matter how loudly they type. What the video can do is make the questions feel less abstract. It's much harder to be glib about "animals belong in the wild" when you're looking at a particular animal in a particular place. It's equally hard to be glib about "what a beautiful bond" when the word "dangerous" is sitting right there in the opening line.

The title doesn't resolve this for you. If anything, it refuses to. And I respect that, because the easiest thing in the world would have been to make a video that tells you how to feel.

Let me put one more idea on the table, because it's the one that stays with me after the screen goes dark.

We usually imagine bravery as an act. Running into a fire. Stepping between a child and a car. A dramatic decision made in a single second.

There's another kind, and it's much less photogenic. It's the bravery of sustained, daily, unglamorous presence. Showing up again tomorrow. Keeping your hands calm when your pulse isn't. Staying attentive on the four-hundredth ordinary morning as if it were the first, because the animal doesn't know it's ordinary and doesn't care.

That kind of courage has no highlight reel. It looks, from the outside, like a person sitting still. It looks like nothing at all.

Which is exactly why the title says "for years." Years is where the courage actually is. Not in the one moment that gets filmed, but in the thousand quiet moments before it that nobody did.

Think about the asymmetry in what's being risked.

On one side there is a person with a family, a name, a body that breaks easily, and a life that most of us would call fragile the moment it's compared to the animal beside it.

On the other side there is an animal that cannot read a headline, cannot understand a legal argument, cannot be reasoned with, and cannot be held responsible for being exactly what it is. If something ever went wrong, the animal would not be the villain of the story, even though it would be the one that paid the heaviest price afterwards. That's a hard truth about creatures like this: when the line is crossed by a mistake, it's almost never the human who loses the most.

So the stakes aren't one-sided. Both sides of this are exposed. Both are depending on the other being careful, one of them knowingly and one of them by the only means an animal has, which is instinct, habit, and whatever passes inside it that we have no word for.

That's the part I find genuinely moving, and I'd rather say it straight than dress it up. Two bodies, two completely different kinds of mind, one patch of ground, and a daily agreement that neither of them ever wrote down.

I want to mention something about how we describe animals' inner lives, because it matters here.

It would be easy, and very tempting, to say what this bear is thinking. To give it a feeling. To write a little monologue about loyalty or love or gratitude. People do it constantly, and it's often a form of kindness.

But the honest position is that we don't know. We can observe behavior. We can notice what seems calm and what seems tense. We can draw careful inferences from what animals do around people they've known for years versus people they've just met. What we cannot do is read the actual experience, and anyone who tells you with certainty that they can is selling something.

I find that more interesting, not less. The gap doesn't make the scene colder. It makes it larger. There is a mind in there. It is doing something. It is experiencing something. And we are standing outside it, looking in through a window that only lets through a little light.

If you want to feel awe, that's a better source than any invented monologue.

Here's something else that rarely gets said.

The people who spend their lives around animals like this tend to be remarkably unsentimental in conversation and remarkably tender in practice. Ask them whether the bear loves them and many will tell you something dry, like it knows where the food comes from. Watch them for an hour and you'll see attention so close and so gentle that "unsentimental" starts to feel like the wrong word entirely.

That mismatch is not hypocrisy. It's discipline. They refuse to claim more than they know, and they give everything they can to what they do know. If you've ever met someone like that, you know the particular quality of their presence. It's steady. It's quiet. It doesn't perform.

I think that's what's actually on screen, if you pay attention to how it feels rather than what it shows. Not a trick. Not a miracle. A practiced, patient, deeply respectful kind of company.

And the unfinished sentence hovers over all of it.

One more thing, and it's about the person holding the phone.

Somebody decided to record this. Somebody stood there with a device in their hand and chose to keep it steady instead of backing away, which tells you something by itself. Nobody films calmly in a place where they feel afraid. The steadiness of a recording is a quiet kind of testimony. It says the people closest to this scene didn't feel the need to hurry.

I don't want to overread that. A video is a few seconds cut from a long stretch of days, and a few seconds can mislead as easily as they can reveal. But when the testimony of the room matches the testimony of the title, it's worth noticing.

Years, steadiness, silence. Three more words to set beside the first three.

Let me try a thought experiment, since I think it explains why this lands harder than it should.

Imagine you're handed two sentences about the same animal.

The first says: this bear is gentle.

The second says: this bear is dangerous, unpredictable and wild, and has been calm around this person for years.

Which one do you believe more?

Almost everyone says the second, and the reason is worth noticing. The first sentence is a claim. The second is a record. The first asks you to trust a description. The second admits every reason you shouldn't, and then offers the one piece of evidence that complicates them: time.

Time is the only argument that really works with wild animals. You can't talk your way into an animal's confidence, and you can't buy it, and you can't fake it for more than a few minutes. The only currency it accepts is repetition. The same behavior, the same calm, the same absence of threat, day after day, until the animal's world includes you as a fixed, uneventful part of the landscape.

There's something almost humbling in that. In a culture that rewards speed, here is a relationship that cannot be hurried by any amount of talent, money, or charm. It takes what it takes.

And even then, it comes with no guarantee.

I keep thinking about the word "around" in that line.

Not "with." Not "friends with." Around.

It's a small, careful word, and I suspect it was chosen on purpose. "Around" claims proximity, not intimacy. It says: I have been in the same space, for a long time, and I'm not going to pretend that means more than it does. It leaves the door open on what the relationship actually is, and it refuses to close it.

That kind of precision is rarer than it sounds. Most captions about animals rush to name the feeling. Best friends. Soulmates. Family. This one stays with the geometry, who is near whom, for how long, under what conditions, and trusts you to feel the rest without being told.

So here is what I'd ask of you before you press play.

Don't watch it for a trick, because there isn't one.

Don't watch it to decide whether the man is wise or reckless, because the video can't tell you that and neither can I.

Don't watch it as a lesson in how to approach wildlife, because it isn't one, and every person who knows anything about bears would tell you so before you finished asking.

Watch it the way you'd listen to someone say a very short sentence that you suspect is carrying a lot more than it admits.

Watch for the stillness. Watch for the lack of hurry. Watch for the specific kind of ease that has nothing to do with relaxation and everything to do with knowing exactly what is at stake.

And then ask yourself the question that I haven't been able to stop asking: what would you have to know, and how long would it take you to learn it, before you could sit that close to something that wild and remain truthful about what it was?

There's a reason a clip like this travels, and it isn't only the animal.

People send it to each other because it says something they can't quite say themselves. Something about respect that doesn't require control. About closeness that doesn't require pretending. About how a very large thing and a very small thing can share a patch of ground without either one pretending to be the other.

Some of us have been in a version of that. A relationship with a person whose depths we never fully reached. A parent we spent decades beside and never entirely understood. A friend who could, on certain days, still surprise us. A place we loved that stayed itself no matter how long we stayed.

What we call love is often just the willingness to remain near something we can't completely know.

A bear makes that willingness visible. It strips away the cover of sentiment and leaves the bare structure: power, uncertainty, patience, and a choice made again and again.

I don't think that's why the video exists. I think it exists because someone had an ordinary day and a camera. But I think it's why it works.

Here is the strange thing about unfinished sentences.

They stay open. The mind keeps trying to complete them. "You can be around them for years..." and then what? And then you still don't know. And then you still have to be careful. And then, one day, something quiet happens that you could never have scheduled and never will be able to explain.

I won't tell you which of those the video shows. I'll only say that the title is honest about its limits, and that honesty is rarer and more valuable than any miracle.

If you have a minute, watch it. If you have two, watch it again, and pay attention to what you notice the second time that you missed the first. It's the kind of thing that rewards that.

And if you've spent time around large animals yourself, if you've worked with them, rescued them, studied them, lived near them, I'd genuinely like to know how you'd finish that sentence.

Maybe that is the real reason the line stops us. It doesn't flatter the animal and it doesn't flatter the man. It simply stands in the middle of the contradiction and lets it breathe, and it trusts that a few honest words are enough to make a stranger lean toward the screen, and wonder what the second half of the sentence could possibly be, after those years.

Dangerous. Unpredictable. Always wild.

And still.

Ethiopia is actively building 1.5 million affordable homes under an ambitious five-to-six-year national housing initiative led by Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed. The project is currently underway to address severe housing shortages and rapid urbanization across the country.

Key Details of the Initiative
• Background and Scale. Originally pledged at the Guba gathering in late 2025 and reinforced in parliamentary addresses in July and November 2026, the plan builds on a previous phase that constructed 1.2 million homes. Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed inspected active construction blocks in Addis Ababa—including sites in Tulu Dimtu and Addis Ketema—reaffirming the government's push to deliver on the target.
• Addis Ababa's Share. The capital city of Addis Ababa is targeting 100,000 housing units across 21 construction sites. Half of these are funded directly by the city administration, while the other half rely on housing cooperatives and private partnerships.
• Modern Construction Tech. To speed up delivery and lower costs, the government is importing modern construction systems, including 3D printing technology capable of building multi-story residential blocks in roughly a month.
• Local Supply Chain Boost. To reduce reliance on expensive imports, Ethiopia has expanded domestic factories for cement, steel, granite, marble, and furniture. The country also opened new domestic glass manufacturing facilities to supply window materials locally.

Financing and Partnerships
• Mortgage Refinancing. In September 2026, the National Bank of Ethiopia partnered with the International Finance Corporation (IFC) to establish Ethiopia's first dedicated mortgage refinancing company. Capitalized at 100 billion birr (including a $200 million contribution from the IFC), it helps everyday citizens afford homes through long-term, income-based mortgage payments.
• Public-Private Partnerships (PPPs). Because state budgets alone cannot cover the demand, the Council of Ministers approved a national policy that heavily mobilizes private developers and international partners alongside government investment.
• Global Urban Support. As reported by Fana Media Corporation and the Ethiopian Broadcasting Corporation, the housing drive is integrated into Ethiopia's broader Urban Agenda Platform (2025–2030) with support from the World Bank and UN-Habitat ahead of Addis Ababa hosting COP32 in 2027.

After all, "the True Expert Tech Bros have Jensen's back, and also the board members are the real villains here." Conveniently, this framing shifts the blame wholly off of the subject of interest who's alleged actions have threatened the stability and future of the world's most valuable company, while downplaying the exact same legal and fiduciary responsibility that the board members share with Jensen. Except the board is in the position of having to navigate a galactic-scale mess while dealing with the relentless henpecking of all the armchair quarterbacks who have all of the opinions but none of the skin in the game.

In other words, Balaji is just running his "Trust The Experts" two-step that became his familiar move in fanatically justifying draconian COVID policies.

Let me offer another plausible alternative for the chorus of True Expert Tech Bros support for Jensen: all of the founders mentioned by Balaji, including Elon, have every reason to keep the bloom on the Nvidia rose and not risk triggering a financial (or preference, or legal) cascade which could unwind the entire AI hardware sector in a relatively short time.

Remember, for everyone dependent on centralized cloud compute, there is no Plan B after Nvidia. It's the single load-bearing pillar for a multi-trillion dollar industry and dependent subsectors.

Perhaps the lesser of two evils for them is trying to prevent the train from gaining too much momentum the wrong direction, delaying the inevitable long enough to stand up or pivot to viable alternatives.

In this scenario, their only choice is: bite the bullet and stay positive about the man (and his former company) even if they privately disagree with his known/suspected misconduct, and continuing taking the ethical credibility hits if worse news emerges in the coming months, thus preserving their core business models for the longer-term.

For Elon in particular, his horizon only starts turning positive in two years, with full derisking from Nvidia at six years. Terafab will be the captive foundry for Tesla/SpaceXAI's demand, and is scheduled to hit volume production of chips in late 2028 with full production capacity reached in 2032.

All the others who are critically dependent on Nvidia have no such immediate options available on any time horizon. Behind the scenes, these same folks who are publicly defending Jensen today are quite likely cursing his name in private for unleashing a likely black swan on the global tech sector.

The silver lining is that these are also all extremely bright, well-resourced folks who will now be pouring immense quantities of time, money, and desperation-driven creativity into solving the thornier problems that were convenient to ignore while they had the cushion of the "Nvidia Dividend".

After all...

1970 - Southern Airways Flight 932 crashed into a hillside near Huntington, West Virginia, killing all 75 people on board - including 37 members of the Marshall University football team, eight coaches, and 25 supporters and boosters. The disaster was the largest sports-related air tragedy in American history. The crash had a profound effect on the Huntington, West Virginia community, as many prominent citizens were among the victims. Marshall University honors the victims annually with a memorial ceremony at the Memorial Fountain. This event includes a moment of silence and reflection, symbolizing the community's commitment to remembering those lost. The fountain, dedicated in 1972, serves as a lasting tribute to the 75 individuals who perished in this tragic event. 🙏
