text:
Who wanted Nvidia’s Huang out? ‘Honeypot’ scandal raises questions over AI power struggle
Jensen Huang’s exit removes a powerful opponent of US chip restrictions, exposing divisions in Washington over how to preserve America’s technological dominance
Published 13 Nov, 2026 (fFULL)
https://t.co/7HAvq0pxTJ
The downfall of Nvidia founder Jensen Huang in a scandal involving a suspected Chinese spy has raised a politically explosive question: who benefits from the removal of one of Washington’s most influential critics of chip restrictions on China?
Huang resigned on Thursday following revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, former head of Nvidia customer, Singapore-based Megaspeed International. Anonymous US intelligence officials reportedly suspect that she was recruited by Beijing to potentially influence the Nvidia CEO to push Washington to ease AI chip export restrictions.
The scandal came at a pivotal moment in the US-China technology war, just days before a planned summit between Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping. With congressional hawks already pushing for tougher restrictions, the timing of Huang’s downfall has fueled questions about the political interests served by his resignation.
RT examines the intrigue surrounding Huang’s exit and the struggle for control of the global AI industry.
So who benefits from Huang’s departure?
Huang’s resignation removes one of Washington’s most prominent advocates of keeping China connected to American AI technology, potentially handing China hawks a major political advantage. The Nvidia founder repeatedly warned that cutting Beijing off from American technology would accelerate China’s push for independence. In a May interview with Fox Business, he pointed to Huawei’s growing influence: “They’re flourishing in our absence.”
His exit has immediately intensified congressional demands for tighter export controls and investigations into Nvidia’s China dealings.
Republican Representative John Moolenaar, who chairs the House Select Committee on China, has seized on the scandal to question whether whether Chinese intelligence had obtained sensitive information through Huang or influenced US technology policy.
“[Huang has] been one of the strongest proponents for not having export controls,” Moolenaar said. “This shines a whole new light on that discussion.”
House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast has also pushed for stronger safeguards, including measures to prevent chip smuggling and restrict access to advanced semiconductor equipment.
Trump defended Huang as a “very honorable guy” and said he believed the executive’s denial that he knew Alice Huang was allegedly involved in espionage. However, the controversy appears to have given advocates of tougher restrictions on China fresh ammunition against one of their most influential opponents.
Who benefits more – China hawks or AI rivals?
Huang’s abrupt exit has also raised questions over whether rival American technology firms could benefit from his downfall.
Independent journalist Lee Fang suggested rival US AI companies could gain, pointing to Huang’s support for cheaper Chinese open-source models that threaten established American competitors. He drew parallels with earlier campaigns targeting Huawei and TikTok.
Venice AI founder Erik Voorhees went further, calling Huang’s removal a “coup.”
Journalist Glenn Greenwald questioned whether extramarital affairs alone explained the removal of one of America’s most powerful technology executives.
“I don’t know who wanted Jensen Huang out but I know that whoever it was wields extreme levels of power,” he wrote on X.
The resignation also provoked a backlash across Silicon Valley. Binance founder Changpeng Zhao called it “a mistake,” Epic Games chief Tim Sweeney described it as “a sad day,” and Elon Musk said hiring Huang would be “an honor.”
“Dark, dark day. Horrible decision for the US and the western world,” wrote Andreessen Horowitz partner Martin Casado.
The media has some questions to answer
Questions have emerged over how the story reached the press. New York Times reporter Tripp Mickle, who helped break the story of Huang’s affair, revealed on The Daily podcast that he and colleague Ana Swanson began investigating Megaspeed after receiving a tip from an unnamed technology industry contact.
The disclosure reinforces suspicions that journalists may have been deliberately steered toward Megaspeed, raising questions about who supplied the tip – and why.
What did Washington know – and when?
The intrigue deepened following reports that senior US officials knew about Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang months before the scandal erupted.
According to Axios, a highly classified intelligence memorandum overseen by Secretary of State Marco Rubio circulated before Trump’s May visit to China. Based on surveillance of Alice Huang and an investigation into suspected chip smuggling involving Singapore-based Nvidia customer Megaspeed, the warning reportedly reached Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. Rubio also reportedly briefed Trump.
Megaspeed operates AI computing infrastructure, allowing customers to rent access to powerful Nvidia processors outside China – a potential route around restrictions on shipping advanced chips directly to the country.
Washington was also approving direct sales to Chinese buyers. In May Reuters reported that around ten Chinese companies had been cleared to purchase Nvidia’s H200 processors, although deliveries had not begun. The approvals were separate from the Megaspeed investigation, and their precise timing relative to the intelligence warning remains unclear.
The dispute reportedly reached the highest levels of the Trump administration. Axios reported that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent confronted Lutnick over his failure to blacklist Megaspeed despite repeated warnings. The Commerce Department denied the confrontation ever happened and Lutnick now faces congressional scrutiny over his department’s handling of chip exports and suspected diversion to China.
If Washington had been warned months earlier, why did the allegations become a public crisis only now?
How did Singapore become entangled in the scandal
Singaporean authorities had been investigating Alice Huang’s former company, Megaspeed International, long before her alleged ties to Chinese intelligence became central to the scandal surrounding Nvidia’s founder.
In a statement Thursday, Singapore’s Home Affairs Ministry said police began investigating Megaspeed in February 2025 over suspected false declarations involving servers shipped through Singapore to Malaysia.
Alice Huang was questioned and had her passport seized in June 2025. By February 2026, however, investigators found insufficient evidence that she had committed the suspected offenses. She received a warning for knowingly providing inaccurate information about her role at Megaspeed and was barred from re-entering Singapore.
Notably, Singapore stressed that she had never been investigated for espionage.
Meanwhile, the alleged Chinese spy narrative has come under growing scrutiny in Washington itself.
According to CNN, US intelligence officials remain divided over whether the evidence establishes that Alice Huang worked for Beijing. Attorney General Todd Blanche said that the Justice Department had reached “no conclusions” about her alleged intelligence ties.
The assessments leave a fundamental question unanswered: how did an unproven espionage allegation gain such traction despite the lack of conclusive evidence?
Why is Nvidia central to US technological dominance?
Founded by Huang in 1993, Nvidia has become the leading supplier of advanced processors powering the global AI boom.
Its chips and software underpin data centers and AI systems worldwide, making the company a strategic asset in Washington’s competition with Beijing.
By controlling exports of advanced processors and semiconductor technology, the US can influence which countries gain access to the computing power needed to develop cutting-edge AI.
Washington argues the restrictions are necessary to prevent China from strengthening its military and intelligence capabilities. Critics see a broader strategy of technological containment aimed at preserving American economic and geopolitical dominance.
That is what made Huang’s position so consequential: he challenged a central instrument of Washington’s effort to maintain its lead over China.
Could US chip restrictions hand China the advantage?
Washington’s campaign to contain China’s technological rise risks achieving the opposite: accelerating Beijing’s drive to build an AI industry beyond American control.
Chinese firms, including Huawei, are developing domestic alternatives to US processors, while Beijing is pushing for technological self-reliance.
In an August regulatory filing, Nvidia warned that US export controls, combined with Chinese restrictions, had effectively excluded it from China’s data-center computing market.
The company argued that its exclusion was allowing competitors to expand their developer and customer networks, potentially challenging American technology worldwide.
That was the central contradiction Huang repeatedly highlighted: cutting China off from Nvidia could weaken American influence while strengthening Chinese competitors.
Washington’s national security hawks argue the opposite – that selling powerful processors to Beijing risks advancing its military and technological capabilities.
Huang’s departure removes a prominent voice from that debate, but not the dilemma: could Washington’s efforts to preserve its technological supremacy ultimately help China escape American dominance?
Who will take control of Nvidia now?
Huang’s resignation has triggered a leadership crisis at Nvidia. According to Wired, an internal post urging the board to consider employee sentiment attracted more than 1,600 comments, many supporting Huang’s return.
Longtime finance chief Colette Kress has taken over as interim CEO while Nvidia searches for a permanent successor.
According to Reuters, Kress and Nvidia veteran Ian Buck, a key figure behind its CUDA computing platform, are among the possibilities. Other names floated include Arm CEO Rene Haas and AMD chief Lisa Su. On Polymarket, Buck has also emerged among the leading contenders, alongside Jensen Huang’s daughter, Madison Huang, who serves at Nvidia as senior marketing director, and Apple hardware chief Johny Srouji, although betting odds offer no indication of the board’s intentions.
Trump has also weighed in, endorsing former Apple CEO Tim Cook, now executive chairman, declaring on Truth Social that “a Legend replaces a Legend.”
The succession debate has extended to Israel, where media have floated Nvidia technology chief Michael Kagan, Mellanox founder Eyal Waldman, and Apple‘s Srouji. All three have strong ties to the Israeli technology sector.
Whoever succeeds Huang will inherit a company caught in the escalating US-China technology confrontation, with the stakes extending far beyond the boardroom. Huang’s replacement will have to choose whether to continue advocating for keeping China within the American technology ecosystem or bring Nvidia closer to Washington’s advocates of tougher restrictions.
The broader question, meanwhile, is not simply who replaces Huang, but whether his departure will also mark a fundamental shift in America’s AI strategy.

Reports that the United States offered Ukraine NATO membership in exchange for withdrawing from the Donbas portray an exploratory question as a credible proposal. The circumstances suggest a different purpose: testing whether Ukraine is prepared to give up territory without first securing a commitment to the NATO membership supposedly offered in return.

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said American negotiators asked, for the first time, whether Ukraine would withdraw from the Donbas if it joined NATO. He also said there is no finalized proposal and that the details of a broader security package remain under discussion.

The distinction matters because the United States cannot deliver NATO membership on its own. Admission requires the agreement of every alliance member. There is no indication that Washington has secured that agreement or that the Trump administration has committed itself to supporting Ukraine’s accession.

More fundamentally, Putin has repeatedly demanded that Ukraine abandon its NATO ambitions. Following his November 12 meeting with Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Russian officials reiterated their demands for an end to NATO expansion and a return toward the alliance’s 1997 configuration. The American envoys were therefore aware of Moscow’s position when the question was raised.

Against that background, the question looks like a way to determine whether Ukraine might withdraw from the remaining Ukrainian-controlled parts of the Donbas under certain conditions, rather than giving a firm “ні,” “нет,” or “no.”

If Ukraine signaled flexibility, Washington would gain a potential Ukrainian concession that could be leveraged during subsequent negotiations, with no guarantee that it would hold up its end of the bargain.

Zelenskyy very shrewdly did not agree to withdraw. Instead, he said that if the United States and its NATO partners confirmed a concrete security package, he would put it before the Ukrainian people. He also said Ukraine would not recognize occupied territory as Russian.

The most credible interpretation is that the United States is probing Ukraine’s willingness to make a territorial concession while offering something it cannot unilaterally deliver.

text:
Impeach Hegseth Before More Damage Is Done

Listen · 17:02 min
12NOV2026
By David French
NYT Gift Article link
https://t.co/32AT96ok1k

Pete Hegseth has violated federal law, he’s violated the laws of war, he’s violated the Constitution, and he should be impeached, convicted, removed from power and barred from serving in federal office ever again.

Sadly, however, the first effort to impeach Hegseth has failed, at least for now. The lame duck Republican-controlled Congress voted 211 to 204 to essentially kill impeachment by referring the charges to a committee, where it will undoubtedly die — unless Democrats revive the effort in 2027.

They should. Impeaching Hegseth isn’t a matter of retribution or vengeance. It’s about imposing accountability for an unconstitutional war. But even more is at stake — impeaching and convicting Hegseth would help restore the primacy of Congress in the American government.

Last month, I wrote that Hegseth should be impeached, and in response I received a number of messages asking a fair question, even from people who very much oppose the Trump administration and Hegseth’s actions as secretary of defense: Why Hegseth in particular? What are the high crimes and misdemeanors he’s guilty of that require his removal?

Let me answer that question in detail.

As a starting point, we’ll turn to the failed resolution filed by Thomas Massie, the eccentric outgoing Republican representative from Kentucky. It contains eight separate charges against Hegseth.

The first three are directly related to the decision to wage the Iran war, accusing Hegseth of attacking Iran without congressional authorization, continuing the war after Congress voted to terminate hostilities and still fighting the war after the 60-day expiration period defined by the War Powers Resolution, a 1973 act of Congress that was supposed to sharply limit the president’s ability to wage war unilaterally.

Two charges are directly related to Hegseth’s conduct of hostilities, accusing him of ignoring laws that are designed to minimize civilian casualties and engaging in extrajudicial killings in his lethal campaign against suspected drug traffickers in the Caribbean and the Pacific.

Massie’s resolution also accuses Hegseth of violating the free speech rights of Senator Mark Kelly (a retired Navy pilot and former astronaut) by attempting to punish Kelly for making a video with several other Democratic lawmakers that said service members had a duty to defy unlawful orders.

The final two charges accuse Hegseth of kidnapping Nicolás Maduro and Cilia Flores of Venezuela and of waging war against the Houthis in Yemen without congressional authorization.

I want to focus on what are, in my view, the three most important charges: the claims that Hegseth defied the War Powers Resolution in the decision to attack Iran and wage protracted war against Iran.

But first, it’s important to state (or restate) that impeachment is a political remedy for misconduct in office. It is not a criminal trial. It does not require proof beyond a reasonable doubt that an executive branch official committed a felony to merit impeachment or conviction.

High crimes and misdemeanors are whatever Congress says they are, but that does not mean that Congress should exercise unbounded authority and use impeachment as a means of targeting political enemies.

If Congress is going to impeach and convict a member of the cabinet, it is prudent to do so for concrete, obvious violations of federal law or other forms of extreme misconduct. And there are few abuses of power more extreme than waging war in defiance of the Constitution and Congress.

But first, a bit of background.

The War Powers Resolution was passed in 1973 in response to Richard Nixon’s extraordinary use of power during the Vietnam War. Nixon notoriously conducted a secret bombing campaign in Cambodia during the war, for example. The resolution was designed to strike a balance between Congress’s exclusive power to declare war and the president’s exclusive authority to command the armed forces.

Presidents don’t have to wait for Congress to act to order troops into combat when they’re being attacked or when an attack is imminent. American forces, for example, were already engaged in large-scale combat with Japanese forces before Congress declared war on Dec. 8, 1941. They had a right to respond to Japanese attacks.

But the existence of an emergency should not permit the president to circumvent Congress for an indefinite or protracted period of time.

The War Powers Resolution squares that circle. If a president initiates military action, he has 48 hours to inform the speaker of the House and the president pro tempore of the Senate.
That notification then triggers a 60-day clock. If Congress doesn’t authorize the military action, the president has to terminate unauthorized hostilities. If Congress passes a concurrent resolution in both houses, the president still has to terminate hostilities.

As of today, the president hasn’t sought a declaration of war, the 60-day clock has expired and both houses of Congress have passed Concurrent Resolution 86, requiring the president to terminate the war. In other words, the Trump administration is in open defiance of the War Powers Resolution.

Presidents of both parties have long argued that the War Powers Resolution is unconstitutional. They’ve claimed it encroaches on the president’s inherent authority to command the armed forces. But — and I cannot emphasize this enough — that is not the president’s call to make.

The Supreme Court has not explicitly ruled on the constitutionality of the resolution, and it probably will not. For generations it has avoided deciding interbranch disputes regarding the use of the armed forces. That means it is up to Congress to assert its authority. It cannot rely on voluntary presidential compliance. It cannot rely on Supreme Court intervention.

If Congress wants to enforce its authority, it has two primary levers: funding and impeachment. And between those two, impeachment is the far better remedy. It is better to remove a lawless secretary of defense from office than it is to defund the troops under his command.

In fact, I’d argue that if Congress wants to reclaim its constitutional role as the sole entity that can declare war, it is a constitutional necessity to impeach and convict senior members of the Trump administration (if not Trump himself) for waging war with Iran.

Reserving the power to declare war to Congress was no minor matter. As Abraham Lincoln wrote all the way back in 1848: “Kings had always been involving and impoverishing their people in wars, pretending generally, if not always, that the good of the people was the object. This our convention understood to be the most oppressive of all kingly oppressions and they resolved to so frame the Constitution that no one man should hold the power of bringing this oppression upon us.”

In addition, as I’ve written before, it is simply wrong to say that the Constitution creates three coequal branches of government. In our representative democracy, the most representative branch of government — Congress — is supposed to reign supreme.

Yes, other branches can certainly check it. (No branch of government has unchecked power.) Presidents can veto legislation. Courts exercise the power of judicial review of congressional statutes. But Congress alone possesses the power of the purse. Congress alone possesses the power to declare war. And Congress alone can impeach and remove presidents, cabinet officials and federal judges.

One of the central problems of our democracy is that generations of congressional abdication of power to the executive branch have turned the structure upside down. It is that presidents have reigned supreme. It’s destabilizing our country. Presidents were never intended to be kings — far from it.

I can think of few better ways for Congress to reassert its place in American government than by removing a secretary of defense who shares responsibility for the most outrageous act of constitutional defiance in warmaking in modern American history.

Against these charges, Hegseth can offer two primary defenses. First, that the administration did nothing wrong or unusual. And second, that he was simply following orders. In other words, Congress, you’re going after the wrong guy.

The first defense relies on the argument that the Trump administration was merely following modern precedents set by other presidents. President Barack Obama, for example, did not receive congressional approval before launching airstrikes against Libya in 2011. Nor did he receive specific congressional approval for his anti-ISIS military operations in 2014.

I also think that Obama should have sought congressional approval before ordering both military actions, but there are very substantial legal differences between the Trump administration’s war against Iran and Obama’s campaigns against Libya and ISIS.

In Libya, NATO forces operated under the authority of a United Nations Security Council resolution authorizing the use of force. The U.N. Charter is a Senate-ratified treaty (in much the same way that the North Atlantic Treaty, which created NATO, is Senate ratified) that empowers the use of military force. In addition, Congress never used its authority under the War Powers Resolution to attempt to terminate hostilities in Libya.

The ISIS mission was conducted under the auspices of two congressional authorizations for the use of force, the 2001 authorization for use of military force against Al Qaeda (in 2004, the precursor to ISIS — Al Qaeda in Iraq — essentially merged with Al Qaeda) and the 2002 authorization for use of force in Iraq, which allowed U.S. forces to “defend the national security of the United States against the continuing threat posed by Iraq.”

In reality, presidents have repeatedly sought congressional approval for prolonged military action, and no modern president before Trump has faced — much less defied — a concurrent resolution requiring an end to a war.
President George H.W. Bush notified Congress in accordance with the War Powers Resolution when he ordered the invasion of Panama in 1989 and ended combat operations before the expiration of the 60-day clock.

In fact, in February 1990, the House passed a resolution declaring that Bush had “acted decisively and appropriately in ordering United States forces to intervene in Panama.”

Bush also obtained congressional approval and a U.N. Security Council resolution authorizing Operation Desert Storm.

President George W. Bush received congressional approval for both the Afghanistan and Iraq wars. His decision to obtain congressional approval for the invasion of Iraq was particularly notable. His own Department of Justice told him it was unnecessary, but he disagreed and went to Congress anyway.

What about Hegseth’s claim that he was merely following orders? In a combative news conference on Tuesday, Hegseth said that every operation in Iran, South America, the Caribbean and Yemen was a “lawful operation ordered by the commander in chief, then ordered by myself.”

It is true that Trump bears primary responsibility for the military operations executed under his command. He deserves impeachment and conviction as well. But Trump does not bear exclusive responsibility.

To make this point, I’m going to turn to the Nuremberg trials. But I want to be very clear: I do not believe that Hegseth’s violations of the law are in any way comparable in scope or savagery to the conduct of Nazis in World War II. I am comparing legal principles, not atrocities.

The Nuremberg trials established a legal principle that’s applicable beyond Hitler’s Germany: Powerful subordinates can and should be held accountable for waging war without legal justification. They share responsibility with the leader of the nation for the actions undertaken in its name.

In Count 1, the Nuremberg prosecutors prosecuted multiple senior Nazi leaders who “participated as leaders, organizers, instigators or accomplices” in the “formulation or execution of a common plan or conspiracy to commit, or which involved the commission of, crimes against peace, war crimes and crimes against humanity.”

Count 2 charged defendants with participating in the “planning, preparation, initiation and waging of wars of aggression, which were also wars in violation of international treaties, agreements and assurances.”

As I said, impeachment isn’t a criminal proceeding, and thankfully, the charges against Hegseth are nowhere near as grave as the charges against the Nazi defendants. But did Hegseth conspire or have a common plan to wage war against Iran without congressional approval and in defiance of the acts of Congress and congressional resolutions? Did he plan, prepare, initiate and wage war in violation of the Constitution, acts of Congress and congressional resolutions?

And consider this: Hegseth had an option unavailable to senior Nazi leaders. He could resign at any time and publicly dissent from the administration’s course of action, without fear for his life.

In addition, American law has long imposed on subordinates an affirmative obligation to refuse to obey clearly unlawful orders.

My focus on the War Powers Resolution should not be taken in any way as a judgment that Hegseth is innocent of the other charges against him. I agree with Andrew McCarthy, my former National Review colleague, who wrote, “I do not believe there is any viable justification for the extrajudicial killings by military force of operators of suspected drug boats.”

If any evidence emerges during impeachment proceedings that Hegseth ordered attacks on sailors who were clinging to the destroyed wreckage of their boat — as The Washington Post reported in 2025 — that’s so clearly illegal that the Department of Defense Law of War Manual uses it as a textbook example of a war crime.

Hegseth’s attempt to punish Senator Kelly for publicly stating that service members have a duty to disobey illegal orders was also laughably unconstitutional. It was a clear abuse of power for which he is individually responsible. If he were impeached on that basis alone, it would be well deserved.

The impeachment charges provide an opportunity for the House and the Senate to think bigger — to recover their power (and, quite frankly, for some of them, their dignity) by at least holding the secretary of defense accountable for his role in waging an unconstitutional war. The president, of course, is primarily responsible — and one day he should face a reckoning for his constitutional crimes — but he is not solely responsible.

Hegseth shares the blame, and no amount of finger-pointing and excuse-making can change the fact that he played his own role in arrogantly leading our nation into an unconstitutional war. Congress must relieve him of his command.

text:
Demographic projections and survey data consistently show a steep decline in active relationship-seeking, cohabitation, and marriage formation among young and middle-aged men. Under the Romantic Canopy, mainstream commentators interpret this withdrawal as a psychological or cultural pathology. Men who decline to bid for long-term domestic contracts are routinely coded as avoidant, emotionally stunted, or intimidated by modern egalitarian norms.

When we examine this demographic shift through the Three-Track Model, however, the decline requires no moralizing and no clinical diagnosis. Post-agricultural marriage was never an organic byproduct of romantic emotion. It was a high-constraint social technology engineered to coordinate biparental investment, property transmission, and paternity certainty by placing heavy external penalties on contract defection.

When modern legal and cultural shifts removed the protective scaffolding of that contract while leaving its upfront liabilities intact for the male provider, the expected return on long-term male investment dropped sharply. Market withdrawal is the mathematical result of running a high-cost post-agricultural contract inside a low-consequence exit environment.

1. Post-Agricultural Marriage as an Evolutionary Social Technology
In evolutionary anthropology, human mating psychology on the Biological Floor is governed by Strategic Pluralism (Gangestad & Simpson, 2000) and Parental Investment Theory (Trivers, 1972). Male mating architecture contains two distinct tracks: a low-cost, opportunistic short-term variety circuit and a metabolically expensive long-term provisioning circuit.

Why did the majority of men across post-agricultural civilizations agree to suppress their short-term track and commit decades of labor and resource acquisition to a single household? As Joseph Henrich, Robert Boyd, and Peter Richerson (2012) demonstrated in Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B, normative monogamous marriage spread across complex societies as an institutional equilibrium. Alongside Laura Fortunato and Marco Archetti’s (2010) models of vertical wealth transmission in intensive agricultural economies, the research shows that institutional marriage solved two critical evolutionary problems:

Paternity Certainty and Return on Investment: Because ancestral males faced paternity uncertainty and high replacement costs if a partner defected, dense legal, religious, and reputational scaffolding made female extra-pair allocation or unilateral exit prohibitively expensive. In exchange for lifetime provisioning, a man received guaranteed paternity certainty, domestic reciprocity, and social status.

Suppression of Intra-Sexual Competition: By restricting elite polygyny and stabilizing nuclear households, socially imposed monogamy gave the broad majority of non-elite men a secure reproductive stake, dramatically reducing male status competition, violence, and social instability (Henrich et al., 2012).

Synthesis: The Romantic Canopy was merely the cultural narrative draped over those structural rails. The narrative claimed that emotional and erotic fusion held the household together, when in reality, dense Institutional Scaffolding was bearing the structural load.

2. The Deregulation of Exit and the Asymmetry of Liability
Over the past half-century, the external scaffolding that enforced the post-agricultural bargain thinned out through unilateral no-fault divorce, reduced economic interdependence, and the elimination of reputational penalties for relationship dissolution. Crucially, however, this deregulation did not remove contractual risk symmetrically across the sexes:

Asymmetric Initiation of Marital Dissolution: Longitudinal demographic research by Michael Rosenfeld (2018) using the How Couples Meet and Stay Together dataset established that women initiate approximately 69% of all legal divorces in the United States. By contrast, in non-marital romantic relationships where state asset-transfer and custody rules do not apply in the same manner, breakup initiation is equal across men and women.

Incentive Structures in Family Law: In a comprehensive empirical analysis of over 46,000 divorce filings, law and economics researchers Margaret Brinig and Douglas Allen (2000) demonstrated that filing behavior directly tracks expected post-dissolution control over children and household assets. Because contemporary family court frameworks reliably award primary physical custody and associated financial transfers to the mother regardless of who initiates the split, the structural penalty for liquidating the contract falls heavily on the male balance sheet.

3. How the Three-Track Model Explains the Expected-Value Collapse
When we combine this asymmetric legal architecture with the internal cognitive mechanics of the Biological Floor and Optimizing Logic, the modern man’s risk calculation becomes entirely transparent.

Across a multi-year marriage, female partner-specific sexual desire predictably declines due to domestic familiarity and erotic habituation (Klusmann, 2002; McNulty, Meltzer, Makhanova, & Maner, 2018; Sims & Meana, 2010). Under historical scaffolding, external norms buffered the household through this trough. Under contemporary Canopy expectations, however, a drop in honeymoon dopamine is coded as proof that the relationship has failed.

Once habituation occurs on the floor, low-crosstalk modularity (Kurzban & Aktipis, 2007; Showers, 1992) and Triversian self-deception (von Hippel & Trivers, 2011) give the female partner two low-cost options that preserve her virtuous Ghost Madonna self-image while shifting the deficit onto the husband:

The Right Fork (Unilateral Erotic Retirement): She can park her erotic module in permanent neutral, reclassify her husband into the non-sexual Household/Utility File (Kornrich, Brines, & Leupp, 2013), and maintain the provisioning contract while withdrawing sexual reciprocity.

Terminal Dissolution (The Adversarial Rewrite): If her internal mate-switching calculator (Buss, Goetz, Duntley, Asao, & Conroy-Beam, 2017) decides to exit the bond entirely, retrospective memory bias (Karney & Coombs, 2000) and moral disengagement via attribution of blame (Bandura, 1999) recode the husband as an adversary, allowing her to liquidate the marriage and recruit state-backed resource and custody transfers with zero reputational cost (Brinig & Allen, 2000; Vaillancourt, 2013).

4. Optimal Foraging and Rational Market Withdrawal
In behavioral ecology and Sexual Economics Theory (Baumeister & Vohs, 2004; Stephens & Krebs, 1986), any organism allocates metabolic effort by weighing expected energetic and reproductive payoffs against the probability of catastrophic loss.

Meanwhile, rising educational and income hypergamy (Lichter, Price, & Swedlund, 2019) has narrowed the pool of men whom women perceive as clearing their minimum provisioning threshold on the floor, while allowing a small fraction of high-status men to access short-term mating opportunities without offering long-term commitment. For the remaining majority of men, the formal marital contract now demands full upfront financial and legal liability while granting the counter-party a state-protected option to withdraw erotic reciprocity or terminate the contract for a net gain.

When the Romantic Canopy looks at declining marriage rates and labels modern men "afraid of commitment," it confuses rational risk assessment with psychological dysfunction.

The male Biological Floor has not mutated, nor have men lost the capacity for pair-bonding. What changed is the institutional math. When a society strips away the legal, economic, and reputational scaffolding that once made long-term male provisioning a protected investment, while retaining unilateral exit incentives for the counter-party, a growing proportion of men simply read the balance sheet and decline to bid.
